Surah 4: An-Nisa'

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed, Allah is ever Watchful over you.﴾

They differed concerning its revelation, on two views:

One of them: that it is Meccan. This was narrated by ʿAṭiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the view of al-Ḥasan, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatadah.

The second: that it is Medinan. This was narrated by ʿAṭa' from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the view of Muqatil. It has also been said: it is Medinan except for one verse that was revealed in Mecca concerning ʿUthman ibn Ṭalhah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to take from him the keys of the Ka'bah in order to hand them over to al-ʿAbbas. That verse is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners﴾. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fear your Lord﴾ has two interpretations:

One: it means obedience, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it means fear (khashyah), as said by Muqatil.

"The single soul" is Adam, and his mate is Ḥawwa' (Eve). The "min" in His saying ﴿and created from it﴾ is for partitive meaning according to the majority. Ibn Bahr said: "from it" means: from its kind (jins).

They differed as to the time at which she was created for him, on two views:

(p-٢) One: she was created after his entry into the Garden, as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: before his entry into the Garden, as said by Kaʿb al-Aḥbar, Wahb, and Ibn Ishaq.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When Allah created Adam, He cast sleep upon him, and created Ḥawwa' from one of his left ribs. She did not hurt him with anything; had he felt pain, he would never have inclined toward her. When he awoke, it was said: "O Adam, what is this?" He said: "Ḥawwa'."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and dispersed from both of them﴾. al-Farra' said: "Baththa" means spread out. Among the Arabs there are those who say: "Abatha Allah al-khalq" (Allah scattered the creation), and they say: "Battahtuka ma fi nafsi" and "Abthathtuka" (I revealed to you what is in my soul).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿whom you ask through﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, al-Burjumi from Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, al-Yazidi, Shuja', al-Ju'fi, and ʿAbd al-Warith, from Abu ʿAmr, read (tasa''alūna) with doubled sin. ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and many of Abu ʿAmr's companions from him read it with single sin.

al-Zajjaj said: The original is "tatasa'alun." Whoever reads with the doubled sin assimilated the ta' into the sin, because these two letters are close in articulation; whoever reads with the single sin deleted the second ta', because two ta's came together.

Regarding the meaning of "tusa'alūna bihi" there are three views:

One: you show compassion to one another through it, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: you make covenants and pledges through it, as said by al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Rabi'. 

(p-٣) The third: you seek your rights through it, as said by al-Zajjaj.

As for His saying "wa'l-arḥām" (and the wombs): the majority read it with a fatḥah on the mim, meaning: fear the wombs lest you sever them. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd explained it this way. Al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read it with a kasrah on the mim, meaning: through it and through the wombs. Al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭa', and al-Nakha'i explained it this way.

al-Zajjaj said: The genitive "al-arḥām" is an error in Arabic grammar, permissible only in cases of poetic necessity, and an error in religion, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not swear by your fathers." al-Farra' went in a similar direction. Ibn al-Anbari said: Ḥamzah intended to report an ancient practice to which their custom had long been accustomed, so the meaning is: "that by which you used to ask one another, and by the wombs" in the Jahiliyyah. Abu ʿAli said: Whoever reads it in the genitive has conjoined to the pronoun governed by the preposition "bi"; this is weak in analogy and rare in usage, so leaving it is better.

As for al-Raqib (the Watchful): Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: al-Raqib is the Guardian (al-Ḥafiẓ). al-Khattabi said: He is the Guardian from whom nothing is hidden, and in the description of human beings it refers to one entrusted with guarding a thing, who watches over it and guards against heedlessness concerning it. From this one says: "raqibtu al-shay' arquburhu ruqbatan" (I watched the thing, I observe it with watchfulness).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 2:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And give the orphans their properties⦘ The occasion of its revelation: "A man from Ghatafan had a great deal of wealth belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the boy reached maturity, he demanded his property, but the uncle withheld it, so he brought the matter before the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed." This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The address in His saying ﴿And give﴾ is to the guardians and the executors (of orphans' affairs). Al-Zajjaj said: They were called orphans even after reaching maturity, by the name that had been theirs, and it was said of the Prophet (ﷺ): "the orphan of Abu Talib."

His saying: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good⦘ Ibn Muhaysin recited "tabaddalu" with a single taa'. Then, regarding the meaning of the statement, there are two views.

The first: that it is substitution in actuality, and there are two views on this.

One of them: that it is taking the good and giving the bad in its place. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi said: One of them would take a fat sheep from the orphan's flock and put a lean one in its place, and take good dirhams and throw in their place bad ones (zuyuf).

The second: that it is profiting at the orphan's expense, while the orphan is naive and has no knowledge. This was said by Ata'.

The second view: that it is not substitution in actuality, but rather taking (the orphan's property) as consumed. There are two views on this too.

One of them: that they would not give inheritance to women and young children, and only the adult men would take the inheritance; so a man's share of the inheritance is good, and what he took of the orphan's right is bad. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The second: that he consumed the orphan's property in place of consuming their own property. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

"Ila" here means "ma'a" (with). "Huwb" means sin. al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Nakha'i recited it with a fatha on the ha'.

Al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz say "huwb" with a damma, while Tamim say it with a fatha.

Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Farra' said: the one with the damma is the noun, and the one with the fatha is the verbal noun (masdar). Ibn Qutayba said: There are three forms in it: hawb, huwb, and hab.

(p-٦) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphan girls﴾ — scholars differed regarding its revelation (tanzil) and its interpretation (ta'wil) into six opinions.

The first: The people used to marry a large number of women in the Jahiliyya, and they did not scruple about failing to be just among them, while they did scruple regarding the affairs of orphans. So it was said to them with this verse: Beware of failing to be just among women, just as you beware of failing in regard to orphans. This meaning is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second: The guardians of orphans used to marry women using the wealth of orphans. When the women became numerous, they inclined toward the orphans' wealth, so they were restricted to four in order to protect the orphans' wealth. This meaning is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, and from 'Ikrima.

The third: Its meaning is: And if you fear, O guardians of orphans, that you will not be just regarding the orphans' dowries when you marry them, then marry others besides them from the strangers whom Allah has made lawful for you. This meaning is related from 'A'isha.

(p-٧) The fourth: Its meaning is: And if you fear, O guardians of orphans, that you will not be just in marrying them, and you are wary of bad companionship with them and of little desire for them, then marry others besides them. This meaning is also related from 'A'isha, and from al-Hasan.

The fifth: They scrupled about the guardianship of orphans, so they were commanded to scruple also about fornication, and were urged toward lawful marriage. This meaning is related from Mujahid.

The sixth: They scrupled about marrying orphans, just as they scrupled about their wealth, so Allah granted them a concession with this verse and restricted them to a number with which justice is possible. It is as if He said: And if you fear, O guardians of orphans, that you will not be just to them, then marry them, but do not exceed four so that you may be just; and if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one. This meaning is related from al-Hasan.

Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of His saying "And if you fear" is: if you know that you will not be just [among the orphans]. It is said: aqsata al-rajul (he acted justly) when he was just, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Those who act justly (al-muqsitun) in this world will be upon pulpits of pearl on the Day of Resurrection." And it is said: qasata al-rajul when he acted unjustly, and from it is the saying of Allah: ﴿And as for the unjust (al-qasitun), they will be fuel for Hell﴾. Regarding the meaning of justice concerning orphans there are two views: one concerning marrying orphans, and the second concerning their wealth.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then marry what seems good to you﴾ — i.e., what is lawful for you.

Ibn Jarir said: By His saying "what seems good to you" He meant the act, not the persons of women, and therefore He said "ma" and did not say "man." They differed over whether the marriage is to orphans or to others, on the two views already mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿two, or three, or four﴾

(p-٨) al-Zajjaj said: It is a substitution (badal) for "what seems good to you," and its meaning is: two by two, three by three, and four by four. Allah addressed the Arabs in the most eloquent of languages, and it is not the way of an eloquent speaker to express nine in number by "two, three, four," because nine has been established for this number, so that would be incoherent speech.

Ibn al-Anbari said: This waw (and) means distribution (tafriq) and is not cumulative. So the meaning is: marry what seems good to you of women, two; and marry three in a state other than the first; and marry four in a state other than the two.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The waw here is for permitting whichever number one wishes, not for combining. This number applies only to free men, not to slaves; this is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i.

Malik said: They are like free men. Our view is supported by the fact that He said "marry" (fankihu), and this is addressed to one who has the right of marriage, while a slave does not have that right by himself. He also said in its context: ﴿then one, or what your right hands possess﴾, and a slave has no ownership, so it is not permitted for him to combine more than two.

(p-٩) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you fear﴾ — there are two views: the first is "you know," and the second is "you dread."

His saying: ﴿that you will not act justly﴾ — Qadi Abu Ya'la said: it means justice in the division (of time and provision) among them.

His saying: ﴿then one﴾ — i.e., marry one. al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Humayd read: "fawahida" (then one) in the nominative, meaning: then one suffices.

His saying: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ — meaning: concubines. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of the verse is: just as you fear that you will not be just among orphans when you take them into your care, so fear also that you will not be just among women when you marry them; so He restricted them to four so that they may be able to be just. Then He said: And if you fear that you will not be just among these four, then marry one, and confine yourselves to what your right hands possess.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is nearer﴾ — i.e., closer (to avoiding injustice). Regarding the meaning of ﴿ta'ulu﴾ (to be unjust/deviate) there are three views.

The first: "tamilu" (to incline/deviate), said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, 'Ata', Ibrahim, Qatada, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and al-Farra'. Abu Malik and Abu 'Ubayd said: "tajuru" (to act tyrannically).

Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjaj said: "tajuru" and "tamilu" have one meaning. Two men from among the Arabs brought a dispute to a man, and he ruled in favor of one of them. The one judged against said: "By Allah, you are indeed ta'ulu against me," meaning: you incline and act unjustly.

(p-١٠) The second: "tadilu" (you go astray), said by Mujahid. The third: "takthura 'iyalukum" (your dependents multiply), said by Ibn Zayd, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi related it in his Tafsir from al-Shafi'i. Al-Zajjaj rejected it, saying: All the people of the language say this view is wrong, because one wife supports her (only one), and permission of the right-hand possessions increases dependents more than four.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 4:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give the women their dowries (ṣadaqāt) as a gift (niḥlah)﴾. The scholars differed over whom this address is directed to, on two views. The first: they are the husbands. This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). They argued that the address to those marrying has already preceded, and this verse is coordinated with it (ma'tuf 'alayhi). Muqatil said: A man used to marry without a dowry, saying, "I will inherit from you and you will inherit from me," and the woman would say, "Yes." So this verse was revealed. The second: it is addressed to the guardians (awliya'). Within this there are two views. One: a man, when he married off a woman who had no husband (ayyimah), would take her dowry for himself and not give it to her. They were forbidden by this verse. This is the view of Abu Salih, and al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba chose it. The second: a man would give his sister to another man and take that man's sister in her place, without a dowry. They were forbidden from this by this verse. Abu Sulayman al-Taymi narrated it from some of his shaykhs. Ibn Qutayba said: "The ṣadaqāt are the dowries (mahr), and the singular of them is ṣadaqah." Regarding His saying ﴿niḥlah﴾, there are four views. The first: it means an obligation (fari
ḍah). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil. The second: it means a gift and a bestowal. This was said by al-Farra'. Ibn al-Anbari said: The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah would not give the women any of their dowries. So when God imposed the dowry for them, it was a niḥlah from God, meaning a gift to the women, an obligation upon the men. al-Zajjaj said: It is a gift from God to the women. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: It has been said that the dowry was only called a niḥlah because the husband does not own anything in exchange for it, since the genital (bud'); after marriage is in the ownership of the woman. Do you not see that if she was had intercourse by mistake (wuṭi'at bi-shubhah), the dowry would be hers and not the husband's? What the husband deserves is only permission (al-istibaḥah), not ownership (al-milk). And it is a bestowal given with good will. It is as if He said: Do not give them their dowries while you are unwilling. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. The fourth: the meaning of "niḥlah" is religious obligation (diyanah). Its estimate is: "And give them their dowries as a religious obligation." It is said: "So-and-so yanḥalu kadha," meaning he adheres to it as a religion (yadin bihi). al-Zajjaj mentioned this from some of the scholars. (p-12) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then if they give you willingly﴾, meaning: the married women. Regarding "lakum" there are two views. One: it means the husbands. The second: it means the guardians. The "hā'" in "minhu" refers to the dowry. al-Zajjaj said: "Minhu" here is for the genus (lil-jins), like His saying ﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾, meaning: avoid the abomination which is an idol. So it is as if He said: "Eat the thing which is a dowry." Thus it is permissible for a man to ask for the entire dowry. "Nafsan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). So the meaning is: if their souls are content with that for you, then eat it, wholesome and agreeable (hanī'an marī'an). Regarding "hanī'" there are three views. One: it is that whose outcome is not feared. The second: that which results in benefit and healing. The third: that which is not spoiled by anything. As for "marī'," it is said: "marii'a al-ṭa'ām" when the food is digested and its outcome is praised.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property⦆ The word "foolish" (al-sufaha') is understood in five ways.

The first: they are women. This was said by Ibn 'Umar.

The second: women and children. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Farra', and Ibn Qutaybah. It is also reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid, in a manner similar to these two opinions.

The third: children. This was said by Abu Malik. These three opinions are transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is reported from al-Hasan that he said: they are the young children.

The fourth: orphans. This was said by 'Ikrimah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one report.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: "Do not give the foolish their property," as evidenced by His saying ﴿and provide for them from it⦆. He said "your property" to refer to the category which God made as property for people. Others said: He attributed it to the guardians (al-wulat), because they are its custodians (qiwam).

The fifth: the statement is to be taken in its general sense, and it refers to every foolish person who deserves to be placed under restraint (hajr). This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and others, and it is the apparent meaning of the verse.

Regarding His saying ﴿your property⦆ there are two views. One: it is the property of orphans. The other: it is the property of the foolish.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿which God made for you as a means of support⦆ al-Hasan recited "al-lati ja'ala Allahu lakum qiwaman." Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu 'Amr recited "qiyaman" with a yaa' and an alif here. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited "qayyiman" without an alif.

Ibn Qutaybah said: qiyaman and qiwaman have the same meaning. You say: "This is the qiwam of your affair and its qiyam," meaning: that by which your affair is sustained. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi mentioned that "qiwaman," "qiyaman," and "qayyiman" all carry the meaning of al-qawwam, the one who maintains the matter. He said: the view of those who say that "al-qiyam" here is the plural of "qiyamah" (value) with respect to something is not correct.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and provide for them from it⦆ that is, from it. Regarding "the kind word" (al-qawl al-ma'ruf) there are three views.

The first: a good promise. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, and Muqatil.

The second: a gracious response. This was said by al-Dahhak. The third: supplication, like your saying: "May God grant you well-being" (afakaku Allah). This was said by Ibn Zayd.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 6:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And test the orphans﴾. The occasion of its revelation: a man called Rifa'ah died and left a young son called Thabit, and his paternal uncle took charge of him. The uncle came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My nephew is an orphan in my care. What is lawful for me from his property, and when should I hand his property over to him?" Then this verse was revealed. Muqatil related something similar. Al-ibtila' (testing) means al-ikhtibar (examination). And what are they tested in? There are three opinions on this.

The first: they are tested in their intellects. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, Sufyan and Muqatil.
The second: they are tested in their intellects and their religion. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. It is also reported from Mujahid as both opinions.
The third: in their intellects, their religion, and their preservation of their property. This was mentioned by al-Tha'alibi.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this testing is before puberty.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, when they reach the age at which they can marry women. ﴿then if you perceive﴾ means: if you know and have clear evidence. The root of anastum is "they saw". Regarding rushd (maturity of judgment) there are four opinions.

The first: righteousness in religion and the preservation of property. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: righteousness in intellect and the preservation of property. This is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

The third: that it is intellect. This was said by Mujahid and al-Nakha'i.

The fourth: intellect and righteousness in religion. This is reported from al-Suddi.

Section

Know that Allah, may He be exalted, made the lifting of restriction over orphans conditional on two things: puberty and maturity of judgment. He commanded the guardians to test them. When their maturity has become evident, it becomes obligatory on them to hand over their property to them.

Puberty occurs through one of five things. Three are shared by men and women: wet dreams (ihtilam), completing fifteen years of age, and the growth of pubic hair. Two are specific to women: menstruation and pregnancy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not consume it wastefully﴾. This is addressed to the guardians. Ibn Abbas said: do not consume it without right. And "bidaran" means: you hasten to consume the property before the child reaches puberty. ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain﴾ from their property, refraining from the orphan's property. Regarding consuming "in a fair manner" (bil-ma'ruf) there are four opinions.

The first: that it means taking it as a loan. This is reported from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Aliyah, Ubaydah, Abu Wa'il, Mujahid and Muqatil.

The second: consuming an amount according to need, without extravagance. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ata', al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The third: that it means taking an amount equal to a wage, if the guardian has done work for the orphan. This is reported from Ibn Abbas and Aishah, and it is the narration of Abu Talib and Ibn Mansur from Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him.

The fourth: that it means taking when there is necessity. If he becomes well-off, he repays it; and if he does not become well-off, he is permitted (to keep it). This is the view of al-Sha'bi.

Section

Scholars differed on whether this verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) or mansukh (abrogated) in two views.

One: it is muhkam. This is the view of Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Aliyah, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and others. According to them, its ruling is that a wealthy guardian may not eat anything from the orphan's property. As for the poor person who cannot find what suffices him, and whose occupation with managing the orphan's property prevents him from earning his sustenance, he may take an amount sufficient for him in a fair manner, without extravagance.

Is he liable to repay when he becomes well-off? There are two views among them.
One: he is not liable, but it is like a wage for his work. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
The second: when he becomes well-off, repayment becomes obligatory. This is reported from Umar and others, and also from Ibn Abbas, as two views.

The second view: that it is mansukh (abrogated) by His saying: ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves by false means﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, but it is not authentic.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then call witnesses against them﴾. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this is by way of precaution for the orphan and the guardian, and it is not obligatory. As for the orphan, if there is evidence against him, he is less likely to claim non-receipt. As for the guardian, if his trustworthiness is evident, the oath is waived when the orphan denies receiving the property. Regarding "al-Hasib" (the Reckoner) there are three opinions.

One: it means the Witness. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Muqatil.

The second: it means the Sufficient, from your saying "ahsabani hadha al-shay'" (this thing has sufficed me); Allah is my Sufficient and yours, that is, our Sufficient, meaning a judge sufficient between us. The poet said:

We nurture the young of the tribe if he is hungry,
and we make him sufficient if he is not hungry.

That is, we give him what suffices him until he says: "Enough for me." This was said by Ibn Qutaybah and al-Khattabi.

The third: it means the Reckoner, the one who calls to account. In this sense he is a companion, a dining companion, and a drinking companion. This was related by Ibn Qutaybah and al-Khattabi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave behind﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari died and left behind three daughters and a wife. Two men from among his paternal cousins, called Qatada and Urfuta, stood up and took his property, and they gave nothing to his wife or his daughters. His wife came to the Prophet (ﷺ), told him of that, and complained of poverty, so this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn Abbas. Qatada said: "They used not to give inheritance to women, so this verse was revealed."

By "men" is meant the males, and by "women" the females, whether they were young or old.

"Nasib" (share): the portion or allotment of something. It is general (mujmal) in this verse, and its amount is known from another place, such as His saying: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-An'am: 141], and His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. "Mafrud" (prescribed): that which Allah has ordained, and it is more binding (akkad) than "wajib" (obligatory).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 4, verse 8:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the kinsfolk, the orphans, and the needy are present at the division﴾. Regarding this division there are two opinions.

The first: it is the division of the inheritance after the death of the deceased. On this view, the address is to the heirs. This is the view of the majority, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Zuhri.

The second: it is the bequest of the deceased made before his death, so that he is commanded to designate something for those who do not inherit from him. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd. The mufassirun (exegetes) said: the intended meaning of "those of kinship" (ulu al-qurba) is those who do not inherit. ﴿Then provide for them from it﴾, that is, give them from it. It was said: feed them. According to the majority, this is recommended (mustahabb). A group held that it is obligatory (wajib) upon the wealth. If the heirs are adults, they themselves undertake giving to them; if they are minors, their guardian of property undertakes it on their behalf. It was narrated from 'Ubayda that he divided the property of orphans; he ordered a sheep to be bought from their wealth and food to be prepared, and said: "Were it not for this verse, I would have liked for it to come from my own wealth." Muhammad ibn Sirin did likewise regarding the orphans in his guardianship. Similarly, it was narrated from Mujahid that what this verse contains is obligatory.

Regarding ﴿kind words﴾ (al-qawl al-ma'ruf), there are four opinions.

The first: the guardian says to them when giving them: "Take; may Allah bless you." This was narrated by Salim al-Aftas from Ibn Jubayr.

The second: the guardian says: "This is the property of orphans, and I have no share in it." This was narrated by Abu Bishr from Ibn Jubayr. In another narration from Ibn Jubayr, he said: "If the deceased had bequeathed something to them, I carry out their bequest for them. If the heirs are adults, they give them a little (yarda'u); and if they are minors, their guardian says: 'I do not own this property; it belongs to the minors.' That is the kind word."

The third: it is the good promise, which is that the heirs' guardians say to them: "These heirs are minors; when they reach maturity, we will command them to recognize your right." This was narrated by 'Ata' ibn Dinar from Ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: they are given from the property, and when dividing the lands and the slaves they are told: "May you be blessed." This is the kind word. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: "We found people doing this."

**Section**

The scholars of naskh (abrogation, i.e., the principle that one ruling may be superseded by a later one) differed regarding this verse into two opinions.

The first: it is muhkam (not abrogated). This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, and al-Zuhri. We have already mentioned that what it contains of command is recommended according to the majority, and obligatory according to some of them.

The second: it is mansukh (abrogated). It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas. It is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Qatada, and others.

(p-22) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them﴾. Scholars differ over whom this verse addresses, and there are three opinions.

The first is that it is addressed to those present with the testator. On this view there are two readings of the meaning. One is: let those who attend a testator concerning his wealth fear that they might urge him to distribute it to someone who does not inherit from him, so that he distributes it and leaves his heirs behind, just as if they themselves were the testators, they would be glad that those present with them urged them to preserve their wealth for their children. This meaning is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second is the opposite of this view: that those present with the testator are forbidden to prevent him from bequeathing to his relatives, and forbidden to urge him to limit himself to his own child. This is the view of Miqsam, Sulayman al-Taymi, and others.

The second opinion is that it is addressed to the guardians of orphans, connected to His saying: ﴿And do not consume them extravagantly and hastily﴾. The meaning of the speech is: deal well with the orphans under your guardianship, just as you would love for the guardians of your own children after you to deal well with them. This meaning is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third is that it is addressed to the executors of wills, who are commanded to carry out the bequest as the testator laid it down, and that the designated provisions be observed with care, like the care of weak offspring, without alteration. Then this was abrogated (naskh: the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) by His saying: ﴿But whoever fears from a testator injustice or sin and brings about reconciliation among them, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 182]. So this verse commands the executor, when he finds a deviation from what is right, to apply the judgment of the Sharia and to reconcile between the heirs. Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah and others mentioned this in "al-Nasikh wa-al-Mansukh" (the abrogating and the abrogated). On this view the verse is abrogated, and on the view before it the verse is muhkam (established, not abrogated).

(p-23) "Al-Di'af" (weak ones) is the plural of "da'if," and they are the young children. Hamzah recited "ḍi'āfan" with imala (inclination) of the 'ayn.

Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: Its rationale is that whatever is of the pattern "fi'al" and whose first letter is an emphatic (musta'li: a letter pronounced with the tongue raised toward the palate) and kasra-vowelled, such as "ḍi'āfun," "qifāfun," and "khifāfun," the imala is good in it, because the voice may rise with the emphatic letter and then descend with the kasra, so it is preferable not to rise again with emphasis after descending with the kasra, so that the sound follows a single course. Likewise Hamzah recited ﴿fear for them (khafū 'alayhim)﴾ with imala of the khā', and the imala here is good, even though the khā' is an emphatic letter, because it seeks the kasra found in "khiftu" and so inclines toward it by imala. And the sound opinion is the correct one.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ — regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

One of them: a man from Ghatafan called Marthad ibn Zayd was in charge of the property of his nephew, and he consumed it, so this verse was revealed. This was related by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The second: Handhalah ibn al-Shamardal was guardian of an orphan and consumed his property, so this verse was revealed. Some of the exegetes mentioned it. The consuming was specifically mentioned because it is the greater part of the intended matter; it was also said that consuming is used to express taking.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning of "unjustly" is that one takes it without right. As for the mention of "bellies," it is for emphasis, as you say: "I saw with my own eye, and I heard with my own ear." Regarding what is meant by their consuming fire, there are two accounts.

One of them: they will indeed consume fire on the Day of Resurrection, so the consuming is named by what their affair will lead to, like His saying: ﴿I am pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. Al-Suddi said: the one who consumes the property of an orphan unjustly will be raised with the flame of the Fire coming out of his mouth, his ears, his nose and his eyes, and whoever sees him will recognize that he was consuming the orphan's property.

The second: it is a metaphor. Its meaning: they consume that which brings them to the Fire, like His saying: ﴿And you had certainly wished for death before you met it; now you have seen it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 143], meaning: you have seen its causes.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will burn in a blaze﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-sayaslawna" with a fatha on the ya'. Al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ya', and Ibn Miqsam agreed with them, except that he doubled the lam. The meaning: they will be burned by the Fire and roasted. Al-Sa'ir: the blazing Fire; and its being kindled (istiar al-nar) is its being set ablaze.

Section

Some people who have no knowledge of tafsir and its jurisprudence have imagined that this verse is abrogated (mansukh), because they heard that when it was revealed, the people became reluctant to mix with orphans, so there was revealed His saying: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]. This is an error; the removal of the hardship was only on condition of intending reform, not as a permission to commit injustice.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 11:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾. There are three reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah fell ill, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited him. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how should I dispose of my wealth?' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The second: "A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with her two daughters and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the father of these two was killed with you at Uhud, and their paternal uncle has taken their wealth.' So it was revealed." Also narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.

The third: "'Abd al-Rahman, the brother of Hassan ibn Thabit, died, leaving a wife and five daughters. His heirs took his wealth and gave nothing to his wife or his daughters. So his wife came complaining to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed." This is the statement of al-Suddi.

(p-26) al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "yuwsikum" (enjoins you) is "yafridu 'alaykum" (prescribes for you), because the bequest (wasiyya) from Him is an obligation. Others said: He mentioned it with the term wasiyya for two reasons.

The first: a wasiyya carries more weight than a mere command, so it is more emphatic.

The second: a wasiyya contains a right belonging to the one who makes it, and so it indicates the emphasis of the matter by attributing it to His right.

al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "yuwsikum" with the doubled letter (shadda).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the male, the like of the share of two females﴾. That is: a son's share of the inheritance is like the share of two daughters. Then He mentioned the share of the females from the beginning, saying: ﴿And if they are women above two﴾, meaning: daughters. Concerning His saying "fawqa" (above), there are two views.

The first: it is superfluous (za'ida), as in His saying: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾ [al-Anfal: 12].

The second: it carries the meaning of "increase." Qadi Abu Ya'la said: He specified what is above two, and one, but did not specify two, because when each one of them is given a third along with a male, it is more fitting that a female share alone should be a third.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if there is one﴾. The majority read it in the accusative (nasb), while Nafi' read it in the nominative (raf'), meaning: "And if one should occur or be found."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for his parents﴾. al-Zajjaj said: abawahu is the dual of ab and abah (two forms for "father"). The original term for the mother would have been "abah," but they dispensed with it in favour of "umm." The pronoun in "li-abawayhi" refers to the deceased, even though he has not been mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then for his mother is a third﴾. That is: if he leaves no heirs other than his two parents, then a third of his wealth goes to his mother, and the rest to the father. He specified the mother by mention because if He had limited Himself to His saying ﴿and his parents inherit him﴾, the one who thinks would have supposed that the wealth would be divided between them in halves. When He specified her with a third, this indicated preference.

(p-27) Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "fali-ummihi" and ﴿fi buṭūni ummahatikum﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], ﴿fi ummiha﴾ [al-Qasas: 59], and in ﴿Umm al-Kitab﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4] with a damma (raf'). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read all of these with a kasra when they are connected, and their argument is that they made the hamza follow what precedes it, whether a ya' or a kasra.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if he has siblings﴾, that is: together with the two parents, they exclude (yahjubun) the mother from the third, returning her to a sixth. They agreed that if there are three siblings, they exclude her. If there are two siblings, is she excluded? On this there are two views.

The first: two siblings do exclude her from the third. This is the view of 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Zayd, and the majority.

The second: only three exclude her. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who based it on His saying: "siblings" (ikhwa). "Ukhuwwa" is a collective noun (ism jam'), and they differed concerning the minimum number of a plural. The majority said its minimum is three; a group said two. The first is more sound. The scholars excluded the mother with two siblings on the basis of an evidence they agreed upon, and two may be called a plural. al-Zajjaj said: All the people of the language say (p-28) that two brothers are a group. Sibawayh reported that the Arabs say: "They placed their saddlebags (rihal)," meaning: the saddlebags of their two mounts.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿After a bequest﴾. That is: these shares are only distributed after the bequest and the debt. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "yuwsa biha" with a fatha on the ṣād in both places. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yuwsi" in both with a kasra. Hafs, from 'Asim, read the first with a kasra and the second with a fatha.

Know that the debt is placed later in wording but earlier in meaning, because the debt is a right upon him, and the bequest is a right belonging to him. Both take precedence over the rights of the heirs when the bequest is within a third of the wealth. The particle "aw" (or) does not necessitate order; it only indicates that if one of them exists, the inheritance comes after it, and likewise if both exist.

(p-29) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

The first: it refers to benefit in the Hereafter. Then there are two views on this:

The first: if the parent is higher in rank than his child, the child is raised up to him, and likewise the child. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it refers to the intercession of some of them for others. This was narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second view is that it refers to benefit in this world. This was said by Mujahid. Then regarding its meaning there are two views:

The first: the meaning is: you do not know whether the death of the parents is nearer, so that the children benefit from their wealth, or the death of the children, so that the parents benefit from their wealth. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: the meaning is that fathers and sons differ in benefit, to the extent that one does not know which of them is nearer in benefit, because children benefit from their parents in their youth, and parents benefit from their children in their old age. This was mentioned by Qadi Abu Ya'la.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the statement is that Allah has prescribed the obligations as He knows to be wise. If He had left that to you, you would not know which of them is more beneficial to you, and you would place wealth where it is not wise. Indeed Allah is Knowing of what sets right His creation, Wise in what He has prescribed.

Concerning the meaning of "kana" (was) there are three views:

The first: its meaning is that He was Knowing of things before creating them, and Wise in what He decrees to arrange of them. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: its meaning is: He has never ceased (lam yazal). Sibawayh said: It is as if the people had witnessed knowledge and wisdom, (p-30) and it was said to them: Indeed Allah is such, meaning: He has never ceased to be as you have witnessed, it is not something newly arising.

The third: the word "kana" in reporting about Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has the same meaning in its past and future, because things are in one state with Him. He mentioned these views. This is from al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if a man leaves property to be inherited, or a woman, and he has no parent or child⁠—﴾ al-Hasan recited "yuwarrithu" (with a fatha on the waw, a kasra on the ra, and shaddah), and regarding "al-kalalah" there are four opinions.

The first: it refers to anyone other than the father and the child. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "A time came upon me when I did not know what al-kalalah is; then it turned out to be: one who has neither a father nor a child." This is the view of ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn ʿAbbas, (p-31) al-Hasan, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAta, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, and al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj reported from the people of linguistics (ahl al-lughah) that "al-kalalah" derives from their saying "takallalahu al-nasab" (lineage encircled him), meaning the one who inherits from him is neither his son nor his father. He said: al-kalalah is other than father and child, and it is merely like a crown (iklil) upon the head. Ibn Qutaybah reported from Abu ʿUbaydah that it is a verbal noun from "takallalahu al-nasab," when it surrounds him. The son and the father are the two extremities of a man; when he dies without leaving either of them, he has died having lost his two extremities, so the loss of the two extremities is called kalalah [and it seems to be a name for the calamity in takallala al-nasab, from which it is derived; similar to this is their saying: "I wajjahtu al-shay'" (I took its face), and "thaghartu al-rajul" (I broke his front teeth)].

The second: al-kalalah is one who has no child. This was narrated by Ibn ʿAbbas from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and it is the view of Tawus.

The third: al-kalalah is anyone other than the father. This was said by al-Hakam.

The fourth: al-kalalah is the distant paternal cousins (banu al-ʿamm al-abaʿid). Ibn Faris mentioned this from Ibn al-Aʿrabi.

They differed over what the term al-kalalah applies to, in three opinions.

The first: it is a name for the living heir. This is the position of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and the majority of scholars who said that al-kalalah is other than father and child, for they said: al-kalalah is a name for the heirs when there is among them no child and no parent. Some Bedouin said: "My property is abundant, and my heir is a kalalah whose lineage is distant from them."

The second: it is a name for the deceased. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, and Abu ʿUbaydah along with a group. Al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: al-kalalah is a name for the deceased, for his state and his description, and for this reason it is in the accusative (intasaba).

The third: it is a name for both the deceased and the living heir. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Regarding what al-kalalah is derived from, there are two opinions.

One: it is a noun derived from encompassing (al-ihatah), and from it comes al-iklil (the crown), because it encircles the head.

The second: it is derived from al-kalal, which is fatigue, as if the one who reaches the inheritance does so from a distance and with exhaustion. Al-Aʿsha said:

"So I swore I would not lament for her from kalalah, nor for one who wearies, until she visits Muhammad."

(p-33) His saying: ﴿and he has a brother or a sister﴾ means: from the mother, by consensus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then they are partners in the one-third﴾. Qatadah said: the male and the female among them are equal in it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿without causing harm﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "ghayra mudarrin" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: he bequeaths thereby without causing harm, that is, to the heirs.

The Quranic phrase "Those are the limits of Allah" (تِلْكَ حُدُودُ اللَّهِ). Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means what Allah has set as limits in His obligatory shares in inheritance. "And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger" in matters of the inheritance shares "He will admit him into gardens" (يُدْخِلْهُ جَنّاتٍ). Ibn ʿAmir and Nafiʿ recited "nudkhiluhu" (نُدْخِلُهُ) with the nūn in both instances, while the rest recited it with the yāʾ (يُدْخِلْهُ) in both.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah﴾, meaning does not accept His apportioning, ﴿He will admit him to Fire﴾. If it is asked: how did He decide with certainty that the disobedient person abides eternally? The answer: when he rejects the judgment of Allah and disbelieves in it, he is a disbeliever who abides eternally in the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those of your women who commit immorality﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "allati" (the feminine relative pronoun, "who") has the plurals "al-lati" and "al-lawati."

The poet said:

"From the al-lawati and the allati and the al-lati, they claimed that I have grown old, my age-mates [having grown old] with me."

The plural "al-lati" is also used both with and without the ta' (ت) at the end.

The poet said:

"From the al-lati who did not perform the pilgrimage, seeking reward, but rather to kill the innocent, heedless one."

Al-fahisha (the immorality) is fornication (al-zina) according to the consensus of the scholars. Regarding His saying: ﴿So call to witness against them four [witnesses] from among you﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: it is addressed to the husbands.

The second: it is addressed to the rulers (al-hukkam), so the meaning is: hear the testimony of four of you. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only made the months four as a veil by which He covers your immoralities. The meaning of "from among you" is: from among the Muslims.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then confine them to their houses﴾. Ibn Abbas said: When a woman committed fornication, she was confined in the house until she died, until Allah made for them a way (sabil), which is flogging (al-jald) or stoning (al-rajm).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 16:

His saying, Most High: ﴿And the two who commit it among you﴾. Ibn Kathir recited "wallaḏāni" (وَاللَّذانِ) with a shaddah on the nun, and "hadhāni" (هَذانَ) in (Ta-Ha) and (al-Hajj), and "hatayni" (هاتَيْنِ) in (al-Qasas): ﴿one of these two daughters of mine﴾, and "fadhānika" (فَذانِكَ) throughout, all with a shaddah on the nun. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited all of that with the nun unstressed (without shaddah). Abu 'Amr stressed "fadhānika" alone.

His saying: "wallaḏāni" means: the two fornicators (al-zani-yayn). Is this general or not? There are two opinions on this.

The first: it is general, covering virgins and married persons, men and women. This was said by al-Hasan and 'Ata'.

The second: it is specific to the two virgins if they commit fornication. This was said by Abu Salih, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Sufyan. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The first is more sound, because this is a specification without evidence.

His saying, Most High: ﴿they come to it﴾ means: the indecency (al-fahisha). His saying: ﴿then harm them﴾ has two opinions.

The first: it is harm by speech and reproach. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Muqatil also said it.

The second: it is reproach and beating with sandals, narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. ﴿But if they repent﴾ from the indecency ﴿and make amends﴾ in their conduct ﴿then leave them alone﴾ regarding their harm. All of this was before the prescribed punishment (hadd).

Section

The punishment for the two fornicators previously was harm to them, and confinement for the woman specifically. Both rulings were abrogated (nasakha). They differed as to what abrogated them. One group said: by the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Take from me, take from me! Allah has made a way for them: for a married person with a married person, a hundred lashes and stoning with stones; and for a virgin with a virgin, a hundred lashes and exile for a year." This is according to the view of those who hold that the Qur'an may be abrogated by the Sunnah.

(p-٣٦) Another group said: it was abrogated by His saying: "The adulterer and the adulteress, flog each one of them a hundred lashes" [al-Nur: 2]. They said: the saying ﴿and the two who commit it﴾ referred to the two virgins, so their ruling was abrogated by flogging, and the ruling on married women was abrogated by stoning.

Another group said: it is possible that the abrogation occurred by a Qur'an whose text was then lifted while its ruling remained, because in the hadith of 'Ubadah is "Allah has made a way for them," and the apparent meaning is that it was made by a revelation whose recitation was not established. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: This is a sound position, and it follows the view of those who do not hold that the Qur'an is abrogated by the Sunnah. He said: It is impossible for the abrogation to occur by the hadith of 'Ubadah, because it is of the solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad), and abrogation is not permitted by such.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Repentance is only accepted by Allah from those who do evil in ignorance﴾. Al-Hasan said: "The repentance that Allah accepts is only the one [mentioned here]. As for 'evil' (al-su'), it refers to acts of disobedience (ma'asi), and it was called 'evil' because of the evil of its consequence."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in ignorance﴾. Mujahid said: "Every disobedient person is ignorant at the time of his disobedience." Al-Hasan, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Suddi and others said: "They were only called 'ignorant' because of their acts of disobedience, not because they are lacking in discernment."

Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of the verse is not that they are ignorant that it is evil, for if a Muslim commits something he is ignorant of, he is not like one who has committed an evil. Rather, two possibilities are implied:

First: they did it while not knowing that it is disliked [by Allah] in it.

Second: they undertook it with insight and knowledge that its consequence is disliked, but they preferred the immediate over the deferred, so they were called 'ignorant' because they preferred the little (of this world) over the abundant comfort and the lasting consequence."

Regarding "soon" (al-qarib), there are three opinions.

The first: that it is repentance in good health. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi and Ibn al-Sa'ib also said it.

The second: that it is repentance before witnessing the Angel of Death. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Mijlaz also said it.

The third: that it is repentance before death. Ibn Zayd and others said it.

(p-38) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾. Regarding "evil deeds" there are three opinions.

The first: it is polytheism (shirk). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah.

The second: it is hypocrisy (nifaq). This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: it refers to the sins of the Muslims. This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri, who cited His saying, ﴿nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ as evidence.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until, when death approaches one of them﴾. Regarding "approaches" there are two opinions.

One: it means the descent of the signs of death (al-suq). This was said by Ibn 'Umar.

The second: it means the angels' being seen (mu'aynat al-mala'ika) at the seizing of the soul. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: After this verse, Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him…﴾ [An-Nisa' 116]. So He forbade forgiveness for whoever dies as a polytheist, and He deferred the people of monotheism to His will [so He did not make them despair of forgiveness]. Based on this, the verse is abrogated (mansukha, from naskh, abrogation) with respect to the believers.

O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion (﴿يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا يحل لكم أن ترثوا النساء كرها﴾).

**The occasion of revelation:** A man used to die, and his guardians (*awliya'*) had more right to his wife. If they wished, they would marry her, and if they wished, they would not marry her. So this verse was revealed. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration from him: In the early days of Islam, when a man died, the nearest of kin to him would stand up and throw a garment over his widow, and thereby acquire the right to marry her.

Mujahid said: When a man died, his eldest son had more right to his wife. He would marry her if he wished, or he would give her in marriage to whomever he wished.

Abu Umama ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf said: When Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, his son wanted to marry his widow after him, and this was a practice among them in the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance). So this verse was revealed.

'Ikrima said: The name of this woman was Kabisha bint Ma'n ibn 'Asim, and this practice was among the Arabs.

Abu Mijlaz said: The Ansar used to do this.

Ibn Zayd said: This was among the people of Madina.

al-Suddi said: This was only for the guardians, so long as the woman did not get ahead of them by going to her own family. If she did go to her family, then she had more right over herself.

**On the meaning of ﴿أن ترثوا النساء كرها﴾** there are two opinions.

The first: that you inherit the marriage of women (i.e., their marriage contract), and this is the view of the majority (*al-jumhur*).

The second: that you inherit their property by compulsion. Ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The close relative of the deceased would throw a garment over a young girl. If she was beautiful, he would marry her; and if she was plain, he would confine her until she died, and then he would inherit her.

**2.** The reciters (*al-qurra'*) differed in vocalising the *kaf* of *al-kurh* (the "k" in *kurh*) with a fatha or a damma in four places: here, in *al-Tawba*, and in two places in *al-Ahqaf*. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha in all of them, and Hamza read it with a damma. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha in *al-Nisa'* and *al-Tawba*, and with a damma in *al-Ahqaf*. Both are dialectal forms (*lughatan*), and we have mentioned them in *al-Baqara*.

**Regarding those addressed by ﴿ولا تعضلوهن﴾ (and do not restrain them),** there are three opinions.

The first: that it is addressed to the husbands. Then, regarding the restraint (*al-'adl*) that is forbidden, there are three opinions:

The first: that a man would dislike keeping company with his wife, while she had a dowry owed to her by him. So he would confine her and beat her so that she would ransom herself (*tafta*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

The second: that a man would marry a noble woman, perhaps she would not suit him, so he would separate from her on condition that she not marry anyone except with his permission, and he would call witnesses to this. Then when she proposed to someone and pleased him, he would grant her permission; otherwise he would restrain her. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that after divorce they would restrain women, as the Jahiliyya used to do, so they were forbidden from this. This is also related from Ibn Zayd. We have mentioned in *al-Baqara* that a man would divorce a woman, then take her back, then divorce her again in this manner forever, without any end, intending to harm her, until the revelation ﴿الطلاق مرتان﴾ (Divorce is twice) [al-Baqara: 229].

The second opinion: that it is addressed to the guardians. Then, regarding what they were forbidden from, there are three opinions:

The first: that in the Jahiliyya, if a man had a close relative, he would throw his garment over her, and she would never marry anyone other than him except with his permission. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that an orphan girl would be in the care of a man, and he would confine her until she died, or until she married his son. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: that the guardians would prevent women from marrying, so that they could inherit them. This is also related from Mujahid.

The third opinion: that it is addressed to the heirs of the husbands of those women, to whom it was said: "It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion." A man would inherit a close female relative and then restrain her until she died, or until she returned her dowry to him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and others. According to this, the speech is connected to the first part of the verse; and according to the opinions that preceded it, the mention of restraint is separate from ﴿أن ترثوا النساء﴾.

**Regarding al-fahisha (the outrageous immorality),** there are two opinions:

The first: that it is disobedience (*nushuz*) toward the husband. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and a group of others.

The second: that it is fornication (*zina*). This was said by al-Hasan, 'Ata' and 'Ikrima and a group of others. Ma'mar related from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: When a woman committed an outrageous act, her husband would take back what he had given her and expel her; then this was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., *naskh*, abrogation) by the prescribed punishment (*hadd*). Ibn Jarir said: This view is not sound, because the *hadd* is the right of God, while ransoming (*ifida'*) is the right of the husband, and one does not cancel the other.

The sound view is that if she commits any outrageous act, whether illicit intercourse or abusive speech, he is permitted to restrain her and constrain her until she ransoms herself.

As for His saying ﴿مبينة﴾ (manifest): Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr (from 'Asim) read *mubayyina* with a fatha on the *ya'*, and *ayatin mubayyinat* with a fatha on the *ya'* in both. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs (from 'Asim) read it with a kasra on the *ya'* in both. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read *mubiyyina* with a kasra, and *ayatin mubayyinat* with a fatha. The mention of "the Ten" (*al-'ashara*, i.e., the ten canonical readers) has already passed.

**His saying ﴿فعسى أن تكرهوا شيئا﴾** (But it may be that you dislike something). Ibn 'Abbas said: Perhaps God will grant you a child from them both, and God will place in her child much good.

The verse encourages keeping a wife despite disliking her, and it draws attention to two meanings.

The first: that a person does not know the aspects of what is good. Many a thing disliked becomes praiseworthy, and a thing praised becomes blameworthy.

The second: that a person can hardly find a beloved who has nothing in him that is disliked; so let him be patient with what he dislikes for the sake of what he loves.

They recited in this sense:

Whoever does not close his eye on his friend,
and on some of what is in him, will die while still reproaching.

And whoever pursues every slip diligently,
will find it, and no companion will remain sound to him through time.

(p-43) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you desire to exchange a spouse﴾. This address is to the men. "Zawj" (spouse) here means the woman. The mention of "qintar" (a great amount of wealth) has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then take not from it anything﴾. This prohibition applies only to the one who has had intercourse with her, or been alone with her, and the verse that follows it has clarified this. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The prohibition against taking back anything of what was given is singled out for the situation of exchange, even though the prohibition is general, lest someone suppose that, since the intimacy has returned to her ownership, she must forfeit her right to the dowry, or lest someone suppose that the new wife has a better claim to the dowry than she does, since she has taken her place.

As for "buhtan" (manifest injustice), there are two views. The first: it is injustice, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Qutaybah. The second: it is falsehood, as said by al-Zajjaj. The meaning of the statement is: Will you take it while committing slander and sin?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 21:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And how could you take it back?﴾ That is: how could you permit yourselves to take it back? In (the word) "al-Ifda" (the act of going in unto / consummation) there are two opinions.

One of them: that it means intercourse (al-jima'), said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Muqatil, and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: seclusion with her (al-khulwah), even if he has not had intercourse with her, said by al-Farra'.

Regarding what is meant by the covenant (al-mithaq) here, there are three opinions.

The first: that it is the (covenant) which Allah took from men on behalf of women: retaining them with kindness (ma'ruf) or releasing them with good conduct (ihsan). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second: that it is the marriage contract (aqd al-nikah), said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The third: that it is the trust of Allah (amanat Allah), said by al-Rabi'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 22:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (the time of ignorance before Islam) used to forbid what Allah had forbidden, except the wife of the father and the combining of two sisters, so this verse was revealed. Some of the Ansar said: Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, and his son Qays proposed to his wife. She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) seeking his permission and said: "I used to consider him a son." So this verse was revealed.

Abu 'Umar, the slave (ghulam) of Tha'lab, said: What we have obtained from Tha'lab, from the Kufans, and from al-Mubarrad, from the Basrans, is that "nikah" (marriage; lit. the joining of two things) in the original language is a term for joining two things. They also called the sexual act itself "nikah" without a contract.

Al-A'sha said:

"And a woman taken in marriage without a dower"

He meant: the captive woman who was had sexually without a dower and without a contract.

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: "Nikah" is sometimes used for the contract. Allah the Most High said: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. It is a true meaning for the sexual act and a figurative meaning for the contract, because it is a term for joining, and joining happens through the sexual act. So the contract was called nikah because it is a means leading to it.

The words of the Most High: ﴿except what has already passed﴾ On this there are six opinions.

The first: it means "after what has already passed," for Allah will forgive it. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Mufaddal. Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is: do not marry what your fathers married, for you would be punished for it, except what has already passed, for Allah has removed it from you.

The second: it means "other than what has already passed." This was said by al-Farra'.

The third: it means "but what has already passed, leave it." This was said by Qutrub. Ibn al-Anbari said: "But what has already passed, for it was an abomination."

The fourth: the meaning is: do not marry women in the manner of your fathers' marriages, that is, in the corrupt forms that are not permitted in Islam, except what has already passed in your jahiliyyah, of a marriage whose like is not permitted to begin in Islam, for that is pardoned for you. This is like the saying of the speaker: "Do not do what she did," meaning: do not do the like of what she did. Mentioned by Ibn Jarir.

The fifth: it means "and" (waw), so its sense is: "and not what has already passed," and the meaning is: cut off what you are upon of marrying the fathers' wives, and do not begin it. This was said by some scholars of the meanings of the Qur'an.

The sixth: it is for exception. The sense of the speech is: do not marry what your fathers married of women in a lawful marriage (whose contract was among them) except what has already passed from them through fornication and illicit intercourse, for those women are lawful to you. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The words of the Most High: "Innahu" (indeed it) refers to the marriage. "Al-fahishah" (the abomination) is what is shameful and ugly. "Al-maqt" (abhorrence) is the most intense hatred. Regarding the meaning of this "maqt" there are two opinions.

One: it is a name for this marriage. In the jahiliyyah they used to call marrying the father's wife "maqt," and they called the child born from it "al-maqti." So they were informed that what was forbidden to them, from marrying the father's wife, had always been disapproved and detested among them. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The second: it necessitates the hatred of Allah for its doer. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

The words: ﴿and evil is the way﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: That is, this deed was ugly as a path.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 23:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The original form of "ummahat" (mothers) is "amat," but the letter "ha'" (ه) was added for emphasis, just as they added it in "ahraqtu al-ma'" (I poured out the water), whose original form is "araqtu."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾. They were called "mothers" only because of the place of prohibition (hurmah) they hold.

The scholars differed over whether a number (of feedings) is considered in breastfeeding or not. Hanbal transmitted from Ahmad that the prohibition is established by a single feeding, and this is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Hasan, Tawus, al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Zuhri, al-Awzaʿi, al-Thawri, Malik, and Abu Hanifa and his companions. Muhammad ibn al-ʿAbbas transmitted from Ahmad that the prohibition is established by three feedings. Abu al-Harith transmitted from Ahmad that it is not established by fewer than five separate feedings, and this is the view of al-Shafiʿi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾. The mothers of wives become forbidden upon the very contract (of marriage) to the daughter, whether or not he has consummated the marriage with the daughter. This is the view of ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿImran ibn Husayn, Masruq, ʿAta, Tawus, al-Hasan, and the majority. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding a man who divorced his wife before consummation: he may marry her mother. This is also the view of Mujahid and ʿIkrimah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your stepdaughters﴾. The rabibah (stepdaughter) is the daughter of a man's wife from another husband. The meaning of "rabibah" is "marbubah" (one who is raised), because the man raises her. The wording was given in general terms, regarding the upbringing being in the man's household, and not as a condition.

His saying: ﴿And the wives of your sons﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Hala'il" means "azwaj" (spouses). "Halilah" has the sense of "muhallah" (one who is lawful), and it is derived from "halal" (lawful). Others said: she was so named because she "yahillu" (is lawful) with him wherever he is. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: "Halil" is the husband and "halilah" is the wife, and they were so named either because they both "yahillan" (become lawful) in one place, or because each of them is "yuhalu" (is a companion to) the other, i.e., "yunazilahu" (dwells with him), or because each of them makes lawful the other's "izar" (garment, i.e., intimacy).

His saying: ﴿Who are from your loins﴾. ʿAta said: He mentioned "loins" only to exclude adopted sons (al-adiya').

As for His saying: ﴿Except what has already passed﴾, the discussion concerning it is along the lines of what preceded in the previous verse. However, they added two other views regarding this. One: "Except what has already passed" refers to the matter of Yaʿqub, peace be upon him, since he combined between the mother of Yusuf and her sister. This is related from ʿAta and al-Suddi, but it is weak for two reasons.

First: this prohibition is tied to our law, and not all laws agree, nor is there any basis for pardoning us for what others did. Second: if the one who said this were asked to authenticate his transmission, it would be difficult for him.

The second view: the benefit of this exception is that the contracts made before (the prohibition) concerning the two sisters are not annulled, and a person may choose one of them. From this is the hadith of Fayruz al-Daylami, who said: "I embraced Islam while I had two sisters (as wives), so I came to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'Divorce one of them.'" Mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

(p-٤٩) **His saying: ﴿And the married women among women﴾.** As for its occasion of revelation, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated: "We took captives on the day of Awtas, and they had husbands. We disliked having intercourse with them, so we asked the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse was revealed, and so we made them lawful to us."

As for the differences among the readers (qira'at): Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read the ṣād with a fatḥah (المُحْصَناتِ) throughout the Qur'an. al-Kisa'i read the ṣād with a fatḥah in this verse alone. The rest of the Qur'an they read with a kasrah (المُحْصِناتِ), and both al-Muḥṣanāt and Muḥṣanāt [occur]. Ibn Qutaybah said: ihsan (chastity, protection) means that a thing guards and protects something from harm. So al-Muhsanat [min al-nisa'] are those with husbands, because husbands have guarded them and kept others away from them. God Most High said: ﴿And the married women among women, except what your right hands possess﴾. Al-muhsanat are also free women, even if they are not married, because a free woman is guarded and guards [others], and is not like a slave woman. God Most High said: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and He said: ﴿Upon them is half the punishment of the free women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], meaning the free women. Al-muhsanat also means the chaste: God Most High said: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning the chaste. God Most High said: ﴿And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12], meaning she kept herself chaste.

Regarding the meaning of al-muhsanat here, there are three opinions.

The first: those who have husbands. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Zayd, al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj.

The second: the chaste, for they are forbidden to men except by a marriage contract or by ownership of the right hand. This is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Abu al-'Aliyah, 'Ata', 'Ubaydah and al-Suddi.

The third: the free women, so the meaning is that they are forbidden after the four whom were mentioned at the beginning of the surah. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ubaydah.

On the first view, regarding His saying: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾, there are two opinions.

One: its meaning is, "except what your right hands possess of captives taken in war." On this basis, 'Ali, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas interpreted the verse, and these men did not regard the sale of a slave woman as a divorce.

The second: "except what your right hands possess of slave women who are married, whether by capture or otherwise." On this basis, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir and Anas interpreted the verse, and these men regarded the sale of a slave woman as a divorce. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Hasan that they said: "The sale of a slave woman is her divorce." But the first is more sound (asahh), (p-٥١) because the Prophet ﷺ gave Barirah the choice, when 'A'ishah freed her, between remaining with her husband, whom her masters had married her to while she was a slave, and separating from him. The Prophet ﷺ did not make 'A'ishah's manumission of her a divorce; if it had been a divorce, his giving her the choice would have had no meaning. What confirms the soundness of the first view is what we have mentioned about the occasion of revelation of the verse.

On the second view: the chaste are forbidden except by ownership, and ownership may be by contract or by ownership of the right hand.

On the third view: free women are forbidden after the four, except what your right hands possess of slave women, for they are not limited to a number.

His saying, Most High: ﴿The decree of God upon you﴾. al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as an emphatic (object), governed by the sense, because the meaning of ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ is: God has prescribed this for you as a decree. He said: it is also permissible that it be in the accusative by way of a command, with "upon you" explaining it, so the meaning is: "Keep to the Book of God." He said: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾, meaning what is after these things, except that the sunnah has forbidden marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt, or together with her maternal aunt. Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu 'Imran read (كُتُبَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكم) with a fatḥah on the kāf, the tā' and the bā', without an alif, and a rafʿ on the hā'. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-uhilla" with a fatḥah on the ḥā'; Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a ḍammah on the alif.

**Section**

Our shaykh 'Ali ibn 'Ubaydullah said: The majority of scholars held that His saying: ﴿And lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾ is a permission expressed in general terms, and that it is a general statement which has been restricted (takhsis), and the restricting element is the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition that a woman be married together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt. This is not by way of naskh (abrogation). A group held that the permission mentioned in the verse is abrogated by this hadith.

His saying, Most High: ﴿That you seek with your wealth﴾, i.e., that you seek, either by a dowry in marriage, or by a price in ownership. ﴿Chaste (muhsinin)﴾: Ibn Qutaybah said: "married." al-Zajjaj said: "contracting marriage." Others said: "seeking chastity, not committing fornication." Al-sifah means fornication (zina). Ibn Qutaybah said: its root is from "safahtu al-qirbah," when I poured out the water-skin, so fornication was called sifah because the man pours out the seed and the woman pours out the seed. Ibn Faris said: sifah is pouring water without a contract or marriage, like something that flows away in waste.

His saying, Most High: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them, give them their wages﴾. In this there are two opinions.

(p-٥٣) One: it is enjoyment within marriage, through the dowries. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and the majority.

The second: it is enjoyment for a specified term without a marriage contract. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to give a legal opinion permitting temporary marriage (mut'ah), but he later retracted that. Some of the commentators among the readers took great pains, saying: the intended meaning of this verse is the marriage of mut'ah, which was then abrogated by what is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he forbade temporary marriage with women. This is an unnecessary strain, because the Prophet ﷺ permitted mut'ah and then forbade it, so his earlier statement was abrogated by his later statement. As for the verse, (p-٥٤) it does not include the permission of mut'ah, because He, Most High, said in it: ﴿That you seek with your wealth, chaste, not committing fornication﴾, which indicates valid marriage. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of His saying ﴿So for what you have enjoyed of them﴾ is "those whom you have married under the condition that has been established," which is His saying ﴿chaste, not committing fornication﴾, i.e., contracting marriage, ﴿then give them their wages﴾, i.e., their dowries. Whoever interprets the verse otherwise has erred and shown ignorance of the language.
