His saying, Most High: ﴿And there is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree to after the obligation﴾. In this there are six opinions.

One: its meaning is, "There is no blame upon you in what the woman has left of her dowry and given to her husband." This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: "And there is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree upon of staying together or separating after the payment of the obligation." This too is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "And there is no blame upon you, O husbands, if you are in difficulty after the obligation to your wives, in what you mutually agree upon, that they reduce it for you or release you from it." This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Taymi.

(p-٥٥) The fourth: "There is no blame upon you if the term of temporary marriage has ended that they extend the term for you and you increase their wage, without a period of waiting (istibra')." This was said by al-Suddi, and it returns to the story of mut'ah.

The fifth: "There is no blame upon you if a woman gives her dowry to a man, or he gives to her whom he has not consummated with half the dowry which is not obligatory upon him." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The sixth: that it is general, covering increase, reduction, postponement and release. This was said by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford (ṭawlan) to marry free believing women﴾. "Ṭawl" means wealth and ability, according to the majority of scholars. "Al-muḥṣanāt" means free women. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, whoever is not able to pay the dower of a free woman. It is said: "So-and-so had ṭawl over so-and-so," meaning he had superiority over him in ability. (p-56)

By "al-fatayāt" (the young women) here are meant the slave women. A female slave is called fatāh (fatāt), and a male slave is called fatā; and the name has also been given to one who is not a slave. I read to our shaykh, the linguist Imam Abu Mansur, who said: "al-mutafattiyah" is a young woman who is nearing adolescence; a young girl of tender age is called fatāh, and a young boy is called fatā. Al-Qutaybi said: fatā does not mean a young man or a youth; rather it means a complete, excellent man among men.

As for the mention of "what your right hands possess" (al-aymān), it is a condition for their permissibility. It is not permissible to marry a slave woman who is a People of the Book; this is the view of the majority, while Abu Hanifa said it is permissible.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: act upon your outward appearance regarding faith, for you are obligated to act upon what appears from some of you to others. He said: regarding His saying ﴿some of you are from others﴾ there are two interpretations. (p-57) The first: He meant lineage, that is, all of you are the children of Adam. It may also mean: your religion is one, because He mentioned here "believing women." This was said to them because the Arabs used to slander lineages and boast of noble descent, and they called the son of a slave woman "hajin" (of mixed, inferior birth). So Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that the status of slaves and others is equal in the matter of faith. He disliked marrying a slave woman, and forbade it when one finds a way to a free woman, because the children of a slave woman by a free man become slaves, and because a slave woman is subject to being treated as a servant in the company of men, and that would be burdensome for the husband.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of the verse is: all of you are the sons of Adam, so let there be no arrogance or disdain in you from marrying slave women in cases of necessity.

Ibn Jarir said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech; its implied sense is: "And whoever among you cannot afford ṭawl to marry the believing women (al-muḥṣanāt), then let some of you marry from others," that is, let this man marry this man's young woman.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So marry them﴾, meaning the slave women, ﴿with the permission of their people﴾, that is, their masters. "Al-ujūr" means the dowers.

Regarding His saying ﴿in a fitting manner﴾ there are two views.

The first: it is positioned first in meaning, so its sense is: marry them with the permission of their people in a fitting manner, that is, in a valid marriage, ﴿and give them their dowers﴾.

The second: the meaning is: and give them their dowers in a fitting manner, like the dowers of their equals. Ibn Abbas said: "muḥṣanāt" means chaste, not fornicators, ﴿nor those who take secret lovers (akhdān)﴾, meaning, friends. In the Jahiliyya they used to forbid what was openly fornication and make lawful what was hidden. In another narration he said: "al-musāfiḥāt" are those who openly commit fornication, and "al-mutakhidhāt akhdānan" are those who have one lover (p-58). Others said: a woman would take a male friend with whom she committed fornication, and would not commit it with anyone else.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they are chaste (uḥṣinna)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read "uḥṣinna" with the alif dammed. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from Asim read it with the alif and the ṣād vowelled with fatḥa. Ibn Jarir said: whoever reads with fatḥa intends "they embraced Islam, so they became guarded in their chastity from what is unlawful through Islam"; and whoever reads with ḍamma intends "when they marry, they become guarded in their chastity from what is unlawful through husbands."

As for "al-fāḥisha" (the immorality), it is fornication; "al-muḥṣanāt" are free women; and "al-'adhāb" is the prescribed punishment (ḥadd). Qadi Abu Ya'la said: Islam and marriage are not a condition for the obligation of the prescribed punishment upon the slave woman; rather it is obligatory even if both are absent. The condition of chastity (iḥṣān) is mentioned only in the context of the ḥadd, so that no one would imagine that she bears half of what a free woman bears when she is not chaste, and the same as a free woman when she is chaste.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ refers to the permissibility of marrying slave women. Regarding "al-'anat" (hardship/sin) there are five views. The first: it is fornication, said by Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: it is ruin (al-halak), mentioned by Abu Ubayda and al-Zajjaj. The third: meeting hardship in love for the slave woman, related by al-Zajjaj. The fourth: that "al-'anat" here is sin (al-ithm). The fifth: that it is the punishment that causes one distress, which is the ḥadd; both were mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this verse indicates the permissibility of marrying believing slave women on two conditions. The first: the absence of the means to marry a free woman.

(p-59) The second: the fear of fornication. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, Masruq, Makhul, Ahmad, Malik and al-Shafi'i. It has been related from Ali, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid and al-Zuhri that they said: one may marry a slave woman even if one is wealthy; and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾. Ibn Abbas and the community said: (it refers to) refraining from marrying slave women; he urged patience in refraining from it because of the enslavement of the children.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾. The lam here carries the meaning of "an" (that). This is the view of a group of the people of Arabic grammar (ahl al-'arabiyyah), and it was chosen by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). Similar to it are ﴿And I have been commanded to be just between you﴾ [al-Shura: 15], ﴿And we have been commanded to submit﴾ [al-An'am: 71], and ﴿They want to extinguish﴾ [al-Saff: 8].

Clarification (al-bayan) from Allah, Exalted is He, comes sometimes through explicit text (bi'l-nass) and sometimes through the indication of the text (bi-dalalat al-nass). Al-Zajjaj said: "al-sunan" means the paths (al-turuq), so the meaning is: He guides you to His obedience, just as He guided the prophets and those who followed them. Others said: the meaning of the speech is: Allah desires to make clear to you the ways (sunan) of those before you, of the people of truth and falsehood, so that you may avoid falsehood and respond to truth, and that He may guide you to the truth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He desires to guide you to that which will be a cause for your repentance.

Concerning those who follow the passions (al-shahawat), there are four opinions.

The first: they are the fornicators (al-zunat). This was said by Mujahid and Muqatil. The second: they are the Jews and Christians. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: they are specifically the Jews. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. The fourth: they are the people of falsehood (ahl al-batil). This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you should incline a tremendous inclination﴾. That is, away from the truth through disobedience.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you﴾. At-takhfif (lightening) is making the obligation easy, or removing part of it. Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: He desires to make it easy for you, by His permission, to marry believing slave-girls for whoever cannot afford to marry a free woman. Regarding what is meant by ﴿the weakness of man﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: that it is weakness in the original creation. Al-Hasan said: it is that he was created from a despicable fluid. The second: that it is little patience regarding women; this was said by Tawus and Muqatil. The third: that it is weakness of resolve in restraining desire; this is the view of az-Zajjaj and Ibn Kaysan.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 4, Verse 29**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾. *Al-batil* (falsehood) is that which is not lawful in the Sharia (sacred law).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except that it be trade﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *tijaratan* with *raf'* (nominative: *tijaratun*). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read it with *nasb* (accusative: *tijaratan*). We have already explained the reason (*'illa*) for this at the end of *al-Baqara*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾. On this there are five opinions.

(p-61) The first: it is on its apparent meaning, and God has forbidden the servant to kill himself. This is the apparent meaning.

The second: its meaning is that some of you should not kill others. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, Qatada, al-Suddi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba.

The third: the meaning is, do not burden yourselves with an action that may lead to their destruction, even if it is an obligation. On this basis, 'Amr ibn al-'As interpreted it in the expedition of Dhat al-Salasil, when he led his companions in prayer while in a state of major impurity (*janaba*) on a cold night. When this was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said to him: "O 'Amr, you led your companions in prayer while you were in a state of major impurity?" He said: "O Messenger of God, I had a wet dream on a cold night, and I feared that if I bathed I would perish, so I remembered His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed.

(p-62) The fourth: the meaning is, do not be heedless of the portion of your souls. Whoever is heedless of its portion is as if he has killed it. This is the view of al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad.

The fifth: do not kill them by committing sins.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice﴾. Regarding what "that" refers to, there are three opinions.

The first: it refers to killing a soul (qatl al-nafs). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'.

The second: it refers to everything that Allah has forbidden from the beginning of the surah up to this point. This was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it refers to killing a soul and consuming wealth falsely (akl al-amwal bil-batil). This was said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 31:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden⦆ (ijtinab, "avoiding," means leaving something aside). Regarding the major sins (kaba'ir) there are eleven opinions.

The first: they are seven. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs narrate from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what are they?" He said: "Associating partners with Allah, sorcery, killing a soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, consuming usury (riba), consuming the property of an orphan, fleeing on the day of the march (al-zahf), and slandering chaste, believing, heedless women."

This hadith has also been narrated by another route from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The major sins are seven: associating partners with Allah is the first of them, killing a soul without right, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan by hastening before they grow up, fleeing from the march, accusing chaste women, and reverting to being a bedouin after the migration (hijrah)."

It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: They are seven, and he counted these.

It is narrated from Ata' that he said: They are seven, and he counted these, except that in place of associating partners and apostasy (al-ta'arrub) he mentioned false testimony and disobedience to parents.

The second: they are nine. Ubayd ibn Umayr narrated from his father, who was one of the Companions, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked, "What are the major sins?" He said: "Nine: the greatest of them is associating partners with Allah, killing a believing soul without right, fleeing from the march, consuming the property of an orphan, sorcery, consuming usury, slandering a chaste woman, disobedience to two Muslim parents, and making lawful the Sacred House, your qibla, both living and dead."

The third: they are four. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs narrate from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The major sins are: associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, killing a soul, and the perjurous oath (al-yamin al-ghamus)."

Anas ibn Malik narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the major sins, or was asked about them, and said: "Associating partners with Allah, killing a soul, and disobedience to parents," and he said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins? The saying of falsehood, or false testimony." It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: The major sins are four: associating partners with Allah, feeling secure from the plan of Allah, despairing of the mercy of Allah, and losing hope in the comfort of Allah. Similar is narrated from Ikrimah.

The fourth: they are three. Imran ibn Husayn narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins? Associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents," - and he was reclining, so he sat up - "and false speech." Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs narrate from the hadith of Abu Bakrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" We said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents," - and he was reclining, so he sat up - "and false testimony." He kept repeating it until we said: "I wish he would be silent." And they both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." I said: "Then which?" He said: "Then that you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." I said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour."

The fifth: they are those mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to this verse. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas.

The sixth: they are eleven: associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, the perjurous oath, killing a soul, consuming the property of an orphan, consuming usury, fleeing from the march, slandering chaste women, false testimony, sorcery, and treachery. This is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

The seventh: they are every sin which Allah concludes with a fire, or wrath, or a curse, or a punishment. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The eighth: they are everything for which Allah has obligated the Fire in the Hereafter and the prescribed punishment (hadd) in this world. Abu Salih narrated this meaning from Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak said likewise.

The ninth: they are everything by which Allah is disobeyed. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ubaydah, and it is a weak opinion.

The tenth: they are every sin for which Allah has threatened the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak in one narration, and al-Zajjaj.

The eleventh: they are eight: associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, killing a believer, slandering a chaste woman, fornication, consuming the property of an orphan, false speech, and taking a man's right by his oath and covenant for a small price. Mihriz narrated it from al-Hasan al-Basri.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will remove from you your misdeeds⦆. Al-Mufaddal narrated from Asim: "yukaffir" and "wa-yudkhilkum" with the ya' in both. The rest read with the nun in both. Nafi', Aban (from Asim), and al-Kisa'i (from Abu Bakr, from Asim) read "mudkhalan" with a fatha on the mim here, while the rest read it with a damma on the mim in al-Hajj. They did not differ on the damma on the mim in "mudkhala sidq" and "mukhraja sidq" [al-Isra': 80]. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: "al-mudkhal" may be a verbal noun (masdar) or a place, whether with fatha or damma. Al-Suddi said: The misdeeds (sayyi'at) here are the minor sins (saghair). And "al-mudkhal al-karim" is Paradise. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-karim" means "al-sharif" (the noble).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others.﴾ Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three reports.

The first: "Umm Salamah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, men go out to fight, but we do not fight, and we only have half of the inheritance.' So this verse was revealed." This was related by Mujahid.

The second: the women said: "We wish that Allah had made fighting (jihad) something for us, so that we might obtain the same reward that men obtain." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Ikrimah.

The third: when ﴿To the male, a portion equal to the share of two females﴾ was revealed, the men said: "We hope that we will be preferred over women through our good deeds, just as we have been preferred over them in inheritance." And the women said: "We hope that the burden (of sin) upon us will be half of what is upon the men, just as we have the inheritance at half their share." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Regarding the meaning of this wishing (tamanni), there are two opinions. One: that a man wishes for the wealth of another; this was said by Ibn Abbas and Ata. The other: that women wish to be men. It has been related from Umm Salamah that she said: "Would that we were men," and so this verse was revealed.

Wishing (tamanni) has several aspects.

The first: that a person wishes that another's wealth would come to him and be removed from the other. This is envy (hasad).

The second: that a person wishes for the like of what another has, without wanting it to be removed from the other. This is ghibta (wholesome emulation), and it may be that attaining it is not a benefit for the one who wishes. Al-Hasan said: "Do not wish for the wealth of so-and-so, nor the wealth of so-and-so. What do you know, perhaps his ruin lies in that wealth?"

The third: that a woman wishes to be a man, and the like of this which does not come to pass. So let the servant know that Allah is most knowing of what is beneficial, let him be content with the decree of Allah, and let his wishes be for an increase in the deeds of the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: that what is meant by "earning" here is inheritance; this is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah.

The second: that it is reward and punishment. The meaning is that a woman is rewarded as a man is rewarded and is sinful as he is sinful. This is the view of Qatadah, Ibn al-Sa'ib, and Muqatil. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi argued for its soundness by saying that inheritance is not obtained through earning, and that the verse was revealed concerning wishing and preference.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, Aban, and Khalaf in his choice of reading recited (wa-salu Allah), (fa-sal alladhina), (fa-sal Bani Isra'il), and (wa-sal man arsalna), and whatever is similar to this of the imperative addressed directly, when preceded by a "waw" or a "fa", is unhamzated according to them. This is also related from Abu Ja'far and Shayba. The rest recited with hamza in all of these, and they did not differ regarding His saying: ﴿and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10] that it is hamzated.

Regarding what is meant by "bounty" (fadl) there are two opinions. One: that bounty is obedience; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Suddi. The other: that it is provision; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. So the meaning is: ask Allah for the blessings you wish for, and do not wish for the wealth of others.

(p-٧١) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for each We have appointed heirs﴾. *Mawali* means the *awliya'* (those entitled), who are the heirs from among the *'asaba* (agnatic kin, the male relatives who inherit residual shares) and others. The meaning of the verse is: for every person there are heirs who inherit what he leaves. The *i'rab* (grammatical analysis) of "the parents and the nearest relatives" allows two readings.

The first is that it is in the nominative as the predicate of an inchoative subject, the implied meaning being: "They are the parents and the nearest relatives." In this case the complete sentence ends at His saying ﴿from what he leaves﴾.

The second is that it is in the nominative as the subject of the verb *tarak* (leaves) referring to the wealth, so that the parents are the *mawla* (heirs).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those with whom your oaths have been made binding﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *'aqadat* with an *alif* ("عاقَدَتْ"). 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *'aqadat* without an *alif* ("عَقَدَتْ"). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: whoever reads with the *alif*, the implied meaning is "those with whom your oaths have made a contract," and whoever omits the *alif*, the meaning is "your oaths bound their alliance," so the *mudaf* (the governed noun) has been omitted and the *mudaf ilayh* (the governing noun) has been put in its place. There are three opinions concerning them.

The first is that they are the people of alliance (*ahl al-hilf*). A man would make an alliance with another man, and whichever of them died, the other would inherit from him. This was abrogated (*naskh*) by His saying: ﴿And blood relatives are nearer to one another﴾. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Atiyyah narrated from him, saying: A man in the Jahiliyyah would attach himself to another man and become his follower. When the man died, the inheritance went to his family, and his follower remained with nothing. So Allah revealed ( والَّذِينَ عاقَدَتْ أيْمانكم ), and he was given a share of the inheritance. Then after that came ﴿And blood relatives are nearer to one another﴾. Among those who said they were the allies were Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The second is that they are those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought into brotherhood, namely the Emigrants and the Helpers. The Emigrants used to make the Helpers their heirs rather than their blood relatives, because of the brotherhood that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had established between them. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Zayd also said this.

The third is that they are those who used to adopt the sons of others in the Jahiliyyah. This is the opinion of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

As for the proponents of the first opinion, they said: the ruling about the allies who used to bind themselves to one another in support and inheritance was abrogated by the last (verses of) al-Anfal. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Malik, Ahmad and al-Shafi'i held this view.

Abu Hanifa and his companions said: this ruling remains (*muhkam*, unabrogated), except that he made the blood relatives closer than the clients of the contract. Some people went to the view that what is meant is: give them their share of support and counsel, without inheritance. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Other people went to the view that the contract was only in the Jahiliyyah for support and nothing else, and Islam did not change that but confirmed it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Any alliance that existed in the Jahiliyyah, Islam only increased it in strength." He meant: support and assistance. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it indicates that the verse is unabrogated (*muhkamah*).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 34:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A man slapped his wife, so she sought redress against him from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas. The commentators mentioned that the man was Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' al-Ansari. Ibn Abbas said: "Qawwamun" means: empowered to discipline women in what is right. Hisham ibn Muhammad narrated from his father regarding His saying: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾, he said: "When they are men." And he recited a verse:

Do you think every man is a man, when a fire blazes at night like a fire?

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with what Allah has preferred some of them over others﴾, meaning: men over women. Men are preferred over women by greater intellect, a fuller share in inheritance, spoils of war, the Friday prayer, congregational prayers, the caliphate, leadership, jihad, and the right of divorce being placed in his hand, among other things.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and with what they spend from their wealth﴾. Ibn Abbas said: meaning the dower (mahr) and the maintenance (nafaqah) they provide for them.

Regarding "the righteous women" (al-salihat) there are two opinions. One: those who are good to their husbands, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: those who act with goodness, said by Ibn al-Mubarak. Ibn Abbas said: "al-qanitat" means those who are obedient to Allah regarding their husbands, and "al-hafizat lil-ghayb" means guarding what is unseen, i.e., the unseen of their husbands. Ata' and Qatadah said: they guard what the husbands are absent from, such as property, and what is obligatory upon them regarding the preservation of themselves for them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with what Allah has guarded﴾. The majority read "Allah" with a nominative ending (raf'), and regarding the meaning on their reading there are three opinions.

The first: by Allah's guarding of them, said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata' and Muqatil. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated from Sufyan, who said: by Allah's guarding of them in that He made them so.

The second: by what Allah has guarded for them, their dowers and the obligation of their maintenance, said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that its meaning is: they guard the unseen by means of that by which the command of Allah is guarded, related by al-Zajjaj. Abu Ja'far read "Allah" with an accusative ending (nasb). The meaning then is: by their guarding Allah in His obedience.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those from whom you fear disobedience (nushuz)﴾. Regarding "fear" there are two opinions.

One: it means knowledge, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it means suspicion, due to the signs of nushuz that appear, said by al-Farra', who recited a verse:

And I did not fear, O Salam, that you would blame me.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Nushuz" is the wife's hatred of her husband; it is said: "nashazat al-mar'ah 'ala zawjiha" (the woman became disobedient to her husband), and "nashasat" when she rubs him and does not feel at ease with him. The root of nushuz is agitation. Al-Zajjaj said: its origin is from al-nashz, which is an elevated place on the ground.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then admonish them﴾. Al-Khalil said: al-wa'z is reminding of good in what softens the heart.

Al-Hasan said: he admonishes her with his tongue; if she refuses, then he forsakes her (hajara). They differed regarding the meaning of forsaking in the bed, into four opinions.

The first: that he abstains from intercourse, narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abi Talhah, and al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil also said so.

The second: that it is abstention from speech, not from intercourse, narrated by Abu al-Duha from Ibn Abbas, and Khasif from Ikrimah, and al-Suddi and al-Thawri also said so.

The third: that it is the saying of harsh words in the bedchamber, related from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Ikrimah. The meaning then is: speak to them in the bedchamber with harsh speech.

The fourth: that it is forsaking her bed and lying with her. Related from al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, Miqsam and Qatadah. Ibn Abbas said: forsake her in the bed; if she responds, well and good, otherwise Allah has permitted you to strike her with a non-severe blow. A group of the people of knowledge said: the verse is in sequence: admonition at the fear of nushuz, forsaking at the manifestation of nushuz, and striking when it recurs and persists in it. It is not permissible to strike at the beginning of nushuz. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this is the school of Ahmad. Al-Shafi'i said: it is permissible to strike her at the beginning of nushuz.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if they obey you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: meaning in the bed, ﴿then do not seek a way against them﴾, i.e., do not fabricate pretexts against them. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: do not burden her with love, for her heart is not in her hand. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: do not seek a way to what is not lawful for you of their bodies and their wealth by pretexts; that is, that you say to her while she is obedient to you: "You are not loving to me," so you strike her or harm her.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Most High, Most Great﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: do not transgress against your wives, for He will avenge them against you. Al-Khattabi said: al-Kabir is the one described with majesty and greatness of station, before whose majesty every great thing becomes small. It is also said: He is the One who is too great to be likened to created beings.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear a breach between the two﴾. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of "fear." The first: it is caution against the occurrence of something whose occurrence is not certain; this was said by al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian and Qur'anic scholar). The second: it is knowledge; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi (Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi). Al-Zajjaj said: "al-shiqaq" (shiqaq, breach/discord) means enmity, and its derivation is from "al-mutashaqqin" (the two opposing parties), each party being in a "shiqq" (side, direction). And "al-hakam" (arbiter) is the one who is trustworthy in what is entrusted to him. Regarding the one commanded to implement the ruling of the two arbiters, there are two opinions. The first: it is the ruler, if the two spouses bring their dispute before him; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak. The second: it is the two spouses; this was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If they both desire reconciliation﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "That is, the two arbiters." Regarding His saying: ﴿Allah will bring about harmony between them﴾, there are two opinions. The first: it refers to the two arbiters; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ata', al-Suddi, and the majority. The second: it refers to the two spouses; this was mentioned by some exegetes.

Section

The two arbiters are agents of the two spouses, and the consent of the two spouses is required regarding what the two arbiters rule. This is the view of Ahmad, Abu Hanifa, and their companions. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: the ruling of the two arbiters does not require the consent of the two spouses.

(p-79) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Worship Allah﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Affirm His oneness (tawhid).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾. Al-Farra' said: He urged them to show kindness to their parents.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and to the neighbor who is a relative﴾. Concerning it there are two views.

One: that it is the neighbor who is related to you by kinship. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and others.

The second: that it is the Muslim neighbor. This was said by Nawf al-Shami. The meaning would then be: the one who is near to you by Islam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and the distant neighbor﴾. Al-Mufaddal related from ʿAsim: "wal-jari al-junubi" with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the nun. Abu ʿAli said: The meaning is "wal-jari dhi al-janb," the modifier having been elided. Concerning the distant neighbor there are three views.

One: that he is the stranger with whom you have no kinship. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and others.

The second: that he is your neighbor on your right, your left, in front of you, and behind you. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that he is the Jew and the Christian. This was said by Nawf al-Shami.

(p-80) Concerning "al-sahib bil-janb" there are three views.

One: that it is the wife. This was said by ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, and Ibn Abi Layla.

The second: that it is the travelling companion. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas in a narration from Mujahid, and by Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Ibn Qutaybah. It is also reported from Saʿid ibn Jubayr as being like both views.

The third: that it is the companion (rafiq). This was related by Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah also said so.

Ibn Zayd said: he is the one who sticks close to you hoping for your goodness. Muqatil said: he is your companion both at home and on a journey.

Concerning ibn al-sabil (the wayfarer) there are views. We have mentioned them in (al-Baqarah).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and what your right hands possess﴾. He means: the slaves. Some of them said: it includes the animals that are beasts. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-mukhtal" is the one who is insolent in his gait, and "al-fakhur" is the one who boasts over people through his arrogance. Mujahid said: it is the one who counts what he has been given and does not thank Allah.

(p-81) Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-mukhtal" is one possessed of conceit and pride. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-mukhtal" is the boastful, the vain, the ignorant. He mentioned self-conceit here only because the self-conceited person disdains his relatives and his neighbors when they are poor.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 37:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who are stingy﴾. The exegetes mention that it was revealed concerning the Jews. As for the occasion of its revelation, Ibn ʿAbbas said: Kardam ibn Zayd, [the ally of Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf], Usama ibn Habib, Nafiʿ ibn Abi Nafiʿ, Bahri ibn ʿAmr, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Rifaʿa ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut, would visit men of the Ansar, among the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They would mix with them and give them sincere advice, saying to them: "Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you [in its loss], and do not hasten to spend, for you do not know what will happen." So this verse was revealed. Regarding that about which they were stingy and commanded people to be stingy, there are two opinions. The first: it is wealth, related by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd. The second: it is concealing the description of the Prophet ﷺ and his prophethood, related by Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they command people to be stingy﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, and Ibn ʿAmir recited bi-l-bukhl (بِالبُخْلِ) with a light pronunciation of the vowel. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited bi-l-bukhl (بِالبُخْلِ) with a vowelled pronunciation (the first letter voweled with a kasra, i.e. bi-l-bukhl pronounced with the short vowel on the second consonant, bukhul), and likewise in Surat al-Hadid.

Regarding ﴿those to whom Allah has given of His bounty﴾ there are two opinions. The first: they are the Jews, who were given knowledge of the description of Muhammad ﷺ and concealed it; this is the view of the majority. The second: they are the owners of wealth who were stingy with it and concealed their riches; this is related by al-Mawardi, among others.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have prepared﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: We made that a ready provision (ʿatad) for them, i.e., established for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people﴾. The scholars differed concerning who this verse was revealed about, in three opinions. The first: they are the Jews. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Muqatil.

The second: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). This was said by al-Suddi, al-Zajjaj, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The third: they are the polytheists of Makkah who spent (their wealth) in hostility toward the Prophet (ﷺ). This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

And al-Qarin: the constant companion, who is the one joined to another. It is on the pattern of fa'il, from al-iqtiran (the conjoining) of two things. Regarding the meaning of the Shaytan being a companion (muqarana), there are two views. The first: his being a companion in action. The second: his being a companion in the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 39:

The words "﴿And what would it harm them﴾": The meaning is: what would it cost those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, and who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, if they were to believe? In the spending mentioned here there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to sadaqah (voluntary charity), as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it refers to zakah (obligatory almsgiving), as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. And in His words "﴿And Allah was ever Knowing of them﴾" there is a warning to them concerning the evil of their intentions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 40:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) by the weight of an atom﴾. We have already explained zulm (wrongdoing/injustice) earlier, and it is impossible for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to commit it. This is because some people said: zulm is acting with what one does not possess, and everything belongs to Him. Others said: it is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and His wisdom does not necessitate an act that has no benefit behind it. Mithqal (weight, measure) of a thing is the weight of that thing. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said, "This is on the mithqal of that," meaning "on its weight." Al-Zajjaj said: it is mif'al, derived from al-thiql (heaviness).

I read to our shaykh, Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: People think that the mithqal is the weight of a dinar and nothing else, and it is not as they think. The mithqal of every thing is its weight, and every weight is called a mithqal, even if it is the weight of a thousand. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if it is the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47]. Abu Hatim said: I asked al-Asma'i about the sanjah (weight piece) of the mithqal of the balance, and he said: it is Persian, and I do not know how to say it, but I say: mithqal. So if you say to a man, "Hand me a mithqal," and he gives you a sanjah of a thousand, or a sanjah of a grain, he has complied.

As for what is meant by dharrah (atom), there are five opinions. The first: it is the head of a red ant, narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. The second: a tiny particle of dust, narrated by Yazid ibn al-Asamm from Ibn Abbas. The third: the smallest of ants, said by Ibn Qutaybah and Ibn Faris. The fourth: the mustard seed. The fifth: the single mote of dust visible in sunlight when it shines through a hole, mentioned by al-Tha'alabi. Know that mentioning the dharrah is a parable with what can be understood, and the intended meaning is that He does not wrong, whether little or much.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And if it is a good deed﴾. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read ḥasanatun with a raised (nominative) vowel. The rest read it with a fatha (accusative). Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it with the raised vowel, the meaning is: "and if you produce a good deed"; and whoever reads it with the fatha, the meaning is: "and if you have done it as a good deed."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He multiplies it﴾. Ibn Amir and Ibn Kathir read yuḍa'‘ifhā with shaddah and without alif. The rest read yuḍā'ifhā with an alif and a kasrah on the ayn. Ibn Qutaybah said: yuḍā'ifhā with the alif means He gives its like many times, and yuḍa'‘ifhā without alif means He gives its like once.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿from Him﴾, that is, from before Him. And al-ajr al-'azim (the great reward) is Paradise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: "How will the state of these people be on the Day of Resurrection?" The state was omitted because the context indicates it. The word "how" (kayfa) is an interrogative particle, and its meaning here is rebuke. The witness (al-shahid) is the prophet of each nation. There are four opinions about what he testifies to.

(p-86) The first is that he testifies that he conveyed the message to his community. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second is that he testifies to their faith. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah. The third is that he testifies to their deeds. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The fourth is that he testifies for them and against them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We bring you as a witness over these﴾. It means: our Prophet (ﷺ). Regarding "these," there are three opinions. The first is that they are all of his community. On this there are two views. One is that he testifies against them. The other is that he testifies for them, so "ala" ("over") here carries the meaning of "li" ("for"). The second opinion is that they are the disbelievers, and he testifies against them regarding the conveyance of the message. This was said by Muqatil. The third is that they are the Jews and Christians. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Would that the earth were levelled over them!﴾ Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr recited: لَوْ تُسَوّى (law tusawwa), with a damma on the ta' and a light sin (takhfif al-sin). The meaning: they wish that they were turned into dust, so that they and the earth would be equal. This is the view of al-Farra' and others. Abu Hurayra said: when God gathers the creatures, He says to the beasts, the animals and the birds: "Be dust!" Then the disbeliever says at that moment: "Would that I were dust!"

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: لَوْ تُسَوّى (law tusawwa), with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on the sin. The meaning: لَوْ تَتَسَوّى (law tatasawwa), and the ta' was assimilated into the sin because of their closeness. Abu 'Ali said: in this reading there is a broadening of usage, because the verb is attributed to the earth, and the intended meaning is not "they wish the earth had become like them," but rather "they wish that they would be levelled into it." Then, regarding the meaning, the exegetes have two views.

The first: its meaning is: they wish that the earth had split open over them, so that they would sink into it. This was said by Qatada, Abu 'Ubayda and Muqatil.

The second: its meaning is: they wish that they had not been resurrected, because the earth had been level with them before they came out of it. This was said by Ibn Kaysan, and al-Zajjaj mentioned something similar. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited: لَوْ تُسَوّى (law tusawwa), with a fatha on the ta', a light sin, and the waw shadda and imala; it has the meaning of تَتَسَوّى (tatasawwa), so they dropped the ta' that Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir had assimilated. As for the meaning of the two readings, it is one.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾. Regarding "statement" there are two views. The first: it is their saying: "By God, we were not polytheists." This is the view of the majority. The second: it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), his description and his attributes, said by 'Ata'. On the first view, the concealment relates to the Hereafter; on the second, it relates to what happened in the world, so the meaning is: they wish that they had not concealed that.

Regarding the meaning of the verse, there are six views. The first: they wish that, when their limbs expose them, they had not concealed their polytheism from God. This meaning is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: when their limbs bore witness against them, they no longer concealed any statement from God after that. This too is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: in one situation they do not conceal any statement, and in another situation they conceal and say: "By God, we were not polytheists." This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that His saying ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ is a new sentence, not connected to His saying "Would that the earth were levelled over them!" This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The meaning of "they will not conceal from God any statement" is: they will not be able to conceal it, because it is manifest before God.

The fifth: the meaning is: they wish that the earth were levelled over them, and that they had not concealed from God any statement.

The sixth: they did not believe that their saying "By God, we were not polytheists" was a lie; rather, they believed that worshipping idols was obedience. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned both views.

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: they reported what they imagined, since they used to think that they were not polytheists, and that does not remove them from having lied.

[p. 89]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf prepared food for us, invited us, and gave us wine to drink. The wine took effect on us, and the time of prayer came. They put me forward to lead, and I recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, and we worship what you worship﴾. So this verse was revealed." In another narration from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, it is stated that the one they put forward and who made mistakes in this surah was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.

Regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿do not approach prayer﴾, there are two views. The first: do not expose yourselves to intoxication during the times of prayer. The second: do not enter into prayer while intoxicated. The first is more sound, because the intoxicated person does not understand what he is saying. Regarding the meaning of ﴿while you are intoxicated﴾, there are two views.

The first: it means intoxicated by wine, as the majority said. The second: it means drowsy from sleep, as al-Dahhak said, and this view is weak. This verse indicated the permissibility of intoxication outside the times of prayer, and then it was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a earlier ruling by a later one) by the prohibition of wine.

[p. 90]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿nor [while you are] junub﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: janabah (ritual impurity from sexual intercourse or seminal emission) means distance. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "rajulun junub" (a man who is junub), "rajulani junub" (two men who are junub), and "rijal junub" (men who are junub), just as it is said "rajul ridan" and "qawm ridan." Regarding the naming of the junub with this designation, there are two views. The first: because his semen is separated from its place. The second: because of what is required of him in terms of abstaining from prayer, recitation of the Qur'an, touching the mushaf, and entering the mosque.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿except as travellers﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: the meaning is: do not approach prayer while you are junub, except if you are travellers unable to find water, in which case perform tayammum (dry ablution with clean earth, a substitute for washing when water is unavailable) and pray. This meaning is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, Mujahid, al-Hakam, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj.

The second: do not approach the places of prayer, which are the mosques, while you are junub, except as those passing through, and do not sit. This meaning is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Zuhri, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Abu al-Duha, Ahmad, al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Qutaybah, and from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, in the same way as the two views. According to the first view, "'abir al-sabil" (one passing through) means the traveller, and "qurban al-salah" (approaching prayer) means performing it. According to the second, "'abir al-sabil" means one passing through the mosque, and "qurban al-salah" means entering the mosque in which prayer is performed.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you are ill﴾. Regarding the occasion of the revelation of this statement there are two views.

The first: "A man from the Ansar was ill and could not stand to perform wudu' (ablution with water). He had no servant, so he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And if you are ill or on a journey﴾." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were afflicted with wounds, which spread among them, and they were afflicted with janabah. They complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the whole verse was revealed: ﴿And if you are ill﴾." This was said by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The apparent meaning of the verse requires the permissibility of tayammum when there is an illness by which one is harmed by using water, whether one fears destruction or does not fear it. Likewise, travel permits tayammum when water is absent, whether the journey is short or long. The absence of water is not a condition for the permissibility of tayammum for the ill; rather, the condition is the occurrence of harm. As for travel, the absence of water is a condition for the permissibility of tayammum, but travel itself is not a condition. Rather, travel was mentioned because water is usually absent during it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself﴾. The word "aw" (or) here means "wa" (and), because if it were not so, the obligation of purification upon the ill and the traveller would not be connected to a state of minor impurity (hadath). Al-ghait means a low, level place in the ground, and the minor impurity was referred to by its location, as said by Ibn Qutaybah. Likewise they said "rawiyah" for a water-skin, though rawiyah is actually the camel on which water is carried; and they said "za'a'in" for women, though za'a'in are actually the litters in which women sit. They called the minor impurity "'adhirah" because they used to deposit it at the courtyards of houses.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿or you have touched women﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read: "aw lamastum" (with an alif) here, and in (al-Ma'idah). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf in his choice, al-Mufaddal from 'Asim, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah from Ibn 'Amir read: "aw lamastum" (without an alif) here and in (al-Ma'idah). Regarding what is meant by mulamasah (touching), there are two views.

The first: it is sexual intercourse, said by 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah.

The second: it is touching with the hand, said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, al-Sha'bi, 'Ubaydah, 'Ata', Ibn Sirin, al-Nakha'i, al-Nahdi, al-Hakam, and Hammad.

Abu 'Ali said: Lams (touching) occurs with the hand, and its use has been extended, so it is applied to other things. Among this is the verse ﴿And we have touched the heaven﴾ [al-Jinn: 8], meaning we sought the unseen of the heaven, and among us are those who steal it and throw it to the soothsayers and inform them of it. Since lams occurs in other than direct contact with the hand, He said: ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾ [al-An'am: 7], specifying the hand so that it would not be confused with the other sense, just as He said: ﴿and the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], because a son may be called a son while not being from the loins.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿then you do not find water, so perform tayammum﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was with the Prophet (ﷺ) on one of his journeys, and her necklace broke. The Prophet (ﷺ) stayed there searching for it, and they were not near water, and there was no water with them. So this verse was revealed, and Usayd ibn Hudayr said: 'This is not the first of your blessings, O family of Abu Bakr.'" Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it. In another narration, also narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim: "'A'ishah borrowed a necklace from Asma', and it was lost. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent men to search for it. The prayer time came upon them, and they had no water, so they prayed without wudu'. They complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the verse of tayammum was revealed."

Tayammum linguistically means intending or aiming, and we have already mentioned it in His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the bad﴾. As for al-sa'id, it is dust (turab), as said by 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Shafi'i said: the name al-sa'id applies only to dust that has dust particles (ghubar). Regarding al-tayyib (the pure or good), there are two views. The first: it is the clean (tahir). The second: it is the lawful (halal).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿then wipe your faces and your hands﴾. The part wiped in tayammum is the same part bounded in wudu'. Regarding the limit of wiping of the hands, there are three views.

The first: it extends to the two wrist joints, where a thief's hand is cut. 'Ammar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Tayammum is one strike for the face and the two palms." This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Ikrimah, al-Awza'i, Makhul, Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Dawud.

The second: it extends to the elbows. Ibn 'Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he performed tayammum and wiped his two forearms. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, his son Salim, al-Hasan, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i, and from al-Sha'bi there are two views like these.

The third: wiping is required from the tips of the fingers to the armpits. 'Ammar ibn Yasir narrated that he said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, and the concession regarding wiping was revealed, so we struck with our hands one strike for our faces, and one strike for our hands up to the shoulders and armpits." This is the view of al-Zuhri.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning﴾. Al-Khattabi said: "al-'Afw" is in the intensive form (for emphasis). Al-'afw is forgiveness of sins and leaving the requital of the one who does wrong. It is said that it is derived from: "'afat al-rih al-athar," meaning when the wind erases the trace, as if the one who pardons sins erases them by overlooking them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ The scholars differed regarding who was meant by this revelation, in three opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut.

The second: it was revealed concerning two men who, whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke, would twist their tongues and criticize him. Both opinions are related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it was revealed concerning the Jews. This was said by Qatadah.

Regarding the portion that they were given, there are two opinions. One: that they knew the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). The second: knowledge of what is in their Scripture without acting upon it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they purchase error﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: this is from ellipsis (ikhtisar), and the meaning is: they purchase error in exchange for guidance. Similar to it is ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ [al-Saffat: 78], meaning: We left for him a good praise, so the praise was omitted because the addressee knows it.

Regarding the meaning of their purchasing error, there are four opinions.

One: it is their exchanging error for faith. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is their exchanging denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) after his appearance for their faith in him before his appearance. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: it is their preferring denial of the Prophet, in order to take bribes and to retain their leadership. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: it is their giving their rabbis their wealth in return for what they do of denying the Prophet (ﷺ). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they desire that you should lose the way﴾. This is an address to the believers. And what is meant by "the way" is the path of guidance.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of your enemies﴾. So He informs you of what they are upon, so do not seek counsel from them, and they are the Jews. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a protector (wali)﴾ for you. Whoever has Allah as his protector, his enemy will not harm him. Al-Khattabi said: "Al-Wali" (the protector) is the helper, and "al-Wali" is the one who takes charge of the matter and manages it, and its root is from "al-waly," which means closeness. "Al-Nasir" (the helper) is on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active participle).

(p-٩٩) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Among those who are Jews﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Rifa'a ibn Zayd, Malik ibn al-Dayf, and Ka'b ibn Usayd, and they were all Jews. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian of Qur'anic language) mentioned two views regarding "min" (from).

The first: it is attached to "those who were given a portion of the Book," so the meaning is: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, from among those who are Jews?﴾

The second: it begins a new clause, so the meaning is: "From among those who are Jews there are people who distort," and his saying "who distort" is a descriptive clause (sifah), and the thing described is omitted. Sibawayh recited:

Time is nothing but two turns; in one of them I die,
and in the other I seek life and strive.

The meaning is: in one of them is a turn in which I die. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: The meaning is: "And Allah suffices as a helper" against those who are Jews, that is, Allah gives them victory over them.

As for "tahrif" (distortion), it means alteration. "Al-kalim" is the plural of "kalimah" (word). It has been said that "al-kalam" (speech) is derived from "al-kalm," which is a wound that splits the skin and flesh, so speech was called kalam because it pierces the ears by reaching them. It has also been said: rather, it is because it splits open the meanings intended across the various kinds of address.

Regarding the meaning of their distorting the words, there are two views. The first: they used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about something, and when they left, they distorted his speech; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is their altering of the Torah; this was said by Mujahid.

(p-١٠٠) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from their places﴾, that is, from their positions and their proper aspects.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. Mujahid said: "We hear your words, and we disobey your command."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And hear without being heard﴾. There are two views concerning it.

The first: its meaning is: "Hear, may you not hear." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: its meaning is: "Hear, while what you say is not accepted." This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. The meaning of "wa-ra'ina" has already been explained in (al-Baqarah).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿distorting with their tongues﴾. Qatada said: "Al-layy" is the twisting of their tongues with that.

Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of "distorting with their tongues" is that they distort "ra'ina" from its sense of "consider us" and of "waiting," into an insult by means of ignorance (ru'unah). Ibn Abbas said: ﴿It would have been better for them﴾ than what they altered, and "aqwam" means "more just," ﴿but Allah cursed them for their disbelief﴾ in Muhammad.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they do not believe except a few﴾. There are two views concerning it.

The first: among them, only a few believe, and they are Abdullah ibn Salam and those who followed him; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

(p-١٠١) The second: they do not believe except with a small belief. This was said by Qatada and al-Zajjaj. Muqatil said: That is their belief that Allah created them and provided for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who were given the Scripture, believe in what We have sent down⦄ (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ آمِنُوا بِما نَزَّلْنا﴾). The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul): "The Prophet (ﷺ) invited a group of the rabbis of the Jews, among them ʿAbd Allah ibn Suriya and Kaʿb [ibn Asad], to Islam, and said to them: 'Indeed you know that what I have brought is the truth.' They said: 'We do not recognize that.' So this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Concerning "those who were given the Scripture" there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Jews; this is said by the majority (al-jumhur). The second: the Jews and the Christians; this is mentioned by al-Mawardi. On the first view, "the Scripture" is the Torah; on the second, it is the Torah and the Gospel. What is meant by "what We have sent down" is the Qur'an, and its confirmation of what they possess has already been explained in (al-Baqara).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before We obliterate faces⦄ (﴿مِن قَبْلِ أنْ نَطْمِسَ وُجُوهًا﴾). Concerning the obliteration of faces there are three opinions.

The first: it is the blinding of the eyes; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and al-Dahhak.

The second: it is the erasing of what is in them of eye, nose, and brow; this meaning is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and is the preference of Ibn Qutayba.

The third: it is turning them back from the path of guidance; this meaning is taken by al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi. Muqatil said: "before We obliterate faces" means: We will turn the religion away from guidance and insight. On this view, the mention of "face" is metaphorical, and what is meant is insight and hearts. On the two views before it, what is meant by "face" is the well-known organ.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then We turn them back upon their backs⦄ (﴿فَنَرُدَّها عَلى أدْبارِها﴾). There are five opinions.

The first: We make them [faces] at the napes, and place their eyes at the napes; this is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAtiyya.

The second: We make them like the napes, having no mouth, no brow, and no eye; this is the view of a group, including Ibn Qutayba.

The third: We make the face a place for hair, like monkeys; this is the view of al-Farra'.

The fourth: We expel them, turning them back from their dwellings and places. Ibn Zayd took a similar view. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning then is: before We obliterate their faces with which they are, and their region in which they are settled, so that We turn them back upon their backs, from the direction from which they came, Badiyya of al-Sham.

The fifth: We return them to misguidance; this is the statement of al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or curse them⦄ (﴿أوْ نَلْعَنَهُمْ﴾). This refers to the owners of the faces. Concerning the meaning of cursing the People of the Sabbath there are two opinions.

The first: He transformed them into apes; this is said by al-Hasan, Qatada, and Muqatil. The second: He drove them out into the wandering (al-tih), so that most of them perished therein; this is mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the command of God is ever accomplished⦄ (﴿وَكانَ أمْرُ اللَّهِ مَفْعُولا﴾). Ibn Jarir said: "the command" here has the meaning of "the commanded thing" (al-ma'mur); it is named by the name of "command" because it came into being from it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 48:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him⟩. Ibn 'Umar said: "When the verse ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins⟩ [az-Zumar: 53] was revealed, they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'And what about shirk?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked that, so this verse was revealed." The meaning of shirk (association of partners with Allah) has already been explained.

The intended meaning of the verse: He does not forgive a polytheist who dies in his polytheism. In His saying, ﴿for whom He wills⟩, there is a great blessing in two respects. The first: it implies that every deceased person who is guilty of a sin other than shirk is not definitively sentenced to punishment, even if he dies persisting in it. The second: making forgiveness conditional on His will is beneficial for the Muslims, in that they remain between fear and hope.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves?﴾ The occasion of its revelation: "Murahhib ibn Zayd and Bahriyy ibn ʿAwn, who were both Jews, came to the Prophet ﷺ with their children, and with them a group of Jews. They said: 'O Muhammad, is there any sin upon these?' He said: 'No.' They said: 'By God, we are no different from them. Whatever sin we commit by day is expiated for us by night, and whatever sin we commit by night is expiated for us by day.' So this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Regarding His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾ there are two opinions. One: "Have you not been informed," said by Ibn Qutaybah. The second: "Do you not know," said by al-Zajjaj. Regarding "those who claim purity for themselves" there are two opinions. One: they are the Jews, as we have mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is what Mujahid, Qatadah and Muqatil said. The second: they are the Jews and the Christians, and this is what al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said. The meaning of "they claim purity for themselves" is: they assume that they are pure. It is said: "zakka al-shay'" when it grows in goodness.

Regarding that by which they claimed purity for themselves there are four opinions.

One: that they absolved themselves of sins, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the Jews said, "Our children who have died will make us pure before God and will intercede for us," narrated by ʿAtiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: the Jews used to put their children forward in prayer to lead them, claiming that they had no sins. This is the statement of ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Abu Malik.

The fourth: the Jews and the Christians said, ﴿We are the sons of God and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and they said, ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. This is the statement of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But God purifies whom He wills﴾, that is, He makes him pure, and God does not wrong anyone by the amount of a fatil. Ibn Jarir said: the root of "fatil" is "maftul" (twisted), transferred from the pattern maf'ul to fa'il, like sarii' (from masru') and dahin (from madhun).

Regarding the fatil there are two opinions. One: that it is what is in the cleft of a date-stone, narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is what Mujahid, ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, ʿAtiyyah, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, Abu ʿUbaydah, Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said. The second: that it is the dirt that comes out between the fingers when they are rubbed, narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is what Said ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik, al-Suddi and al-Farra' said.

Allah's words: ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾, which is their saying ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones﴾, and their saying ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, and their saying: "We have no sin," and similar things in which they lied. ﴿And sufficient is that as a manifest sin﴾: that is, their telling of lies is sufficient for them as a sin ﴿manifest﴾, whose falsehood becomes clear to whoever hears it.

(p-106) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are four reports.

The first: a group of Jews came to Quraysh, and they asked them: "Is our religion better, or the religion of Muhammad?" The Jews said: "Rather, your religion is." So this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Ibn Abbas.

The second: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab came to Makkah, and Quraysh said to them: "Are we better, or Muhammad?" They said: "You are." So this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Ikrimah in one narration. Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning Ka'b, Huyayy, and two other men from Banu al-Nadir who said to Quraysh: "You are more rightly guided than Muhammad."

(p-107) The third: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who is the one who said to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "You are more rightly guided than Muhammad," so this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ikrimah in one narration.

The fourth: Huyayy ibn Akhtab said to the polytheists: "We and you are better than Muhammad," so this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Ibn Zayd. The ones mentioned in this verse are the Jews.

Regarding "al-Jibt" there are seven statements.

The first: it is magic. This was said by Umar ibn al-Khattab, Mujahid, and al-Sha'bi. The second: it is idols; this was narrated by Atiyyah from Ibn Abbas. Ikrimah said: al-Jibt is an idol. The third: it is Huyayy ibn Akhtab; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak and al-Farra' also said it. The fourth: it is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf; this was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and by Layth from Mujahid. The fifth: it is the soothsayer (kahin); this was reported from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Sirin and Makhul also said it. The sixth: it is the Shaytan; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one narration, and by Qatadah and al-Suddi. The seventh: it is the sorcerer; this was said by Abu al-Aliyah and Ibn Zayd. Abu Bishr narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: al-Jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia.

Regarding the meaning of "al-Taghut" here there are six statements.

The first: it is the Shaytan; this was said by Umar ibn al-Khattab, Mujahid in one narration, al-Sha'bi, and Ibn Zayd. The second: it is a name for those who stand before the idols and interpret for them in order to mislead the people; this was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. The third: it is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak and al-Farra' also said it. The fourth: it is the soothsayer; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, and al-Suddi. The fifth: it is the idol; this was said by Ikrimah, who said: al-Jibt and al-Taghut are two idols. The sixth: it is the sorcerer; this was reported from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Sirin, and Makhul. These statements indicate that they are two names for two referents.

The lexicographers, including Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj, said: every object of worship besides Allah, whether a stone, a image, or a devil, is a jibt and a taghut.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say to those who disbelieve﴾ meaning: to the polytheists of Quraysh: "You are more rightly guided ("ahda") than those who believe," meaning the Prophet and his companions, "in the way ("tariqan")" in religion and belief.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verses 52–53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or do they have a share in the kingdom?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is denial, so the implied sense is: they have no share in it. Al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿then they would not give the people a speck (naqir)﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, its sense being: "And if they had a share in it, they would not give the people a speck (naqir)."

Regarding "al-naqir" there are four views.

(p-109) The first: that it is the small pit (nuqta) on the back of the date stone. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba, among others, said the same.

The second: that it is the husk that lies in the middle of the date stone. This was narrated by al-Taymi from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also reported from Mujahid that it is the thread that lies in the middle of the date stone.

The third: that it is the mark a man makes on a thing with the tip of his thumb (naqara al-rajul al-shay' bi-tarafi ibhamihi). This was narrated by Abu al-'Aliya from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that it is the seed (habba) of the date stone which lies in its middle. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

Al-Azhari said: "al-fatil," "al-naqir," and "al-qitmir" are used as proverbs for a thing that is trivial and insignificant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verses 52–53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or do they have a share in the kingdom?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is denial, so the implied sense is: they have no share in it. Al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿then they would not give the people a speck (naqir)﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, its sense being: "And if they had a share in it, they would not give the people a speck (naqir)."

Regarding "al-naqir" there are four views.

(p-109) The first: that it is the small pit (nuqta) on the back of the date stone. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba, among others, said the same.

The second: that it is the husk that lies in the middle of the date stone. This was narrated by al-Taymi from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also reported from Mujahid that it is the thread that lies in the middle of the date stone.

The third: that it is the mark a man makes on a thing with the tip of his thumb (naqara al-rajul al-shay' bi-tarafi ibhamihi). This was narrated by Abu al-'Aliya from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that it is the seed (habba) of the date stone which lies in its middle. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

Al-Azhari said: "al-fatil," "al-naqir," and "al-qitmir" are used as proverbs for a thing that is trivial and insignificant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they envy the people﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the People of the Book said, "Muhammad claims that he has been given what he has been given through humility, yet he has nine wives. So what kingship is greater than this?" So it was revealed. This was narrated by al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-110) Regarding "am" (or), there are two views. The first: it has the meaning of the interrogative alif. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: it has the meaning of "bal" (rather). This was said by al-Zajjaj. The mention of "envy" (hasad) has already passed in (Surat al-Baqarah). The envious ones here are the Jews. Regarding what is meant by "the people" here, there are four views.

The first: the Prophet ﷺ. This was narrated by 'Atiyyah, from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil also said this.

The second: the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, and 'Umar. This was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: the Arabs. This was said by Qatadah. The fourth: the Prophet and the Companions. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding ﴿that which Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ there are three views.

The first: Allah's permission to His Prophet to marry whatever women he wished, without limit in number. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi. The second: that it is prophethood. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and al-Zajjaj. The third: the sending of a prophet from among them, according to the view of those who said that they are the Arabs.

(p-111) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We had already given the family of Ibrahim the Book﴾, meaning: the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms. All of it was among the family of Ibrahim, and this Prophet is among the descendants of Ibrahim. Regarding "wisdom" (al-hikmah) there are two views.

The first: prophethood. This was said by al-Suddi and Muqatil. The second: understanding of the religion (al-fiqh fi al-din). This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding ﴿a great kingdom﴾ there are five views. The first: the kingdom of Sulayman. This was narrated by 'Atiyyah, from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the kingdom of Dawud and Sulayman over women: Dawud had one hundred wives, and Sulayman had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. This was narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi said this too. The third: prophethood, said by Mujahid. The fourth: support through the angels, said by Ibn Zayd among others. The fifth: the combination of governing worldly affairs and the legislation of the religion, mentioned by al-Mawardi.
