Allah's words: ﴿So among them is one who believed in him﴾ — concerning whom the pronoun "hu" (him/it) and the plural "them" refer, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Jews whom our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) warned. This is the view of Mujahid and Muqatil, and al-Farra' along with others.

According to this view, there are three opinions regarding the pronoun in "bihi" (in him).

The first: it refers to what Allah sent down to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Mujahid. Abu Sulayman (al-Khattabi) said: "The speech is then connected to His words ﴿over what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, which is prophethood and the Qur'an."

The second: it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), so it is connected to His words ﴿Or do they envy the people?﴾, meaning by "the people" Muhammad (ﷺ). The intended meaning of His words ﴿So among them is one who believed in him﴾ is Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

The third: it refers to the report about the family of Abraham. This was said by al-Farra'.

The second view is that the pronoun in His words "minhum" (among them) refers to the family of Abraham. According to this, there are two opinions regarding the pronoun in "bihi." The first: it refers to Abraham; this was said by al-Suddi. The second: it refers to the Book; this was said by Muqatil.

Allah's words: ﴿And among them is one who turned away from him﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Ibn Ya'mur and al-Jahdari read "man sadda 'anhu" with the sad vowelled with a damma (ṣaddа, i.e., "ṣadda" in the active form with a raised ṣād). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Jawza', Abu Raja' and al-Jawni read it with a kasra on the ṣād.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 56:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Soon We will drive them into a Fire﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, We will roast them in a fire. It is related that a Jewish woman presented the Prophet ﷺ with a roasted sheep, that is, a "muslayah" (roasted) one. Regarding His saying ﴿We will exchange their skins for other skins﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: they are truly other than the original skins. On this view it need not be asked: how can skins that enjoyed sins be exchanged for skins that did not enjoy them? For the skins are merely an instrument in conveying the punishment to them, just as they were an instrument in conveying pleasure; it is they who are punished, not the skins.

The second: they are the very same skins, restored after they have been burned, just as they are restored after decay in the graves. The otherness then refers to the attribute, not the essence, so the meaning is: We will exchange them for skins that are not burned, as you say: "I fashioned from my ring another ring." Al-Hasan al-Basri said regarding this verse: The Fire consumes them seventy thousand times every day; whenever it has consumed them, it is said to them: "Return," and they return.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 57:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will admit them to shade, deep and extending.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: It is the shade that protects from heat and wind, and not every shade is like that. So God, Exalted is He, informed that the shade of Paradise is deep and extending, with no heat in it nor cold. If it is asked: Is there cold or heat in Paradise, such that they need shade against it? The answer is: No. Rather, He addressed them with what they can comprehend of its like, as in His saying: ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. And another answer: It is an indication of the perfection of its description and the firmness of its structure, for if cold or heat had any power over it, there would be in its buildings and trees a shade that is not deep and extending.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 58:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

(p-114) The first: "When the Prophet ﷺ conquered Makkah, he asked Uthman ibn Abi Talhah for the key of the House (the Ka'bah). Uthman went to give it to him, but al-Abbas said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, combine it for me with the siqayah (the watering duty).' Uthman withheld his hand, fearing that he would give it to al-Abbas. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Bring the key.' Al-Abbas repeated his words, and Uthman withheld his hand. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Show me the key, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day.' He said: 'Take it, O Messenger of Allah, by the trust of Allah.' So he took the key and opened the House. Then Jibril descended with this verse, and he called Uthman and handed it back to him." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid, al-Zuhri, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil also said this.

The second: it was revealed concerning the rulers (al-umara'). This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. Zayd ibn Aslam, his son, Makhul also said this, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi preferred it, saying: "It commanded the rulers to render the trust concerning the wealth of the Muslims."

The third: it was revealed in a general sense. This is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah, and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la preferred it. Know that the revelation of a verse upon a particular occasion does not prevent the generality of its ruling, for it is general in deposits and other trusts. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The trust is in ablution, in prayer, in fasting, and in speech; and the gravest of these is in deposits."

(p-115) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How excellent is what He admonishes you with﴾. He says: how excellent is the thing with which He admonishes you. We have discussed it in (al-Baqarah).

**Translation of the commentary on Qur'an 4:59**

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on His words, ﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾: There are two opinions about the occasion of its revelation.

The first is that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Hudhafa ibn Qays al-Sahmi, when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him on a *sariyya* (a small military detachment). Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-116) The second is that "ʿAmmar ibn Yasir was with Khalid ibn al-Walid in a *sariyya*. The people fled, and a man from among them came to ʿAmmar and said: 'I have embraced Islam. Will it benefit me, or should I go as my people went?' ʿAmmar said: 'Stay, for you are safe.' So the man returned and stayed. Then Khalid came, seized the man, and ʿAmmar said: 'I have granted him protection, and he has embraced Islam.' Khalid said: 'Do you grant protection against me while I am the commander?' They disputed, and they both came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas.

His words, ﴿and obey the Messenger﴾: Obedience to the Messenger during his lifetime is carrying out his commands and avoiding his prohibitions. After his death, it is following his *sunna* (the Prophetic way and practice).

On ﴿those in authority among you﴾ there are four opinions.

The first is that they are the rulers. This was said by Abu Hurayra, by Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration, by Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

(p-117) The second is that they are the scholars. Ibn Abi Talha narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it is the view of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliya, ʿAta', al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Dahhak. Khasif narrated it from Mujahid.

The third is that they are the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Abi Najih narrated it from Mujahid, and Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani also said this.

The fourth is that they are Abu Bakr and ʿUmar. This is the view of Ikrima.

His words, ﴿If you dispute about anything﴾: Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "you differ." And each party says "the saying" (*al-qawl al-qawli*). The derivation of *munaza'a* (dispute) is that each one pulls (*yantazi'u*) the proof toward himself.

His words, ﴿then refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾: There are two opinions on how this referral is to be done.

The first is that referring it to Allah means referring it to His Book, and referring it to the Prophet means referring it to his *sunna*. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatada, and the majority. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this referral may be of two kinds. One is to what is explicitly stated in its wording and meaning. The other is referral to them through indication (*dalala*), and considering it by way of analogy (*qiyas*) and parallels (*nazair*).

The second opinion is that referring it to Allah and His Messenger means that one says, regarding a matter one does not know: "Allah and His Messenger know best." This was mentioned by a group, among them al-Zajjaj.

As for what is meant by *ta'wil* (outcome or interpretation), there are four opinions. The first is that it means recompense and reward, the view of Mujahid and Qatada. The second is that it means the final outcome (*al-'aqiba*), the view of al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj. The third is that it means confirmation (*al-tasdiq*), like His words, ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream﴾ [Yusuf: 100]; Ibn Zayd said this in one narration. The fourth is that its meaning is: your referring it to Allah and His Messenger is better than your own interpretation, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 60:

Allah's words: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they have believed﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning "a man of the hypocrites who had a dispute with a Jew. The Jew said, 'Let us go to Muhammad,' and the hypocrite said, 'Rather, let us go to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf.' The Jew refused, so they both came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he ruled in favor of the Jew. When they left, the hypocrite said, 'Let us go to Umar ibn al-Khattab.' So they came to him and related the matter to him. He said, 'Wait until I come out to you both.' He entered the house, took up his sword, then came out and struck the hypocrite with it until he cooled, and said, 'This is how I judge between whoever does not accept the judgment of Allah and His Messenger.' Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

The second: Abu Burda al-Aslami was a soothsayer (kahin) who judged between the Jews, and some Muslims went to him for arbitration, so this verse was revealed. Narrated by Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas.

The third: a Jew and a hypocrite had a dispute between them. The Jew called the hypocrite to the Prophet (ﷺ), because he does not take bribes, and the hypocrite called him to their judges, because they take bribes. When they disagreed, they agreed to appoint a soothsayer as arbiter, and this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Sha'bi.

The fourth: a man from Banu al-Nadir killed a man from Banu Qurayzah, and they disputed. The hypocrites among them said, "Go to Abu Burda the soothsayer." The Muslims from both groups said, "Rather, to the Prophet (ﷺ)." The hypocrites refused and went to the soothsayer, and this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Suddi.

Al-za'm and al-zu'm are two dialectal forms, and they are used most often for a statement whose truth is not verified. As for Allah's words ﴿who claim that they have believed in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you﴾, there are two views. One is that it refers to the hypocrite. The second is that the one who claimed to believe in what was revealed to you is the hypocrite, and the one who claimed to believe in what was revealed before you is the Jew. Al-taghut: it is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, as stated by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' and Muqatil.

Allah's words: ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾. Muqatil said: to disavow the soothsayers. And "al-dalal al-ba'id" (far-off error): the lengthy one.

Allah's words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down"﴾. Mujahid said: this verse and the one before it were revealed concerning a dispute between a Jew and a hypocrite. The ha' and the mim in "lahum" (to them) refer to those who claim [to believe]. "What Allah has sent down" means the rulings of the Qur'an. "And to the Messenger" means: to his judgment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So how [will it be] when a disaster befalls them﴾ — that is: how will they devise and scheme when a punishment from Allah befalls them? Concerning what is meant by "disaster" there are two opinions. One: it is a threat and a warning. The second: it is the killing of the hypocrite whom ʿUmar killed. Concerning ﴿that which their hands have sent ahead﴾ there are three opinions. The first: their hypocrisy and their mockery. The second: their rejection of the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ). The third: their earlier sins.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We intended only good and reconciliation﴾ — with the meaning: "We intended nothing but."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except good and reconciliation﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: when ʿUmar killed their companion, they came seeking retribution for his blood, swearing that they intended by demanding his blood nothing but good toward us, and what agrees with the truth in our affair.

The second: "We intended by seeking judgment from ʿUmar nothing but good and reconciliation."

The third: they came apologizing to the Prophet (ﷺ) for having taken their dispute to someone other than him, saying: "In our turning away from you we intended nothing but good, by bringing closer the judgment, and reconciliation between the litigants, without imposing the bitter truth."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾, meaning: of hypocrisy and deviation.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: their concealing what is contrary to what they say. ﴿So turn away from them﴾, and do not punish them, ﴿and admonish them﴾ with your tongue, ﴿and say to them in themselves a far-reaching word﴾, meaning: set forth to them, "If you do the second [offence], I will punish you."

Al-Zajjaj said: one says, "The man became eloquent (balagha, balaghah), so he is eloquent (baligh)" when he conveys with the expression of his tongue the full reality of what is in his heart.

The scholars have spoken about the definition of "eloquence" (al-balaghah). Some of them said: "Eloquence" is conveying the meaning to the heart in the best form of wording. It was also said: "Eloquence" is the goodness of expression together with the soundness of the meaning. And it was said: "Eloquence" is brevity together with clear comprehension, and fluency without wearying the listener.

Khalid ibn Safwan said: The best speech is that whose words are few and whose meanings are many, and the best speech is that whose beginning makes one eager to hear its end. Another said: Speech only deserves the name of eloquence when its wording outpaces its meaning and its meaning outpaces its wording, and its wording does not reach your hearing before its meaning reaches your heart.

Section

Some people have held that the "turning away" mentioned in this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Translation of the passage:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed﴾. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said: "man" (مَن) is inserted for emphasis (li-l-tawkid). The meaning is: "And We did not send a messenger except to be obeyed."

Regarding His words ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾ there are two views. The first is that it means "the command," as said by Ibn Abbas. The second is that it means the permission itself, as said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "except to be obeyed," in that Allah has permitted him to do so.

(p-123) His words, the Most High: ﴿And if they, when they had wronged themselves, had come to you﴾ refer to the two litigants whose mention preceded. Ibn Abbas said: "They wronged themselves by their displeasure at the Messenger's judgment" ﴿came to you and asked Allah's forgiveness﴾ for their conduct.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 65:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe﴾ — regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: it was revealed concerning a dispute between al-Zubayr and a man from the Ansar over the water channels of al-Harrah. The Prophet ﷺ said to al-Zubayr: "Irrigate [your land], then release the water to your neighbour." The Ansari became angry and said: "O Messenger of Allah, [did you say this] because he is the son of your paternal aunt?" The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed colour, and then he said to al-Zubayr: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the walls [of the field]." Al-Zubayr said: "By Allah, I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning that." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The second: it was revealed concerning the hypocrite and the Jew who took their dispute to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, whose story has already passed. This was said by Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe﴾ — meaning: they will not be believers until they make you the judge. It has also been said that "la" (no) is a rejection of their claim that they are believers, and the meaning is: "fa-la" — that is, the matter is not as they claim, that they have believed, while they oppose your judgement. Then he began a new statement, saying: "By your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves," i.e., in what they differ about.

Regarding "al-haraj" (constriction, discomfort in the heart) there are two views. The first: it is doubt; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. The second: it is narrowness (constriction); this was said by Abu Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His saying, ﴿and submit in full submission﴾, there are two views. The first: they submit to what you have commanded them, so they do not oppose you; this is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Zajjaj, and the majority. The second: they submit what they dispute to your judgement; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

**His saying, Exalted is He:** ﴿And if We had prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves," ...﴾

**Occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul):** A man from the Jews said, "By Allah, Allah had prescribed for us, 'Kill yourselves,' so we killed ourselves." Thabit ibn Qays ibn al-Shammas said, "By Allah, if Allah had prescribed that for us, we would have done it." Then this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Suddi.

Al-Zajjaj said: *law* (لَوْ) is used to show that one thing is prevented by the prevention of another. You say, "If Zayd had come to me, I would have come to him." The meaning is that your coming was prevented because his coming was prevented. *Kataba* (كَتَبْنا) here means *faradna* (فَرَضْنا), "We imposed." The meaning is: "If We had imposed upon the believers, for your sake, 'Kill yourselves.'"

Abu 'Amr read *an-iqtulu anfusakum* (أنِ اقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم) with a kasra on the *nun*, and *awi-khrujuu* (أوِ اخْرُجُوا) with a damma on the *waw*. Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i read *an-iqtulu aw-khrujuu* (أنِ اقْتُلُوا أوِ اخْرُجُوا) with a damma on the *nun* and the *waw*. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with a kasra. The meaning is: "If We had imposed upon them, as We imposed upon the people of Musa, ..., none would have done it except a few of them." This is the reading of the majority. Ibn 'Amir read *illa qaliláan* (إلّا قَلِيلًا) in the accusative (naṣb).

**"And if they":** meaning the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), who claim that they have believed, yet they seek judgment from the *Taghut* (false deities or idols) and turn people away from you. ﴿They had done what they were admonished﴾ with it, that is, what they were reminded of concerning obedience to Allah and adherence to His command, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ and firmer for their affairs. Al-Suddi said: ﴿and firmer in steadfastness﴾ means firmer in affirmation (tasdiq).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 69–70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

(p-126) The first: "Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, was intensely devoted to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One day the Messenger of Allah saw him and recognized the sadness in his face, so he said: 'O Thawban, why has your face changed?' He said: 'I have no ailment, except that when I do not see you, I long for you, and I remember the Hereafter, and I fear that I will not see you there. So this verse was revealed.'" This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "It is not fitting for us to be separated from you in this world, for if you are separated from us, you will be raised above us." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Masruq.

The third: "A man from the Ansar came to the Prophet while he was sad, and said: 'Why do I see you sad?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tomorrow you will be raised with the Prophets, and we will not reach you.' So this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever obeys Allah" in the obligatory duties, "and the Messenger" in the Sunnah.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Siddiq" means one who is very truthful, just as it is said: fisseeq (a great transgressor), sikkir (a great drunkard), shirrib (a great drinker), khimmir (a great consumer of intoxicants), sikkit (one who is very silent), fijjir (a great libertine), ishshiq (one who loves excessively), (p-127) dalil (one who is very misguided), and zalim (a great oppressor), when that quality is abundant in him. This is not said of one who did the thing once or twice, until it becomes abundant in him or becomes a habit. As for "shuhada'" (martyrs), it is the plural of "shahid," which is the one slain in the way of Allah.

Regarding his being named "shahid," there are five opinions. The first: because Allah, the Exalted, and His angels bear witness to him for Paradise; this was said by Tha'lab. The second: because the angels of mercy witness him. The third: because he falls to the earth, and the earth is the witness; Ibn Faris the linguist mentioned both of these opinions. The fourth: because he upholds the testimony of truth in the matter of Allah until he is killed; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The fifth: because he witnesses what Allah has prepared for him of honor by being killed; this was said by our shaykh Ali ibn Ubayd Allah.

As for "salihun" (the righteous), they are the designation for everyone whose inner state and outward conduct are sound. The majority hold that the Prophets, the truthful (siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous are general terms covering all who possess this description.

(p-128) Ikrimah said: What is meant here by the Prophets is Muhammad, by the truthful is Abu Bakr, by the martyrs are Umar, Uthman, and Ali, and by the righteous are the rest of the Companions.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "rafiqan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it stands in place of "rufaqa'" (companions). A poet said:

Therein are the carcasses of the exhausted camels; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skins, they are hard.

Another said:

In your throats is a bone, and we have choked on it; he means: in your throats are bones.

﴿That is the bounty﴾ which was granted to those mentioned ﴿from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾ of the intentions and inner purposes.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 69–70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

(p-126) The first: "Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, was intensely devoted to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One day the Messenger of Allah saw him and recognized the sadness in his face, so he said: 'O Thawban, why has your face changed?' He said: 'I have no ailment, except that when I do not see you, I long for you, and I remember the Hereafter, and I fear that I will not see you there. So this verse was revealed.'" This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "It is not fitting for us to be separated from you in this world, for if you are separated from us, you will be raised above us." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Masruq.

The third: "A man from the Ansar came to the Prophet while he was sad, and said: 'Why do I see you sad?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tomorrow you will be raised with the Prophets, and we will not reach you.' So this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever obeys Allah" in the obligatory duties, "and the Messenger" in the Sunnah.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Siddiq" means one who is very truthful, just as it is said: fisseeq (a great transgressor), sikkir (a great drunkard), shirrib (a great drinker), khimmir (a great consumer of intoxicants), sikkit (one who is very silent), fijjir (a great libertine), ishshiq (one who loves excessively), (p-127) dalil (one who is very misguided), and zalim (a great oppressor), when that quality is abundant in him. This is not said of one who did the thing once or twice, until it becomes abundant in him or becomes a habit. As for "shuhada'" (martyrs), it is the plural of "shahid," which is the one slain in the way of Allah.

Regarding his being named "shahid," there are five opinions. The first: because Allah, the Exalted, and His angels bear witness to him for Paradise; this was said by Tha'lab. The second: because the angels of mercy witness him. The third: because he falls to the earth, and the earth is the witness; Ibn Faris the linguist mentioned both of these opinions. The fourth: because he upholds the testimony of truth in the matter of Allah until he is killed; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The fifth: because he witnesses what Allah has prepared for him of honor by being killed; this was said by our shaykh Ali ibn Ubayd Allah.

As for "salihun" (the righteous), they are the designation for everyone whose inner state and outward conduct are sound. The majority hold that the Prophets, the truthful (siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous are general terms covering all who possess this description.

(p-128) Ikrimah said: What is meant here by the Prophets is Muhammad, by the truthful is Abu Bakr, by the martyrs are Umar, Uthman, and Ali, and by the righteous are the rest of the Companions.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "rafiqan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it stands in place of "rufaqa'" (companions). A poet said:

Therein are the carcasses of the exhausted camels; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skins, they are hard.

Another said:

In your throats is a bone, and we have choked on it; he means: in your throats are bones.

﴿That is the bounty﴾ which was granted to those mentioned ﴿from Allah, and sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾ of the intentions and inner purposes.

(p-129) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Take your precaution﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first is: be wary of your enemy.

The second is: take up your weapons.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿then go forth in groups﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: That is, in companies (jamaʿat), the singular of which is thubah. He means a group after a group. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-thabat" means separate companies.

Zuhayr said:

؎ We have set out in the morning with a troop of noble men, drunk, able to do whatever we wish.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿then go forth in groups﴾, that is, in bands (ʿusaban), detachments (sarayā) dispersed. ﴿Or go forth all together﴾, meaning all of you together.

Section

It has been transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that this verse, along with His saying ﴿Go forth, light or heavy﴾ [al-Tawba: 41] (p-130) and His saying ﴿Unless you go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawba: 39], are abrogated (naskh, meaning abrogation) by His saying ﴿And the believers should not go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 122]. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The ruling in this matter depends on what the imam (ruler) sees fit, and there is nothing abrogated in this regard.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verses 72–73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, among you is one who will surely lag behind﴾. The scholars differed over who this verse was revealed about, giving two views.

The first: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who used to drag their feet regarding jihad. If the expedition (sariyyah) suffered a misfortune, the one among them who had lagged behind would say, "Allah has blessed me, since I was not with them." And if they gained booty, he would say, "Would that I had been with them!" This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: It was revealed concerning the Muslims whose knowledge of the rulings of the religion was limited, so they hesitated (tathabbuta) due to their scant knowledge, not due to weakness of faith. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and others. According to the first view, their attribution to the believers with the words "among you" (minkum) is based on the fact that they pronounced Islam and its rulings applied to them. According to the second view, the attribution is literal. Ibn Jarir said: the lam in "liman" (la-man) is a lam of emphasis.

Al-Zajjaj said: The lam in "layubatti'anna" (la-yubatti'anna) is the lam of oath, as in your saying: "Indeed among you is one who swears by Allah that he will surely lag behind." It is said: "abta'a al-rajul" and "bata'a," where the meaning of "abta'a" is "delayed," and the meaning of "bata'a" is "was heavy (slow)." Abu Jaʿfar recited "layubatti'anna" with the hamzah lightened. Regarding the meaning of "layubatti'anna" there are two views: the first is that he himself will lag behind, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas; the second is that he will cause others to lag behind, said by Ibn Jurayj. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-musibah" means the misfortune, and "al-fadl min Allah" means conquest and booty.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿as though there had never been between you and him any affection﴾. Ibn Kathir, Hafs, and al-Mufaddal, from ʿAsim, read "ka-an lam takun" with the ta', because the subject it is attributed to is feminine in form. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "yakun" with the ya', because the feminine marker is not real (ḥaqiqi). Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is: "He will surely say, 'Would that I had been with them,' as though there had never been between you and him any affection," i.e., as though he had not made a pact with you to fight alongside you. It is also possible that this statement is a parenthetical insertion, so the meaning is: "And if a bounty from Allah befalls you, he will surely say, 'Would that I had been with them!' But if a misfortune befalls you, he says, 'Allah has blessed me,' as though there had never been between you and him any affection." In that case, "mawaddah" means: as though he had not made a pact with you regarding faith.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 74:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who sell the life of this world﴾. Here "yashrūna" (sell) means "yabtaghūna" (seek), according to the consensus of the scholars. They recited the verse of poetry:

"And I bought a cloak—would that I had been a bird of death after a cloak!"

"Burd" here is a slave boy whom he sold. The meaning of the verse is: let the fighting of the fighters be sincerely for the sake of God, seeking the Hereafter.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then he is killed or he is victorious﴾. This came out in the manner of what is usual (the likely outcome), and one who was neither victorious nor killed may also be rewarded.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 75:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the oppressed men﴾. Al-Farra' said: its implied sense is "and in (the cause of) the oppressed." This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-mustad'afun" (the oppressed) is in the genitive position, and the meaning is "in the way of Allah and the way of the oppressed," i.e., "What is the matter with you that you do not strive for the deliverance of these people?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "They were Muslim people who were in Makkah and could not emigrate." And "al-qaryah" (the town) is Makkah according to the consensus of the scholars. Al-Farra' said: "al-zalim" (the oppressive) was put in the genitive because it is a qualifier of "ahl" (its people). When "ahl" returned to "qaryah," the action of what was attributed to it took the place of its own action. You say: "I passed by the man whose house is spacious" (مَرَرْتُ بِالرَّجُلِ الواسِعَةِ دارُهُ).

(p-١٣٣) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a protector﴾. Abu Sulayman said: they asked Allah for a protector from Him who would take charge of bringing them out of it, and a helper who would prevent them from the polytheists. Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, Allah, mighty and majestic, made the Prophet, peace be upon him, their protector, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd over them, and he was a helper to them, giving the weak his due from the strong.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 76:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut﴾. Al-Taghut here means: Satan.

Abu 'Ubayda said: Al-Taghut here is in the sense of a group (jama'ah), like His saying, "and the flesh of the swine" (lahm al-khinzir), meaning: the flesh of swine (lahm al-khanazir).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan is ever weak﴾. He means: his scheming and his handiwork [are weak], (kana da'ifan) in that he forsook his companions on the Day of Badr.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 77:

(p-134) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered those who were told, "Restrain your hands"﴾ — the scholars differed regarding who it was revealed about, giving two opinions.

The first: It was revealed concerning a group of the Emigrants (muhajirun) who used to love to be permitted to fight the polytheists while they were in Mecca, before fighting was made obligatory. So they were forbidden from that. When permission was granted to them, some of them disliked it. This meaning was related by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and it is the view of Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

The second: It was revealed describing the conditions of a people who lived in earlier times, warning this Ummah against being like them. This meaning was related by Atiyyah, from Ibn Abbas. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: It seems to allude to the story of those who said, "Send us a king." Mujahid said: It concerns the Jews.

As for "restraining the hand," what is meant by it is refraining from fighting; that was in Mecca, and "was prescribed" (kataba) in the sense of "was made obligatory," and that was in Medina. This is according to the first opinion.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then when a party of them﴾ — regarding this party there are three opinions.

The first: They are the hypocrites (munafiqun). The second: They were believers, but when fighting was made obligatory, they became hypocrites out of cowardice and fear. The third: They were believers, but their natures overcame them, so their souls recoiled (p-135) from fighting.

His saying ﴿fear men﴾ — regarding what is meant by "men" there are two views. The first: the disbelievers of Mecca. The second: all the disbelievers.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or with even greater fear﴾ — it was said: "aw" here means "wa" (and), and "kutibat" means "furidat" (was prescribed). And "lawla" means "halla" (why not). Al-Farra' said: When you do not see a noun after it, it is interrogative, in the sense of "halla"; and when you see a nominative noun after it, it is the one whose answer is the lam, as you say: "Lawla Abdullah, la-darabtuka" (Were it not for Abdullah, I would have struck you). Ibn Qutaybah said: When you see it without an answer, it means "halla," as you say: "Lawla fa'alta kadhā" (Why did you not do such-and-such?), and similar to it is "lawla"; but when you see an answer following "lawla," it does not mean "halla"; rather it is the one used for a matter that occurs upon the occurrence of something else, as in His saying, ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah﴾ ﴿he would have remained in its belly﴾ [al-Saffat: 143]. I say: As for "lawla" with an answer, it is frequent in speech, and they recited in this regard:

Had it not been for modesty, and that my head has been overtaken by greyness, I would have visited Umm al-Qasim.

As for the "lawla" meaning "halla," they recited from it:

You count the slaughter of camels as the best of your glory, O sons of Dawtara — why not (hallaa) the armored warrior?

He meant: "Why do you not prepare the armored warrior?" The "kammi" is one who is clad in weapons.

Regarding "the near term" there are two opinions.

The first: It is death, as if they had said: "Why did You not leave us to die a natural death and spare us from being killed?" This is the view of al-Suddi and Muqatil.

The second: It is a delay of time, as if they had said: "Why did You not postpone the obligation of jihad from us a little, until we become numerous and strong?" This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little"﴾ — meaning: the duration of life in it is short.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you will not be wronged even a thread﴾ — Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "yazlamun" with the ya'. Nafi', Abu Amr, and Asim read it with the ta'. The mention of "enjoyment" (mata') and "thread" (fatil) has already passed.

(p-137) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that the hypocrites said concerning the martyrs of Uhud: "If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed." So this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. *Al-burūj* (the fortresses) means the strongholds, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding *al-mushayyadah* (the fortified or lofty), there are five opinions.

The first is that it means the strongly fortified, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The second is that it means the elaborately built, as said by Abu Malik, Muqatil, and Ibn Qutaybah. The third is that it means plastered, as said by Hilal ibn Khabbab and al-Yazidi. The fourth is that it means built with *al-shayd*, which is gypsum (*al-jiss*), as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The fifth is that it means towers in the sky, as said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Thawri. Al-Suddi said: they are white palaces built in the sky.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if a good befalls them﴾. The scholars differed about who "them" refers to, in three opinions. The first is that they are the hypocrites and the Jews, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that they are the hypocrites, as said by al-Hasan. The third is that they are the Jews, as said by Ibn al-Sirri.

Concerning *al-ḥasanah* (the good) and *al-sayyi'ah* (the evil), there are two opinions.

The first is that *al-ḥasanah* is fertility and rain, and *al-sayyi'ah* is drought and high prices. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-138) The second is that *al-ḥasanah* is conquest and booty, and *al-sayyi'ah* is defeat and wounds, and the like. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From you﴾ (*min 'indika*), there are two opinions. The first is: "because of your ill omen," as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is: "because of your poor management," as said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: All is from Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: the good and the evil. As for the good, He bestowed it upon you, and as for the evil, He tested you with it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So what is wrong with these people﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i paused (*waqf*, a pause at the end of a word in recitation) on the alif of *fa-mā* in His saying: ﴿fa-mā li-hā'ulā'i al-qawmi﴾, ﴿mā li-hādha al-kitābi﴾, ﴿mā li-hādha al-rasūli﴾, and ﴿fa-mā li-alladhīna kafarū﴾. The rest paused on the lām (*al-lām*, the letter lām in these words). As for *al-ḥadīth* (the statement or speech) here, it is said that it means the Qur'an, as if He said: they do not comprehend the Qur'an so that they would believe in it and know that all is from Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 79:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾. Regarding the one addressed by this statement there are three opinions. The first: it is general, so its implied meaning is: whatever befalls you, O human being. This is what Qatadah said. The second: it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended meaning is someone other than him. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Whatever good befalls you, Allah has brought it; and whatever evil befalls you, it is by what Allah has caused," so both verbs refer back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Regarding "good" (hasanah) and "evil" (sayyi'ah) there are three opinions. The first: the good is what He granted him on the Day of Badr, and the evil is what befell him on the Day of Uhud. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. The second: the good is obedience, and the evil is disobedience. This was said by Abu al-Aliyah. (p-139) The third: the good is blessing, and the evil is affliction. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah, and something similar is narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, and it is the most sound, because the verse is general. Kurdab narrated from Ya'qub: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah﴾ with the nun doubled, the mim in the accusative, and the name "Allah" in the genitive, ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ with the mim in the accusative and the sin in the nominative.

Ibn Abbas recited: ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ with the mim in the accusative and the sin in the nominative.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from yourself﴾ means: due to your sin. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and the majority. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned another possibility regarding it, saying: the meaning is "Is it from yourself?", so the interrogative alif has been elided, as it is elided in His saying ﴿and this is a favour﴾, meaning: "or is this a favour?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the mention of the Messenger emphasizes His saying "We have sent you," and the ba' in "with Allah" is emphatic. The meaning is: "and Allah suffices as a witness."

(p-140) "Witness" (shahidan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification), because when you say "Allah suffices," without stating in what respect the sufficiency lies, you are left vague.

Regarding the intended meaning of Allah's witnessing here, there are three opinions. The first: He is a witness for you that you are His messenger. This was said by Muqatil. The second: He is a witness against their statement. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The third: He is a witness for you regarding the conveyance, and against them regarding their denial and hypocrisy. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. If it is said: how did Allah censure these people when they said that good is from Allah and evil is from the Prophet, peace be upon him, and He answered them with His saying: ﴿Say: all is from Allah﴾, then returned and said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾? Did the people say anything other than this? There are two answers to this.

One: they attributed the evil to the Prophet ﷺ out of pessimism regarding him, so He answered them, saying: all is by Allah's decree. Then He said: whatever good befalls you is from Allah, meaning from His bounty, and whatever evil befalls you is due to your sin, even though all is from Allah by decree.

The second: a group of scholars of meanings said: there is an elided, implied element in the speech, its implied meaning being: "What is wrong with these people that they hardly understand any statement? They say: whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself," so this is from their own saying. Elision in the Qur'an is abundant, and among it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], meaning: they say, "Our Lord." Similar is ﴿or has an injury to his head, then a ransom﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], meaning: "then he shaves, then a ransom." Similar is ﴿As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said:] Did you disbelieve?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106], meaning: "it will be said to them." Similar is ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying:] "Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24], meaning: they say, "Peace." Similar is ﴿Or if the dead were made to speak by it, [it would be this Qur'an]﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], meaning: "this Qur'an would be the one." Similar is ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Nur: 20] (p-141), meaning: "He would have punished you." Similar is ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12], meaning: they say. Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"Indeed, whoever fears death, it will find him wherever he goes,"

meaning: wherever he went. Another said:

"I swear, if any thing had come to us from His messenger other than you, but we did not find for you a means of repelling it,"

meaning: "we would have repelled it."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever loves me has loved Allah.' The hypocrites said: 'This man has come close to associating partners with Allah.' So this verse was revealed," as related by Muqatil. The meaning of the statement: whoever accepts what the Messenger brought, has indeed accepted what Allah commanded; and whoever turns away, i.e., (p-142) turns aside from his obedience. In "al-Hafiz" there are two opinions. One is that it means the Watcher (al-Raqib), related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that it means the Reckoner (al-Muhasib), related from al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah.

Section

The exegetes said: this was before the command to fight, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 81:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They say, "Obedience."﴾ It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who would profess faith in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that they would be safe. When they went out, they opposed him. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Farra' said: The nominative in "ṭā'ah" (obedience) is according to the meaning: "Your command is obedience."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A group of them plotted﴾. Abu 'Amr and Hamza read "bayyata" with the "tā'" (ت) silent and assimilated into the "ṭā'" (ط). The rest read the "tā'" with a fatḥah (نَصَبَ). Abu 'Ali said: the tā', the ṭā' and the dāl are from the same articulatory region (ḥayyiz), so assimilation is good. As for "min bayn" (from among), it is because the two letters are separated and their points of articulation differ. Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning is: ﴿When they go out from your presence﴾, i.e., they went out. ﴿A group of them plotted something other than what you say﴾, i.e., they said and planned at night something other than what they had given you in the day. The poet said:

"They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they devised,
and they had come to me with a hideous matter."

The Arabs say: "This is a matter that has been decided at night," and "it was finished at night." From this is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

"They resolved their affair in the evening, but when
they rose in the morning, a clamour was theirs."

Some of them said: "bayyata" means "baddala" (to change), and they recited:

"And he changed my word before the Sovereign;
may Allah fight you, O ungrateful servant."

Regarding his saying ﴿other than what you say﴾, there are two views.

The first: "other than what the group before you says," and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Qutayba. The second: "other than what you say, O Muhammad," and this is the view of Qatada and al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But Allah records what they plot﴾. There are three views concerning it. The first: He records it in the deeds that the angels write down; this was said by Muqatil and others. The second: He sends it down to you in His Book. The third: He preserves it for them so that they may be recompensed for it; al-Zajjaj mentioned both views.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "So turn away from them": do not punish them, trust in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Allah suffices as a trustee for you. He said: Then this turning away was abrogated (nusikha), and he was commanded to fight them.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in His beginning with mention of them collectively, and then saying ﴿a group of them﴾, while they are all hypocrites? The answer is in two respects, which the people of tafsir mentioned.

The first: He informed about those among them who stayed awake at night and planned their affair, to the exclusion of the others. The second: He mentioned those whom He knew would remain upon their hypocrisy, rather than those whom He knew would return.

(p-144) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Tadabbur" (reflection) is looking into the outcome (ʿāqibah) of a thing. And "al-dabr" is the bee, so called "dabr" because it follows up (yuʿaqqibu) what it benefits from. And "al-dubr" is abundant wealth, so called "dubr" because of its abundance, since it remains for the descendants (al-aʿqāb) and the successors (al-adbār).

Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an﴾, so that they contemplate it, and see that some of it confirms other parts, and that none of creation is able to produce its like. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Al-Qur'an" derives from your saying: "The she-camel never cast (qarat) a fetus (sallan) at all," meaning she never gathered a young one in her womb. Abu ʿUbaydah recited:

"Hijan of color, she never gathered (taqraʾ) a fetus..."

It was called "Qur'an" because it gathers (jamaʿa) the surahs and combines them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: that it is contradiction (al-tanaqud). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Zayd, and the majority.

The second: (p-145) falsehood (al-kadhib). This was said by Muqatil and al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it is discrepancy in which the level of eloquence varies, between eloquent speech and inferior speech, since speech that is long must inevitably contain some inferior parts, whereas the Qur'an contains only eloquent speech. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi, along with a group of others.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 83:

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two reports.

The first: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) withdrew from his wives, Umar entered the mosque and heard the people saying, 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) has divorced his wives.' So he entered upon the Prophet, peace be upon him, and asked him, 'Have you divorced your wives?' He said, 'No.' So he went out and called out: 'Truly, the Messenger of God has not divorced his wives.' Then this verse was revealed. He was the one who deduced the matter (istinbat, 'drawing out' or 'deriving' a ruling from a text)." Muslim alone narrated it, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, from Umar.

The second: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent out a military expedition (sariyyah) and it either succeeded or was defeated, they would talk about it and spread it, and would not wait until the Prophet himself was the one to speak of it. Then this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Regarding those referred to by this verse, there are two views. The first: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). This is the view of Ibn Abbas and the majority. The second: they are the people of hypocrisy and the weak among the Muslims. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the meaning of "security" (al-amn) there are four views.

The first: the success of the expedition in gaining victory and booty. This is the view of the majority.

The second: that it is the news that comes to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he has prevailed over a people, so that he feels secure from them. This was stated by al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it is what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) resolves upon regarding truce and safe-conduct for a people. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The fourth: that it is security that comes from a place of safety (ma'man), which is Medina. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, citing it from the hadith of Umar.

Regarding "fear" (al-khawf) there are three views.

The first: that it is the setback that befalls the expedition. This was mentioned by a group of exegetes.

The second: that it is the news that comes that a people are gathering against the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he fears them. This was stated by al-Zajjaj.

The third: what the Prophet resolves upon regarding war and fighting. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿they spread it﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: they circulated it. Ibn Jarir said: the pronoun in "it" refers back to the matter.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿But if they had referred it﴾, meaning the matter, ﴿to the Messenger﴾, so that he would be the one to inform them of it, ﴿and to those of authority among them﴾. Concerning them there are four views.

The first: that they are like Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. This was stated by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that they are Abu Bakr and Umar. This was stated by Ikrima.

The third: that they are the scholars. This was stated by al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Juraij.

The fourth: that they are the commanders of the expeditions. This was stated by Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

Regarding ﴿those who seek to draw it out﴾ there are two views.

The first: that they are those who follow it up among the ones who spread it. This was stated by Mujahid.

The second: that they are those of authority. This was stated by Ibn Zayd. "Istinbat" (drawing out) in the language means extraction. Al-Zajjaj said: its origin is from the Nabat, which is the water that comes out of a well when it is first dug. It is said of this: "So-and-so struck water (anbata) in Ghadra'," meaning he extracted water from soft clay. The Nabat were so named because of their extracting (istinbat) what comes out of the earth.

Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of the verse is: when there comes to them news of an expedition of the Muslims, of good or of ill, they spread it. Had they remained silent until the Messenger and those of authority took charge of the report about it, then they would have confirmed it if it was true, or nullified it if it was false, since those among the people of authority who investigate it would know its reality.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And were it not for the grace of God upon you﴾.

Regarding the meaning of "grace" (al-fadl) there are four views: the first, that it is the Messenger of God; the second, that it is Islam; the third, that it is the Qur'an; the fourth, that it is those of authority.

Regarding "mercy" (al-rahmah) there are four views: the first, that it is revelation; the second, gentleness (al-lutf); the third, blessing (al-ni'mah); the fourth, divine success (al-tawfiq).

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾. Regarding the meaning of this exception there are three views.

The first: that it refers back to the spreading. Its sense is: "They spread it, except a few." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, and was chosen by al-Farra' and Ibn Jarir.

The second: that it refers back to those who draw it out. Its sense is: "Those among them who draw it out know it, except a few." This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatada, and was chosen by Ibn Qutayba. According to these two views, there is an inversion of order (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse.

The third: that it refers back to following Satan. Its sense is: "You would have followed Satan, except a few of you." This is the view of al-Dahhak and was chosen by al-Zajjaj. Some scholars said: the meaning is: Had it not been for God's grace in sending the Prophet to you, you would have gone astray, except for a few of you who would correct themselves by their intellects, recognizing God and recognizing the error of one who worships other than Him, such as Qass ibn Sa'ida.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 84:

The words of His, the Exalted: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "The Prophet (ﷺ), when he called the people to the appointment with Abu Sufyan at Badr al-Sughra after Uhud, some of them disliked that, so this verse was revealed" (p-149). Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Regarding the "fa" in "fa-qatala" there are two opinions.

One of them: it is the response to His words, ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or conquers﴾.

The second: it is connected to His words, ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ Ibn al-Sarri mentioned both. "The way of Allah" means jihad.

The words of His, the Exalted: ﴿You are not held responsible except for yourself﴾, i.e., except for striving with your own self. "Harrid" means "hadderd" (urge on, incite). Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "'asa" (perhaps) in the language is the sense of hope and apprehension, and the granting of hope from Allah is obligatory. And "al-ba's" means severity. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And Allah is stronger in punishment." Qatadah said: "al-tankil" means punishment.

(p-150) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession﴾. Regarding the meaning of "intercession" there are four opinions.

The first: it is a person's intercession on behalf of another person, to bring him some benefit or to deliver him from some affliction. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. The second: it is reconciling between two people, as said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The third: it is supplication for the believing men and believing women, as mentioned by al-Mawardi. The fourth: the meaning is, "Whoever becomes an intercessor (shaf') for the single ones (witr) of your companions, O Muhammad, so that he intercedes for them in the jihad against their enemy and their fighting in the way of Allah," as said by Ibn Jarir and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding the evil intercession there are three opinions.

The first: it is spreading tale-bearing (al-namimah), as said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The second: it is supplication against the believing men and believing women, which the Jews used to do, as mentioned by al-Mawardi. The third: the meaning is, "Whoever intercedes for the single ones (witr) of the people of disbelief, so that he fights the believers," as said by Ibn Jarir and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-kifl" in the language means a share, and it is derived from their saying: iktafala al-ba'ir, when you place something over its hump, or over the place of a back that has a cloth on it, and ride upon it. It was called "kifl" because it does not use the whole back, but uses only a portion of it.

Regarding "al-muqit" there are seven opinions.

The first: that it means the one who has power (al-muqtadir). Uhayhah ibn al-Jullah said:

Wa dhi dhaghinin kafaftu al-nafsa 'anhu / wa kuntu 'ala masa'atihi muqitan
(And one harboring rancor, whom I restrained myself from, / and I was, despite his displeasure, one with power over him.)

To this meaning went Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jarir, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Khattabi.

The second: that it means the Preserver (al-hafiz). This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah and al-Zajjaj said the same. He said: "It is closer to 'the preserver,' because it is derived from al-qut, as one says: qatta al-rajulu yaqutuhu qutan, when his soul is preserved by that which sustains him. And al-qut is the name of the thing that preserves one's soul [and there is no surplus in it beyond the measure of preservation]; so the meaning of al-muqit is the preserver who gives a thing according to the measure of need for preservation." The poet said:

Ali al-fadlu am 'alayya idha huw / sibtu anni 'ala al-hisabi muqitu
(Is the favor mine, or upon me, when I am reckoned / that I am, by reckoning, one who provides sustenance?)

The third: that it means the Witness (al-shahid). This was narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi chose it. The fourth: that it means the Reckoner (al-hasib). This was narrated by Khasif from Mujahid. The fifth: the Watchful (al-raqib). This was narrated by Abu Shaybah from 'Ata'. The sixth: the Everlasting (al-da'im). This was narrated by Ibn Jurayj from 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir. The seventh: that it means the Giver of sustenance (mu'tii al-qut), as said by Muqatil ibn Sulayman. Al-Khattabi said: "al-muqit" can mean "the giver of sustenance." Al-Farra' said: "It is said qatahu and aqatahu."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 86:

(p-152) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾ — concerning "greeting" (tahiyyah) there are two opinions.

The first: it is the salam (peace), so said Ibn 'Abbas and the majority (al-jumhur). The second: it is supplication (du'a'), mentioned by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and al-Mawardi. As for "better than it" (ahsan minha), it is adding to it; and returning it is saying the like of it. Al-Hasan said: when your Muslim brother says, "Peace be upon you," return the salam and add, "and the mercy of Allah," or return what he said and do not add. Al-Dahhak said: when he says, "Peace be upon you," you say, "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah." And when he says, "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah," you say, "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah and His blessings," and this is the furthest extent of the salam. Qatadah said: "with something better than it" applies to the Muslim, or "return it" applies to the People of the Book.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning those who doubted the Resurrection (al-ba'th). Al-Zajjaj said: The lam in "la-yajma'annakum" is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), like your saying: "By Allah, He will surely gather you." He said: It is possible that the Day of Resurrection (al-qiyamah) was so named because people rise (qiyam) from their graves, and it is possible that it was named so because of their standing (qiyam) for the reckoning.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ He described Himself with this only because all of creation is susceptible to lying, whereas it is impossible with respect to Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 88:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So what is [the matter] with you regarding the hypocrites, [that you have become] two groups?﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are seven reports.

The first: "Some people embraced Islam, then a plague struck them in Medina and its protected pasture (hima), so they left. A group of Muslims met them and said, 'What is the matter with you, that you have gone out?' They said, 'A plague struck us in Medina and we became ill from it (ijtawaynaha).' They said, 'Do you not have in the Messenger of Allah an example (uswah)?' Some of them said, 'They have become hypocrites,' and some said, 'They have not become hypocrites,' so this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman from his father.

The second: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to Uhud, some people who had gone out with him turned back, and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) split over them: one group said, "We should kill them," and another group said, "We should not kill them." So this verse was revealed. This is in the two Sahihs, from the statement of Zayd ibn Thabit.

The third: Some people in Mecca spoke the words of Islam while they were assisting the polytheists. (p-154) They went out of Mecca for some need of theirs. Some of the Muslims said, "Go out to them and kill them, for they support your enemy." Others said, "How can we kill them when they have spoken the same words that we have spoken?" So this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Atiyya from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: Some people came to Medina and showed Islam, then returned to Mecca and showed polytheism, so this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The fifth: Some people declared faith in Mecca and refrained from emigration, so the believers differed about them, and this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Dahhak.

The sixth: Some of the hypocrites wanted to leave Medina, and they said to the believers, "Indeed, illnesses have struck us in Medina, so perhaps we will go out and recover, for we were people of the desert (badiya)." They set out, and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) differed about them, so this verse was revealed. This is the statement of al-Suddi.

The seventh: It was revealed concerning the affair of Ibn Ubayy when he spoke about Aisha what he spoke. This is the statement of Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So what is [the matter] with you﴾ is addressed to the believers. The meaning: What is your position in differing about their affair? "Fi'a" means a faction (firqa). Regarding the meaning of "arkasahum" (ﷻ) there are four statements.

The first: He returned them (radda-hum). This was narrated by Ata from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Qutayba said: "rakastu (p-155) al-shay'" and "arkastuhu" are two dialects, meaning he overturned them and returned them to their disbelief. This is the statement of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

The second: He caused them to fall (awqa'ahum). This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

The third: He destroyed them (ahlakahum). This was stated by Qatada.

The fourth: He led them astray (adallahum). This was stated by al-Suddi.

As for "bima kasabu" (what they earned), it is their disbelief and apostasy. Abu Sulayman said: He only said, "Do you wish to guide one whom Allah has led astray?" because some of the believers said, "They are our brothers," and spoke with our words.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿you will never find for him a way﴾ has two statements. One: a way to the proof (hujja), stated by al-Zajjaj. The other: a way to guidance (huda), stated by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 89:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved﴾. Allah, mighty and majestic, informed the believers of what lies in the hearts of that group, so that they would not think well of them, would not argue on their behalf, and would firmly hold to their enmity.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾, meaning: do not befriend them, for they are your enemies. ﴿Until they emigrate﴾, meaning: until they return to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas said: ﴿But if they turn away﴾ from emigration (hijrah) and monotheism (tawhid), ﴿then seize them﴾, meaning: take them captive, and kill them wherever you find them, within the sacred area and outside it.

Section: Qadi Abu Ya'la said: Emigration (hijrah) was obligatory until Mecca was conquered. Al-Hasan said: The obligation of emigration remains. Know that people regarding emigration fall into three categories. The first is one for whom it is obligatory: he who cannot openly display Islam in the land of war, out of fear for his life, and who is able to emigrate. It is obligatory for him, based on His words: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ The second is one for whom it is not obligatory but recommended: he who is able to display his religion in the land of war. The third is one for whom it is not recommended: the weak person who can neither display his religion nor move, such as the decrepit old man and the chronically ill, for emigration is not recommended for him because it would cause him hardship.

(p-157) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except those who join﴾. This exception refers to the killing, not to the alliance.

There are two views on the meaning of "yasilun" (join).

The first is that it means "they connect with and seek refuge in" [a people]. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami had made a truce with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he would neither help him nor help anyone against him. Whoever joined Hilal from his own people or from others, they had the same protection of neighbourhood as Hilal had."

The second is that it means "they trace their lineage to" [a people]. Ibn Qutayba said this and recited:

"When she traces her lineage, she says: 'Abu Bakr ibn Wa'il,' while Bakr and the noses (of pride) are humbled."

He means: when she claims kinship, she says "Abakran," that is, "O family of Bakr."

(p-158) There are four views about the people mentioned.

The first is that they are the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat; Ibn 'Abbas said this. The second is that they are Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami, Suraqa ibn Malik, and Khuzayma ibn 'Amir ibn 'Abd Manaf; 'Ikrima said this. The third is that they are the Banu Mudlij; al-Hasan said this. The fourth is that they are Khuza'a and the Banu Mudlij; Muqatil said this. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-mithaq" means the covenant.

(p-159) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or they come to you﴾. There are two views on this.

The first is that its meaning is: "or they join a people who have come to you"; al-Zajjaj said this along with a group of others.

The second is that it refers back to those who were sought to be killed, so its implied meaning is: "or they return and enter among you." This has the same sense as the view of al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿their breasts are constricted﴾. There are two views on this. The first is that it contains an implied "qad" (indeed). The second is that it is a predicate following another predicate: his saying "jaa'ukum" (they come to you) is a complete predicate, and "hasirat" (are constricted) is a new predicate. Al-Zajjaj related both views. al-Hasan, Ya'qub, and al-Mufaddal, from 'Asim, read ﴿hasirat sudooruhum﴾ as a circumstantial clause (hal). "Hasirat" means "were constricted." The meaning of the statement is: their breasts were constricted from fighting you because of the treaty between you and them, or from fighting their own people, meaning Quraysh.

Mujahid said: Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir is the one whose breast was constricted from fighting you or fighting his people.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He informs that He only restrained them through the terror that was cast into their hearts. Regarding "al-salam" (peace), there are two views. The first is that it means Islam; al-Hasan said this. The second is that it means reconciliation; al-Rabi' and Muqatil said this.

Section

A group of the exegetes said: the treaty and truce with the polytheists mentioned in this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by the "verse of the sword" (ayat al-sayf), which is the command to fight. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: When Allah strengthened Islam, they were commanded not to accept from the polytheists of the Arabs anything except Islam or the sword.

(p-160) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will find others﴾ — the commentators differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, giving four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, who professed Islam in words so that they would be safe from the believers by their statement, and safe from their own people by their disbelief. This was related by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning the Banu 'Abd al-Dar. This was related by al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it was revealed concerning a people who wished to obtain a guarantee of safety from the Prophet ﷺ, saying: "We will not fight you, nor will we fight our people." This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, who was secure among the Muslims and the polytheists, and who would carry news between the Prophet (peace be upon him) and them. Then Nu'aym embraced Islam. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The meaning of the verse: you will find a people who show agreement with you and with their own people, in order to be safe from both groups. Whenever they are called to polytheism, they return to it. So if they do not withdraw from you in fighting, and do not offer you peace, and do not restrain their hands from fighting you, then seize them, that is, take them captive, and kill them wherever you encounter them. And against these We have placed for you a clear proof (authority) for killing them.

(p-161) * Section

The people of tafsir said: the leniency toward those mentioned in this verse has been abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 92:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by error﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: "'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah embraced Islam in Makkah before the Hijrah of the Messenger of Allah. Then he feared to show his Islam to his people, so he left for Madinah. His mother said to her two sons, Abu Jahl and al-Harith, the sons of Hisham, who were his maternal brothers: 'By Allah, I will not be shaded by a roof, nor will I taste food or drink until you bring him back to me.' So the two of them set out in pursuit of him, and with them al-Harith ibn Zayd, until they came to 'Ayyash while he was secured in a fortress. They said to him: 'Come down, for your mother has not sheltered under a roof, nor tasted food or drink, and we give you our covenant that we will not stand between you and your religion.' So he came down, and they bound him and each of them lashed him one hundred lashes. They brought him to his mother, and she said: 'By Allah, I will not untie you from your bonds until you disbelieve.' So he was thrown, bound, in the sun until he gave them what they wanted. Then al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: 'O 'Ayyash, if what you were upon was guidance, then you have abandoned it, and if it was misguidance, then you have embarked upon it.' He became angry and said: 'By Allah, I will not meet you alone except that I will kill you.' Then 'Ayyash escaped after that and emigrated to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Madinah. Then al-Harith embraced Islam after him and emigrated, but 'Ayyash did not know. One day he met him and killed him. He was told: 'Indeed he had embraced Islam.' So he came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of what had happened, and said: 'I did not perceive his Islam.' Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. This is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and the majority.

The second: "Abu al-Darda' killed a man who had said, 'There is no god but Allah,' during one of the expeditions. Then he came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned to him what he had done, and this verse was revealed." This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer at all." The exception (al-istithna') is not from the first part; rather the meaning is: "except that a believer errs." Abu 'Ubaydah narrated from Yunus that he asked Ru'bah about this verse, and he said: "It is not permissible for him to kill him intentionally or by error, but 'illa (except) has been placed in the position of waw (and)." The poet said:

Every brother who parts from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads (stars)

meaning: "and the two Farqads." Some scholars of meanings said: The sense of the verse is: "However, he may kill him by error, but that is not what Allah has granted him, for error is not subject to permission or prohibition." It was also said: The exception applies to what the verse contains regarding the deserving of sin and the obligation of retaliation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Freeing a slave is obligatory upon the killer from his own wealth. The scholars differed regarding freeing a young slave who cannot yet properly perform prayer and fasting. It is narrated from Ahmad that it is permissible, and Ibn Abi Talhah narrated likewise from Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the view of 'Ata' and Mujahid. It is also narrated from Ahmad that only one who fasts and prays is acceptable, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas in one narration, and of al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim, and Qatadah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and a compensation (diyah) paid to his family﴾. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: This verse does not state who bears this diyah, and the jurists agree that it is the 'aqilah (the paternal kinsmen) of the killer, who bear it on his behalf by way of consolation, and it is due upon the 'aqilah over three years, one third each year. The 'aqilah are the male relatives through lineage, and the offender himself bears nothing of it. Abu Hanifah said: he is like one of the 'aqilah. And the diyah for a soul has six equivalents: from gold, one thousand dinars; from silver, twelve thousand dirhams; from camels, one hundred; from cattle, two hundred cows; from sheep, two thousand sheep; and regarding garments, there are two narrations from Ahmad, one of which holds that they are a basic measure, so it would be two hundred garments. This is the diyah of a free male Muslim, and the diyah of a free Muslim woman is half of that.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿unless they remit it as charity﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: unless the heirs of the slain give up the diyah as charity to the killer.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you and he is a believer﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: its meaning is: "And if the slain by error was from a disbelieving people, then there is the freeing of a slave without diyah, because his heirs are disbelievers." The second: "And if he was residing among his people and was killed by one who did not know of his faith, then there is the freeing of a slave and no diyah, because he destroyed himself by residing among the disbelievers." Both views are narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The first is the view of al-Nakha'i, and the second is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
