According to the first, "min" is partitive, and according to the second it means "in."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it refers to a man from the dhimmis (protected people) who is killed by error, so the killer owes diyah and expiation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i. Our companions have detailed discussion regarding the amount of diyah that is owed.

The second: it refers to a believer who is killed while his people are polytheists with whom there is a treaty; his diyah goes to his people, and his inheritance to the Muslims. This is the view of al-Nakha'i.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months﴾. They differed over whether this fasting replaces only the slave when it is unavailable, or replaces both the slave and the diyah. The majority said: it replaces the slave alone. Masruq, Mujahid, and Ibn Sirin said: both. The scholars agreed that if the fasting of the two months is interrupted by breaking the fast without an excuse, one must begin again. As for when illness or menstruation interrupts it, according to us the consecutiveness is not broken, and this is the view of Malik. Abu Hanifah said: illness breaks it, while menstruation does not; he distinguished between them on the basis that it is customarily possible to fast two months without illness, but not without menstruation. According to us, the woman is excused in both cases.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a repentance from Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: Allah ordained that as a repentance from Him.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾, i.e., He has always been Knowing of what sets right His creation in terms of obligations, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He decides between them and manages in their affairs.

**The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 4, Verse 93**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "Maqis ibn Subabah found his brother Hisham ibn Subabah slain among the Banu al-Najjar, and he was a Muslim. So he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him about that. The Messenger of Allah sent a messenger from the Banu Fihr and said to him: 'Go to the Banu al-Najjar, convey my greetings to them, and say to them: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commands you that if you know the killer of Hisham, you should hand him over to Maqis ibn Subabah, and if you do not know of any killer, you should give him his blood money.' The Fihri conveyed that to them. They said: 'By Allah, we do not know of any killer for him, but we will give his blood money.' So they gave him one hundred camels. Then the two of them turned back toward Madinah. Satan came to Maqis ibn Subabah and said: 'Will you accept your brother's blood money? It will be a disgrace upon you as long as you live. Kill the one who is with you in place of your brother, and take the excess of the blood money.' So he struck the Fihri with a rock and crushed his head. Then he mounted one of the camels, drove the rest of them back toward Makkah, and he was saying:

*I killed Fihr in exchange for him, and I carried his blood money,*
*the chiefs of the Banu al-Najjar, the lords of Fari'.*

*I have attained my vengeance and lay down reclining,*
*and I was the first to return to the idols.*

Then this verse was revealed. Afterwards, the Prophet ﷺ declared his blood forfeit on the day of the Conquest, and he was killed." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Regarding His saying (*muta'ammidan*, "intentionally") there are two views. The first: intentionally because he is a believer, which was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: intentionally with regard to killing him, which was mentioned by some of the exegetes (*mufassirin*). Regarding His saying (*fa-jaza'uhu Jahannam*, "then his recompense is Hell") there are two views. The first: that it is his recompense definitively. The second: that it is his recompense if he is recompensed (by it).

The scholars differed over whether a believer who intentionally kills a believer has repentance (*tawbah*) or not. The majority held that he has repentance, while Ibn 'Abbas held that he has no repentance.

**Section**

The scholars differed regarding this verse: is it *muhkam* (definitive, not abrogated) or *mansukh* (abrogated, *naskh*)? One group said: it is *muhkam*, and they argued that it is a report (*khabar*), and reports do not admit of abrogation (*naskh*). Then these divided into two groups. One of them said: it is upon its apparent meaning, and the killer of a believer is eternal in the Fire. The second group said: it is general (*'amm*), and specification (*takhsis*) has entered it, with the proof that if a disbeliever killed him and then the disbeliever embraced Islam, the punishment is entirely removed from him in this world and the Hereafter. Thus, when it is established that it is of the general that has been specified, then whichever proof is suitable for specification must be acted upon. Among the causes of specification is that his killing is considered lawful (*mustahall*), so he deserves eternity for considering it lawful.

Another group said: it is specified with regard to one who does not repent, and they cited His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 70]. Others said: it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48].

(p-169) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are four reports.

The first: "The Prophet ﷺ sent a *sariyya* (a small raiding detachment) in which was al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. When they reached the people, they found that they had dispersed, but one man remained who had much wealth and did not leave. He said, 'I testify that there is no god but Allah,' and al-Miqdad moved toward him and killed him. A man from among his companions said to him, 'Did you kill a man who testifies that there is no god but Allah? I will certainly mention that to the Prophet ﷺ.' When they came before the Prophet ﷺ, they said: (p-170) 'O Messenger of Allah, a man testified that there is no god but Allah, and al-Miqdad killed him.' He said, 'Call al-Miqdad to me.' He said to him, 'O Miqdad, did you kill a man who said there is no god but Allah? How will you deal with "there is no god but Allah" tomorrow!'

He said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are abundant spoils. Thus you were before, and Allah bestowed His favour upon you, so investigate carefully﴾. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said to al-Miqdad: 'He was a believer who concealed his faith among a disbelieving people, and he manifested his faith, and you killed him? Thus you too used to conceal your faith in Makkah before.'" Narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "A man from Banu Sulaym passed by a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, with a flock of sheep. He greeted them with peace, and they said, 'He only greeted you with peace in order to seek refuge from us.' So they set upon him, killed him, and took his sheep, and brought them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed." Narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-171) The third: "Some people of Makkah heard that a *sariyya* of the Messenger of Allah was coming to them, so they fled. But a man among them who had embraced Islam, called Mirdas, remained behind. The commander of the *sariyya* was a man called Ghalib ibn Fadala. When Mirdas saw the horsemen, he exclaimed 'Allahu akbar,' came down to them, and greeted them with peace. Then Usama ibn Zayd killed him and drove off his sheep. They returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was greatly distressed by that, and this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Suddi said: Usama was the commander of the *sariyya*.

The fourth: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Abu Hadrad al-Aslami, Abu Qatada, and Muhallam ibn Jaththama in a *sariyya* toward Idam. They met 'Amir ibn al-Adbat al-Ashja'i, who greeted them with the greeting of Islam. Muhallam ibn Jaththama attacked him and killed him, and took his camel and water-skin as spoils. When they came before the Prophet ﷺ and told him, he said, 'Did you kill him after he said "I have believed"?!' And this verse was revealed." Narrated by Ibn Abi Hadrad from his father.

As for the exegesis: His saying ﴿when you go forth in the cause of Allah﴾ means: when you travel and go on military campaign.

As for His saying ﴿fa-tabayyanu﴾ (investigate carefully), Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read *fa-tabayyanu* with the letter nun, from *tabyin* (making something clear) before proceeding with it. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf (p-172) read *fa-tathabbatu* with the letter tha', from *thabat* (steadfastness) and abandoning haste. They also read it thus in *al-Hujurat*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to one who offers you peace (al-salam)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr, Hafs from 'Asim, and al-Kisa'i read *al-salam* with an alif and a fathah on the sin. Al-Zajjaj said: it may mean *al-taslim* (the greeting), and it may mean *al-istislam* (submission). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Khalaf, Jiblla from al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read *al-salam* with fathah on the sin and lam, without an alif, and it is from *al-istislam*. Aban ibn Yazid from 'Asim read it with kasrah on the sin and sukun on the lam, without an alif, and *al-salam* means peace treaty (*al-sulh*). The majority read *lasta mu'minan* with kasrah on the mim. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliya, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, and Abu Ja'far read it with fathah on the mim, from *al-aman* (safety/security).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿seeking the goods of worldly life (ʿaraḍ al-ḥayat al-dunya)﴾. *ʿArad* means whatever wealth is in it, whether little or much. The exegetes said: what is meant by it is what they seized as spoils from the man they killed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with Allah are abundant spoils (maghanim kathira)﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

One: it is the reward of Paradise, as said by Muqatil.

The other: it is the doors of provision in this world, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus you were before﴾. Concerning this there are three views.

One: its meaning is: thus you used to feel safe from your own believing people through this word, so do not frighten the one who says it. Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: thus you used to conceal your faith in Makkah, just as this man concealed his faith. Narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: thus you were before, as polytheists. Said by Masruq, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd.

(p-173) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and Allah bestowed His favour upon you﴾. Concerning the favour by which He bestowed, there are four views.

One: the Hijra (emigration), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the public declaration of faith, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The third: Islam, said by Qatada and Masruq. The fourth: repentance granted to the one who killed that man, said by al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so investigate carefully (fa-tabayyanu)﴾ is an emphasis of the first.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 95:

The Almighty's words: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers are not equal﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: This verse was revealed concerning a people who, whenever a military expedition (ghazwah) was called, would ask permission to stay behind.

Zayd ibn Thabit said: "I was sitting beside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when tranquility (sakinah) came over him. Then it lifted from him, and he said, 'Write: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers and the strivers (mujahidun) are not equal﴾,' up to the end of the verse. Ibn Umm Maktum stood up and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, what about one who is unable to strive?' By Allah, he had not finished his words before tranquility came over the Messenger of Allah again. Then it lifted from him, and he said, 'Read.' I read: ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those who strive, are not equal.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾, and so he added it."

(p-174) The Almighty's words: ﴿Those who sit at home﴾, meaning: from jihad. The meaning is that the one who strives is more excellent. Ibn Abbas said: By this jihad is meant the battle of Badr. Muqatil said: the expedition of Tabuk.

The Almighty's words: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Hamzah recited "غَيْرُ" with a damma on the ra' (raf'). Nafi', Ibn Amir, al-Kisai, Khalaf and al-Mufaddal recited it with a fatha (nasb). Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: whoever reads it with the raf', makes "غَيْرُ" an attribute (sifah, adjective) of "al-qa'idin" (those who sit), and whoever reads it with the nasb, makes it an exception (istithna', exclusion) from "al-qa'idin." Regarding "al-darar" (harm) there are two views.

One: it is incapacity due to chronic disability (zamanah), sickness and the like. Ibn Abbas said: they are a people whom sicknesses and ailments kept from the expeditions. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Qutaybah said: they are the people of chronic disability. Al-Zajjaj said: the harm is that one be blind, or blind in sight, or chronically disabled.

The second: it is excuse. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Allah has preferred the strivers with their wealth and their lives over the sitters﴾. Regarding the "darajah" (degree) over these sitters there are two views.

One: they are those who sit because of harm. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil.

The second: those who sit without harm. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn Jarir said: the darajah is the excellence. As for "al-husna" (the best reward), it is Paradise according to the consensus of the scholars.

(p-175) The Almighty's words: ﴿And Allah has preferred the strivers over the sitters﴾. Ibn Abbas said: the sitters here are "other than those with a harm." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are those who have no excuse at all.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 96:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Degrees from Him﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Darajat" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for His saying "a great reward," and it explains the reward. There are two opinions regarding what is meant by the degrees.

The first: they are the degrees of Paradise. Ibn Muhayriz said: "The degrees are seventy degrees, the distance between each two degrees being the gallop of a well-bred, trained horse for seventy years." Muqatil also went to something similar.

The second: the meaning of the degrees is the virtues (fada'il). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this. Qatadah said: "It used to be said: Islam is a degree, emigration within Islam is a degree, struggle (jihad) within emigration is a degree, and being killed in jihad is a degree."

Ibn Zayd said: "The degrees are the seven that Allah mentioned in Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah), when He said: ﴿That is because they do not suffer thirst...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and they do not cross a valley except that it is written for them﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:120-121]."

(p-176) If it is asked: What is the wisdom in Allah mentioning one degree at the beginning of the statement and degrees at its end? There are two answers to this.

The first: the single degree is the preference of the mujahidin over those who sit back from among those with a excuse (ulu al-darar) in rank, and the "degrees" is the preference of the mujahidin over those who sit back from among those other than those with an excuse, in many stations. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas.

The second: the first degree is the degree of praise and honor, and the "degrees" are the stations of Paradise. This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ — concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: "Some people in Makkah had professed Islam. When the Prophet ﷺ set out for Badr, Quraysh did not leave anyone behind but made them go out with them. Those who had professed Islam were killed, and this verse was revealed concerning them." This was related by ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning some people who spoke the words of Islam, then went out with Abu Jahl, and were killed on the Day of Badr. They offered excuses without any valid excuse, so God refused to accept them from them.

The second: some people were hypocrites on the Day of Badr and doubted, and they said: "Their religion has deceived these people." They remained with the polytheists until they were killed, and this verse was revealed concerning them. This was related by Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it was revealed concerning a people who stayed behind from the Messenger of God ﷺ and did not go out with him. Whoever of them died before joining the Prophet, the angels struck his face and his back. This was related by al-ʿAwfi, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Regarding "tawaffi" (taking in death) there are two views.

One of them: that He seized the souls at death; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil. The second: the gathering to the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan. Muqatil said: by "the angels" is meant the Angel of Death alone.

In another place he said: the Angel of Death and his assistants, who are six: three who attend to the souls of the believers, and three who attend to the souls of the disbelievers. Al-Zajjaj said: "wronging themselves" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning is: they take them while they are in the state of wronging themselves. The original form is ẓālimīn (wronging), but the nūn was dropped for lightness. As for their wronging themselves, according to what is mentioned in their story, there are four possible views.

One: that they abandoned emigration (hijrah). The second: their return to disbelief. The third: doubt after certainty. The fourth: aiding the polytheists.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In what were you?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: it is a question of reproach, and the meaning is: were you among the polytheists or among the Muslims?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: We were oppressed in the land﴾ Muqatil said: We were subdued in the land of Makkah, unable to mention faith. The angels said: ﴿Was not the earth of God spacious, so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ meaning Madinah, ﴿emigrate therein﴾ meaning: to it. The angels' saying to them shows that they were able to emigrate.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 98–99:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Except the oppressed among men﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Muslims said concerning the oppressed Muslims in Makkah, "These are in the same position as those who were killed at Badr," and so this verse was revealed. This was said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said: "al-mustad'afin" (the oppressed) is in the accusative as an exception from His saying: ﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾. Abu Sulayman (Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi) said: "al-mustad'afun" are the elderly (dhu al-asnan), the women, and the children.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are not able to devise a plan﴾, meaning: they are not able to find a plan for leaving Makkah, nor have the means (nafaqah), nor the strength.

Concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor are they guided to a way﴾, there are two opinions. (p-179) One: they do not know the road to Madinah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and Mujahid. The second: they do not know any way to head toward, so if they went out they would perish. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Concerning "'asa" (perhaps), there are two opinions. One: it carries the meaning of certainty (al-ijab), said by al-Hasan. The second: it carries the meaning of hope (al-tarajji), so the meaning is that they hope for pardon. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 98–99:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Except the oppressed among men﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Muslims said concerning the oppressed Muslims in Makkah, "These are in the same position as those who were killed at Badr," and so this verse was revealed. This was said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said: "al-mustad'afin" (the oppressed) is in the accusative as an exception from His saying: ﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾. Abu Sulayman (Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi) said: "al-mustad'afun" are the elderly (dhu al-asnan), the women, and the children.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are not able to devise a plan﴾, meaning: they are not able to find a plan for leaving Makkah, nor have the means (nafaqah), nor the strength.

Concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor are they guided to a way﴾, there are two opinions. (p-179) One: they do not know the road to Madinah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and Mujahid. The second: they do not know any way to head toward, so if they went out they would perish. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Concerning "'asa" (perhaps), there are two opinions. One: it carries the meaning of certainty (al-ijab), said by al-Hasan. The second: it carries the meaning of hope (al-tarajji), so the meaning is that they hope for pardon. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿he will find in the earth many a refuge (muragham) and abundance﴾ is said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid to mean: one who moves away from what he dislikes.

Ibn Qutayba said: al-muragham and al-muhajir are one and the same. It is said: "raghamtu" and "hajartu" (I opposed/I emigrated). Its origin is that when a man embraced Islam, he left his people as a *muragham*, meaning one who angers them, and a *muhajir*, meaning one who cuts off from them (from *al-hijran*, abandonment). So the path (the way of life he adopted) was called *muragham*, and the going to the Prophet ﷺ was called *hijrah* (migration), because it was by a man abandoning his people. [al-Ja'di said: "Honored is the muragham and the madhhab (path)."]

Regarding "abundance" (sa'ah), there are two views. The first is that it means abundance in provision, said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority.

The second is the ability to openly practice the religion, said by Qatada.

The phrase ﴿And whoever leaves his home emigrating toward Allah and His Messenger﴾ — they agreed that it was revealed concerning a man who set out as a *muhajir* and died on the way, and they differed about him in six views.

The first: he was Damrah ibn al-'Is, who was blind and wealthy. He said: "Carry me." He was carried while sick, and he died at al-Tan'im, so this statement was revealed concerning him. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: he was al-'Is ibn Damrah ibn Zinba' al-Khuza'i. He ordered his family to carry him on his litter, and when he reached al-Tan'im, he died, so this verse was revealed concerning him. This was narrated by Abu Bishr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: he was Ibn Damrah al-Jundu'i, who fell ill and said to his sons: "Take me out of Makkah, for its distress has killed me." They said: "Where?" He pointed with his hand toward Madinah, meaning hijrah. They took him out, and he died on the way, so this was revealed concerning him. This was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq. Muqatil said: he was Jundub ibn Damrah.

The fourth: his name was Sabrah. When the words were revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves...﴾ up to ﴿many a refuge﴾, he said to his family while he was sick: "Carry me, for I am wealthy and I have enough wealth to bring me to Madinah." When he passed the sanctuary (haram), he died, so this was revealed concerning him. This was said by Qatada.

The fifth: he was a man from Banu Kinanah who emigrated and died on the way. His people mocked him, saying: "He has neither reached what he intended, nor stayed among his family until he was buried." So this was revealed concerning him. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The sixth: he was Khalid ibn Hizam, brother of Hakim ibn Hizam, who set out as a *muhajir* and died on the way. This was mentioned by al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar. His saying "waqa'a" (fell/occurred) means: wajaba (became due, incumbent).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening [some] of the prayer﴾. Mujahid narrated from Abu 'Ayyash al-Zuraqi, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at 'Usfan, and over the polytheists was Khalid ibn al-Walid. [He] said: We prayed the Zuhr, and the polytheists said: We have had a chance at them; if only we had charged upon them while they were in prayer. So the verse of shortening was revealed between Zuhr and 'Asr."

"Daraba fi al-ard" (striking in the land) means travel; "junah" (blame) means sin; "qasr" (shortening) means reduction; and "fitnah" means killing. Regarding qasr there are two views. (p-182) One: it is shortening in the number of rak'ahs. The second: it is shortening in its limits (its conditions and observances). The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that shortening is not permitted except in fear, and the matter is not so; rather, the verse was revealed concerning the majority of the journeys of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and most of them were not free from fear of the enemy. It was also said: His saying, ﴿that you shorten from the prayer﴾ is a complete statement, and His saying, ﴿if you fear﴾ is a new sentence, and its meaning is: "and if you fear."

The scholars differed over whether the prayer of the traveller of two rak'ahs is shortened or not. A group said: it is not shortened; rather, that is the obligation for the traveller. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Abu Hanifah. According to this view, "qasr" of the prayer means it becomes one rak'ah, and this is not permitted except when both travel and fear are present, because for these scholars the two rak'ahs in travel, when there is no fear, are a complete prayer, not a shortened one. They argued with what Ibn 'Abbas narrated: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed at Dhu Qarad, and the people were arranged behind him in two rows: one row behind him, and a row facing the enemy. He prayed with those behind him one rak'ah, then those went back to the place of these, and those came and he prayed with them one rak'ah, and they did not make up (the rest)." And from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Allah prescribed the prayer through the tongue of your Prophet: in residence four, in travel two, and in fear one rak'ah."

The second view: that it is shortened, and it is not the original form. This is the view of Mujahid, Tawus, Ahmad, and al-Shafi'i. "Ya'la ibn Umayyah said: I said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: I wonder at people shortening today, when they are secure, and Allah the Exalted only said: ﴿if you fear﴾. 'Umar said: I wondered at what you wondered at, so I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: It is a charity which Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity." (p-184)

Section

Shortening is permitted for the traveller only when his journey is lawful, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: it is permitted for him to shorten in a journey of disobedience. As for the duration of residence which, if he intends it, he completes the prayer, and if he intends less than it, he shortens: our companions (the Hanbali scholars) said: a stay of twenty-two prayers. Abu Hanifah said: fifteen days. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: four days.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 102:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "When the polytheists saw the Prophet ﷺ and his companions had prayed the Dhuhr, they regretted that they had not attacked them. Some of them said to others: Leave them, for they have a prayer that is dearer to them than their fathers and their sons," meaning the ʿAsr. "When they stood up for the ʿAsr prayer, they charged upon them. When they stood for the ʿAsr prayer, Gabriel descended with this verse." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you are among them﴾ is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and it does not indicate that the ruling is restricted to him. It is like His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. Abu Yusuf said: The prayer of fear is not valid after the Prophet ﷺ. The hāʾ and mīm in "fīhim" refer to those who travel in the land.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer for them﴾, that is, begin it for them. ﴿Then let a group of them stand with you﴾, that is, to stand (in position). Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Whenever it becomes dark for them, they stand﴾ [al-Baqara: 20].

﴿And let them take their weapons﴾. Regarding "them" there are two views:

One: they are the ones who remain behind, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they are those praying with him, mentioned by Ibn Jarir. He said: This weapon is like the sword, which a person hangs on his shoulder, and the dagger which he fastens to his forearm.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they have prostrated﴾, meaning those praying with him, ﴿then let them be﴾ — regarding the referent of "them" there are two views. One: they are the group that did not pray, who were commanded to guard the praying group; this is the meaning of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement. The second: they are those praying with him, who were commanded, when they prostrated, to withdraw to the guard.

The scholars differed on how they withdraw after prostration. Some said: If they complete a rakʿa with the imam, they complete one rakʿa for themselves, then they give the salam and withdraw, and their prayer is complete.

Others said: They withdraw after one rakʿa. These differed: some of them said: If they pray one rakʿa with the imam and give the salam, it suffices them. Others among them, including Abu Hanifa, said: Rather, they withdraw from that rakʿa to the guard while they are still in their prayer, so they stand facing the enemy in place of the other group that did not pray, and that group comes. They differed regarding the other group. Some said: When the imam prays with them, he lengthens the tashahhud until they complete the missed rakʿa, then he gives the salam with them. Others said: Rather, he gives the salam at the end of his prayer with them, and when he gives the salam they complete what they missed. Others said: Rather, he prays one rakʿa with the second group and gives the salam himself, while they do not give the salam, but return to face the enemy; then the first group comes, completes the remainder of its prayer and gives the salam, and goes off, and the other group comes and completes its prayer. This is the position of Abu Hanifa.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: It means those who prayed first. Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that it means those who are facing the enemy, because the one praying is not a fighter; and it is permissible that the congregation was commanded to carry weapons, because it is more intimidating to the enemy and more likely that they will not advance against them. "Al-junah" means sin, and it derives from "janaḥtu," when one deviates from a place and takes a side away from the right course. The meaning is: If you put down your weapons, you do not deviate from the truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there is upon you a hardship from rain﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They were granted leave to lay down the weapons because of their weight upon the sick and because of the rain, and he said: Take your precaution so that they do not catch you unaware.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 103:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾ means: the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf), and "qaḍaytum" here carries the meaning of "faza'tum" (you were frightened).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then remember Allah﴾ — regarding this remembrance there are two opinions.

The first: it is the remembrance of Allah outside the prayer. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority. They said: it is glorification (tasbīḥ), magnification (takbīr), supplication (duʿāʾ), and thanksgiving (shukr).

(p-188) The second: it is the prayer itself, so the meaning is: pray standing, and if you are not able, then sitting, and if you are not able, then on your sides. This is the view of Ibn Masʿud. Regarding what is meant by ṭumaʾnīna (tranquillity/security), there are two opinions.

The first: it is the return to one's homeland from travel, the view of al-Ḥasan, Mujahid, and Qatada. The second: it is security after fear, the view of al-Suddi, al-Zajjaj, and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding "iqāmat al-ṣalāh" (establishing the prayer) there are two opinions. The first: completing it, said by Mujahid, Qatada, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: it is establishing its bowing (rukūʿ) and prostration (sujūd), and what is obligatory in it that may be omitted in a state of fear; this is the view of al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times﴾ means: an obligation (farḍan). Regarding "al-mawqūt" there are two opinions. The first: it means "al-mafrūḍ" (the obligatory), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. The second: it means "al-muwaqqat" (prescribed at specific, fixed times), the view of Ibn Masʿud, Qatada, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Ibn Qutayba.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 104:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not falter in pursuit of the enemy people﴾. The people of tafsir said: the occasion of its revelation was that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded his companions, when they returned from Uhud, to go in pursuit of Abu Sufyan and his companions, but they complained of the wounds they had suffered, so this verse was revealed.

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: The meaning of "tahinu" (do not falter) is "tada'ifu" (become weak). It is said: wahana, yahinu, when he became weak, and every weakness is wahn. "Ibtagha al-qawm" means he sought them out for war. And "al-qawm" here means the disbelievers. ﴿If you suffer pain﴾, that is, you are in pain, for they find pain from what the wounds and fatigue inflict upon them, just as you find it, and yet you hope for what they do not hope for. Regarding this "hope," there are two views. The first: it is expectation (amal), said by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the consensus of the trustworthy linguists. The second: it is fear, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Al-Farra' (a grammarian) said: "Khawf" used in the sense of "raja'" (hope) is only found together with a negation, [so when this is the case, fear is in the manner of hope and fear, and hope is likewise], as in His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from Allah?﴾ [Nuh 71:13] and His saying: ﴿who do not expect the days of Allah﴾ [al-Jathiyah 45:14]. The poet said:

Do not hope when you meet the one who exceeds [in strength], whether they are seven who met together or one alone.

And al-Hudhali said:

When the bee has stung him, he does not hope for its sting, and he opposes it in a house of woven cloth, crowded.

It is not permissible to say "raja'tuka" (I hoped in you) while meaning "khiftuka" (I feared you), nor "khiftuka" while meaning "raja'tuka."

Al-Zajjaj said: Hope came to include the meaning of fear only because it is an expectation which may be feared not to be fulfilled. So according to the first view, the meaning is: you hope for victory, the establishment of your religion, and Paradise. And according to the second, you fear from the punishment of Allah what they do not fear.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 105:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: "Ṭu'mah ibn Ubayriq stole a coat of mail belonging to Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man. The coat of mail was in a sack containing flour, and the flour began to spill through a tear in the sack, until it reached the house. Then he hid it with a man from the Jews. The coat of mail was searched for at Ṭu'mah's, but it was not found with him, and he swore: 'I have no knowledge of it.' Its owners said: 'Yes, by Allah, he entered upon us and took it, and we followed his trail until he entered his house, and we saw the trace of the flour.' When he swore, they left him, and they followed the trace of the flour until they reached the dwelling of the Jewish man and seized him. He said: 'Ṭu'mah gave it to me.' The people of Ṭu'mah said: 'Go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and let him argue on behalf of our companion, for he is innocent.' They came to him and spoke to him about that, and he intended to act accordingly and to punish the Jew, so these verses were all revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "A man from the Jews deposited a coat of mail with Ṭu'mah ibn Ubayriq, and he betrayed it. When he feared that they would discover it, he cast it into the house of Abu Mulayl al-Ansari. The people of Ṭu'mah argued on his behalf and came to the Prophet ﷺ, asking him to clear him and to call the Jew a liar, so the verses were revealed." This is the saying of al-Suddi and Muqatil.

The third: "The storeroom of Rifa'ah ibn Zayd was breached, and his food and weapons were taken, and the Banu Ubayriq, who were three—Bashir, Mubashshir, and Bishr—were suspected. Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man went to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a household among us, among whom there is harshness, breached the storeroom of my uncle Rifa'ah ibn Zayd and took his weapons and his food.' He said: 'Look into this matter.' Then a group from the people of the Banu Ubayriq went to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man and his uncle have targeted a household of ours, accusing them of theft, while they are a household of Islam and righteousness.' The Prophet ﷺ said to Qatadah: 'You accused them of theft without clear evidence!' So these verses were revealed." This was said by Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man.

Al-Kitab (the Book): the Qur'an. Al-Haqq (the truth): the judgment with justice.

﴿That you may judge between the people﴾: i.e., that you may decide between them.

Concerning His saying ﴿by what Allah has shown you﴾ there are two opinions.

One: it is what He taught him, and what He taught him was that he should not accept one person's claim against another except with proof. The second: it is what his ijtihad (independent reasoning) leads him to, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Do not be a disputant, nor a defender of a traitor. They differed over whether he actually argued on his behalf or not, on two views.

One: that he stood up to speak and excused him; narrated by al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he intended to do so but did not do it; said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: This verse indicates that it is not permissible for anyone to dispute on behalf of another in establishing or negating a right, when he does not know the reality of the matter, because Allah the Exalted rebuked His Prophet for the like of that.

Allah's words: ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾. Concerning that for which he was commanded to seek forgiveness, there are two opinions.

One: that it is his standing up on behalf of the one who had been wronged (i.e., his defending him, as the man was defended against the treacherous). The second: that it is his resolve to do so (i.e., his intention to act thus).

(p-193) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. That is, they betray themselves, making their souls betrayers by committing treachery.

ʿIkrimah said: What is meant by them is Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq and his people who argued on his behalf.

In the report of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: A group from Ṭuʿmah's clan set out by night to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Indeed, our companion is innocent."

"Al-istikhfa'" means concealment, and the meaning is: they conceal themselves from people so that they will not be made aware of their treachery and their lying, but they do not conceal themselves from Allah, for He is with them by His knowledge. Anything that is plotted or discussed at night is called "bayyata." The majority of scholars hold that what is referred to by "concealment" and "planning by night" is the people of Ṭuʿmah.

What they planned was their scheming to clear their companion through lying. Al-Zajjaj said: It is the thief himself. The one who planned it said: "Accuse the Jew of stealing the coat of mail, and swear that I did not steal it, so that my oath will be accepted and the Jew's oath will not be accepted."

(p-193) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. That is, they betray themselves, making their souls betrayers by committing treachery.

ʿIkrimah said: What is meant by them is Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq and his people who argued on his behalf.

In the report of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: A group from Ṭuʿmah's clan set out by night to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Indeed, our companion is innocent."

"Al-istikhfa'" means concealment, and the meaning is: they conceal themselves from people so that they will not be made aware of their treachery and their lying, but they do not conceal themselves from Allah, for He is with them by His knowledge. Anything that is plotted or discussed at night is called "bayyata." The majority of scholars hold that what is referred to by "concealment" and "planning by night" is the people of Ṭuʿmah.

What they planned was their scheming to clear their companion through lying. Al-Zajjaj said: It is the thief himself. The one who planned it said: "Accuse the Jew of stealing the coat of mail, and swear that I did not steal it, so that my oath will be accepted and the Jew's oath will not be accepted."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 109:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Ha" (ha, an interjection of alerting) is for drawing attention, and it is repeated at its beginning. The meaning is: "Here you are, you who argued." And "al-mujadalah" and "al-jidal" (arguing, contention) mean intense dispute, while "al-jadal" means intense twisting. The discourse refers to those who pleaded on behalf of the thief. As for His saying, "on their behalf" (ʿanhum), it refers to the thief. And "ʿalayhim" is used in the sense of "lahum" (on their behalf). And "al-wakil" (the guardian, the one entrusted) is the one who stands in charge of a matter on behalf of the one who entrusted him. So it is as if He said: "Who, from among you, will take up their case before their Lord on the Day of Judgment?!"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 110:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does an evil or wrongs himself﴾, the scholars differed concerning its revelation into three opinions.

One of them: it was revealed as an address to the thief and an offer of repentance to him. This was narrated by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Zayd and Muqatil also said so.

The second: it was revealed concerning those who argued on his behalf among his people. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it intends by it every wrongdoer who sins. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Its general application does not preclude that it was revealed on a specific occasion. Concerning this "evil" (su') there are three opinions.

One of them: that it is theft. The second: polytheism (shirk). The third: that it is everything for which one incurs sin. Concerning this "wronging" (zulm) there are two opinions. One of them: that an innocent person was accused of a charge. The second: what is less than polytheism.

Allah's saying: ﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾, that is: whoever commits a wrongdoing, ﴿then he earns it only against himself﴾. He means: its burden returns only upon him. Muqatil said this. And this (verse) also concerns Tu'mah.

[p-195] The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or a wrong﴾. The majority of scholars (jumhur al-'ulama') hold that it was revealed concerning the story of Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul when he slandered 'A'ishah, peace be upon her, with the false accusation (al-ifk).

Regarding His words ﴿a sin or a wrong﴾, there are four opinions.

The first: "al-khati'ah" is the thief's false oath, and "al-ithm" is his theft of the coat of mail and his casting of the accusation onto the Jew. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: "al-khati'ah" is the guilt that attaches to him for it, and "al-ithm" is his slander of the innocent. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: "al-khati'ah" may occur intentionally or unintentionally, while "al-ithm" is specific to intention. This was said by Ibn Jarir and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Al-Zajjaj mentioned that "al-khati'ah" is like the killing by mistake, in which sin is lifted.

The fourth: when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, named some disobediences "khati'ah" and others "ithm", it informs that whoever earns something that falls under either of these two names and then casts it onto an innocent person has borne a slander (buhtan). This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj also. As for His words ﴿then casts it onto an innocent person﴾, it means he casts onto an innocent person what he himself committed.

If it is said: "khati'ah" and "ithm" are two things, so how does He say "bihi" (it) in the singular? There are four answers regarding this.

The first: He meant "then casts both of them (bihima)", and the mention of "ithm" was sufficient by repeating the reference to it rather than to "khati'ah", as in His words ﴿they dispersed toward it﴾, where He singled out the trade, and the meaning is: toward trade and amusement.

The second: the pronoun returns to the earning (al-kasb). Since "yaksib" indicated the earning, He referred to it by a pronoun.

The third: the pronoun returns to the meaning of sin and wrong, as if He said: whoever earns a sin and then casts it. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, who related these opinions.

The fourth: the pronoun returns to "ithm" alone. This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

Regarding the meaning of "the innocent" whom this thief slandered, there are two opinions. [p-196]

One: he was a Jew. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Sirin, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. 'Ikrimah and Qatadah named him Zayd ibn al-Samir.

The second: he was a Muslim. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. They differed about who that Muslim was. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was 'A'ishah when Ibn Ubayy slandered her. Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man said it was Labid ibn Sahl. Al-Suddi and Muqatil said it was Abu Mulayl al-Ansari.

As for buhtan (slander), it is the lie that bewilders by its enormity; it is said: "baha al-rajul" (the man was bewildered) when he became perplexed. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he has borne a slander (buhtan) by his casting of the innocent person, and a manifest sin (ithman mubinan) by his false oath.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ — regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

One: that it relates to the story of Tu'mah and his people, when they confused the Prophet ﷺ concerning the matter of their companion. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas through the transmission of Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: "The delegation of Thaqif came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'We have come to you to pledge allegiance to you on condition that we do not perform hashr and not perform 'ashr, and that you allow us to enjoy al-'Uzza for a year.' He did not answer them, and this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of al-Dahhak.

Regarding what is meant by the bounty of Allah and His mercy, there are two views. One: prophethood and protection from error (al-'isma). The second: Islam and the Qur'an, related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Muqatil said: "Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you, in that He clarified to you the matter of Tu'mah and turned you away from confirming the traitor through the Qur'an, a group among them would have certainly sought to mislead you." Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "indeed, they had resolved (to do so)."

If it is asked: how does He say, ﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, a group would have resolved﴾ when they had indeed resolved to mislead him? The answer: were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, the effect of what they intended would have appeared. As for the group, according to the narration of Ibn al-Sa'ib from Ibn 'Abbas, it is the people of Tu'mah; and according to the narration of al-Dahhak, it is the delegation of Thaqif.

Regarding "misleading" there are two views. One: error in judgment. The second: being led astray from the truth.

Al-Zajjaj said: "They do not mislead except themselves, because they act as those who are astray, so the misguidance returns to them." As for "the Book," it is the Qur'an.

Regarding "wisdom" there are three views. One: judgment through revelation, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the lawful and the unlawful, said by Muqatil. The third: the explanation of what is in the Book, the inspiring of what is right, and the placing of the correctness of the answer into the heart, said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Regarding His saying ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ there are three views.

One: that it is the Sharia, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: the reports of the former and later peoples, said by Abu Sulayman. The third: the Book and the wisdom, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding His saying ﴿And the bounty of Allah upon you has been ever great﴾ there are three views.

One: that it is the favor of faith. The second: the favor of prophethood. These two are from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that it is general, encompassing all the bounty with which Allah specified him, said by Abu Sulayman.

(p-198) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are the people of Tu'mah. Muqatil said: They were all Jews, who conferred together concerning the matter of Tu'mah. Mujahid said: It is general, covering the secret talk of all people. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of najwa (secret talk) is what a group or two people confide in alone, whether secret or open. The linguistic meaning of "najawtu al-shay'" is: I freed it and cast it off. It is said: "najawtu al-jild" when one strips the hide off a camel or other animal. The poet said:

"I said, 'Get away from it, as the hide gets away' — indeed, its hump and back-ridge will satisfy you both from it."

And "najawtu fulanan" means: when you test someone's breath (istankahtahu). The poet said:

"I tested Mujalladan, and I found from him a smell like the breath of a dog that died long ago."

(p-199) All of this derives from najwah, which is what rises from the ground. The poet, describing a torrent, said:

"Whoever is on its elevated ground is like whoever is on its low ground, and the one who walks hidden is like the one who walks in the open."

By "their secret talk" is meant what they plan among themselves of speech.

As for His saying: ﴿except one who enjoins charity﴾, it may mean: except in secret talk of one who enjoins charity. It may also be an exception not from the first part, meaning: "But whoever enjoins charity — in their secret talk there is good." As for His saying "enjoins charity," the meaning is: urges toward it.

As for ma'ruf (what is good/right), there are two views. (p-200) One is that it means the obligatory (al-fard); this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second is that it is general, covering all acts of righteousness; this is the view chosen by Qadi Abu Ya'la and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 115:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ — regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions.

One of them: when the Qur'an was revealed exposing Ṭu'mah (Ṭu'mah ibn Ubayriq) and explaining his wrongdoing, and he feared for himself disgrace and the cutting off of his hand, he fled to Makkah and joined the people of polytheism, and this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Ibn Zayd, and al-Suddī. Muqātil said: When he arrived in Makkah he stayed with al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿIlāṭ al-Sulamī, who treated him well as a guest. He then learned that there was gold in the house, so he went out at night and breached the wall of the house. They became aware of him and surrounded the house, and when they saw him they wanted to stone him, but al-Ḥajjāj felt ashamed because he was his guest, so they left him. He went out and joined the Ḥurrah of Banū Sulaym, worshipping their idol, until he died in polytheism. So there was revealed concerning him: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. Another said: Rather, he went out with merchants and stole something from them, so they pelted him with stones until they killed him. It was also said: He boarded a ship, stole money on it, was discovered, and was thrown into the sea.

The second opinion: that a group came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and embraced Islam, then apostatized, and this verse was revealed concerning them. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbās. The meaning of the verse: whoever opposes the Messenger regarding monotheism and the prescribed punishments, after monotheism and the ruling have become clear to him, and follows other than the way of the Muslims — ﴿We will leave him to what he has turned to﴾, i.e., We will leave him to what he has chosen for himself; ﴿and burn him in Hell﴾: We will cause him to enter it.

Ibn Fāris said: you say "ṣalaytu al-laḥma uṣlīhi" (I roasted the meat) when you have grilled it; if you mean that you burned it completely, you say "aṣlaytuhu."

﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾, i.e., a place of return to which one is taken.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions. (p-202) One of them: it was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq when he fled from Makkah, and he died upon polytheism. This is the opinion of the majority, among them Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: "A certain old man from among the Bedouins came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I am deeply immersed in sins, but I have not associated anything with Allah since I came to know Him, and I am truly regretful and seeking forgiveness. What is my state?' Then this verse was revealed." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. As for its interpretation (tafsir), it has already been discussed earlier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They invoke besides Him none but females.﴾ The "إنَّ" (in) here means "ما" (not), and "يَدْعُونَ" (they invoke) means "يَعْبُدُونَ" (they worship). The "هاء" (the pronoun "-hi," "Him") in "دُونِهِ" (besides Him) refers back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The well-known reading is "إناثًا" (*inathan*, "females"). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abdullah ibn Umar, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu al-Jawza' read "إلّا وثنًا" (*illa wathanan*, "but an idol"), with a fatha on the waw and the tha' and without an alif. Ibn Abbas and Abu Razin read "أُنُثًا" (*unuthan*), with a damma on the hamza and the nun and without an alif. Abu al-Aliya, Mu'adh al-Qari', and Abu Nahik read "أُناثا" (*unathan*), with a damma on the hamza and an alif after the tha'. Abu al-Siwar al-Adawi and Abu Shaykh al-Hana'i read "أوثانًا" (*awthanan*, "idols"), with a fatha on the hamza, followed by a waw and an alif after the tha'. Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, and al-Jawni read "إلّا أُنْثى" (*illa unthā*), in the pattern "فُعْلى" (*fu'lā*). Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read "إلّا وُثُنا" (*illa wuthunan*), with a damma on the waw and the tha' and without an alif. Muwarriq al-Ijli read "أُثُنًا" (*uthunan*), with a damma on the hamza and the tha' and without an alif.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads "إناثًا" (*inathan*) has it as the plural of "أُنْثى" (*unthā*) and "إناث" (*inath*). Whoever reads "أُنْثًا" (*unthan*) has it as the plural of "إناث" (*inath*). Whoever reads "أُثُنًا" (*uthunan*) has it as the plural of "وثن" (*wathan*, "idol"), and the original form is "وثن" (*wathan*). However, when the waw is vowelled with a damma, it is permissible to replace it with a hamza, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:11]. The original form is "وُقِّتَتْ" (*wuqqitat*, "were appointed"). It is also permissible that "أُثُنٌ" (*uthunun*) originally was "أُثْنٍ" (*uthnin*), and the damma was made to match the damma that follows. It is also permissible that it was "أُثُنَ" (*uthuna*), like "أسَدٍ" (*asad*) and "أُسْدٍ" (*usd*, "lions").

As for the exegetes, they have four opinions on the meaning of "الإناث" (*al-inath*, "the females").

The first is that "الإناث" means the dead (or lifeless things). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan in one narration, and Qatada. Al-Hasan said: Everything without a soul, such as a stone or a piece of wood, is "إناث." Al-Zajjaj said: All lifeless things are referred to in the feminine, just as the feminine is referred to. You say: "الأحجار تعجبني" (*al-ahjaru ta'jibuni*, "the stones please me") and "الدراهم تنفعني" (*al-darahimu tanfa'uni*, "the dirhams benefit me").

The second is that "الإناث" means the idols. This is the view of Aisha and Mujahid.

The third is that "الإناث" means al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat, all of which are feminine. This is the view of Abu Malik, Ibn Zayd, and al-Suddi. Abu Raja' related from al-Hasan that he said: No tribe of the Arabs existed without having an idol that they called "أُنْثى بني فلان" (*unthā Banī Fulān*, "the female of the so-and-so clan"). Then this verse was revealed.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: they invoke only what they name with the names of females.

The fourth is that "الإناث" means the angels, whom they claimed were the daughters of Allah. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Regarding the meaning of "الشيطان" (*al-shaytan*, "the devil"), there are three opinions.

The first is that it is a devil that dwells in the idol. Ibn Abbas said: With every idol there is a devil that appears to the custodians and speaks to them. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: With every idol there is a jinn (*jinniyya*).

The second is that it is Iblis. Worshipping him means obeying him in what he embellishes for them. This is the view of Muqatil and al-Zajjaj.

The third is that it refers to the idols they worshipped. Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

As for "المَرِيد" (*al-marid*, "the rebellious"), al-Zajjaj said: "المَرِيد" is "المارِد" (*al-marid*), meaning the one who goes out of obedience. Its meaning is that he has become defiant in evil. It is said: "مَرَدَ الرجل يَمْرُدُ مُرُودًا" (*marada al-rajulu yamrudu murudan*, "the man became defiant") when he transgresses and goes out of obedience. The sense of "المُرُود" (*al-murud*) is that he reaches the point at which he departs from the whole category of those who are like that. Its root meaning in the language is the smoothness of a thing. From this, a person is called "أمرد" (*amrad*, "beardless") when there is no hair on his face. Likewise, a tree is called "شجرة مرداء" (*shajara marda'*, "a bare tree") when its leaves have fallen, and a rock is called "صخرة مرداء" (*sakhra marda'*, "a smooth rock") when it is smooth.

Regarding His saying: ﴿Allah has cursed him﴾, there are two opinions.

The first is that it is the beginning of a supplication against him with the curse. This is the view of those who say that it refers to the idols.

The second is that it is a report of a curse that already happened. This is the view of those who say that it refers to Iblis. Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: Allah has already cursed him. Ibn Abbas said: The meaning of the statement is that Allah repelled him and expelled him from the Garden. And he said, that is Iblis: "Surely I shall take from among Your servants an appointed portion." Ibn Qutayba said: That is, a share that I have assigned to myself from them, so that I may lead them astray. Muqatil said: The appointed portion is that from every thousand people, one will be in the Garden, and the rest in the Fire.

Al-Zajjaj said: "الفَرْض" (*al-fard*) in the language means cutting. "الفُرْضة" (*al-furda*) is the breach that occurs in a river. "الفَرْض" (*al-fard*) on a bow is the notch in which the string is tied. "الفَرْض" (*al-fard*) in what Allah has imposed on the servants means that He has made it a decisive, binding obligation upon them.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 119:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "From the path of guidance." Others said: "He has no means of misleading except calling them to it." Regarding His saying, ﴿And I will surely arouse in them false desires﴾, there are four opinions.

The first: it is the lies he tells them. Ibn 'Abbas said: he says to them, "There is no Paradise, no Fire, and no Resurrection."

[p. 205] The second: it is the procrastination of repentance. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is making them imagine that they will obtain a share of the Hereafter. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: it is adorning false hopes (amani) for them. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they will surely slit the ears of the cattle﴾. Qatada, 'Ikrima, and al-Suddi said: this is splitting the ear of the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit as a sign of consecration in pre-Islamic practice). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "yubattikunna" is "they will split." It is said: "batakat al-shay' abtikuhu batkan," meaning "I cut it," and "batkuhu" and "batakahu" are like "qat'uhu" and "qata'a." This refers to the bahira: in the Jahiliyya, when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring and the fifth was a male, they would slit the she-camel's ear, refrain from benefiting from her, not drive her away from water or pasture, and if someone weary met her, he would not ride her. Iblis made it seem to them that this was an act of worship drawing them near to God, Exalted is He.

Regarding the intended meaning of ﴿changing the creation of God﴾, there are five opinions.

The first: it is changing the religion of God. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by al-Hasan in one narration, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil. It was also said: the meaning of changing the religion is making lawful what is unlawful and making unlawful what is lawful.

The second: it is changing the natural form by castration. This was narrated by 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is related from Anas ibn Malik, and from Mujahid, Qatada, and 'Ikrima, as two similar opinions.

The third: it is alteration by tattooing. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, and of al-Hasan in one narration.

[p. 205] The fourth: it is changing the command of God. This was narrated by Abu Shayba from 'Ata'.

The fifth: it is the worship of the sun, the moon, and stones, and the prohibition of what they forbade of the cattle, while God created those things for benefit. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of God﴾. Regarding the intended meaning of "wali" (guardian), there are two opinions.

One: it means "lord." This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is from "muwalah" (allegiance). This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. If someone says: From where does Iblis have knowledge of the outcomes, such that he said, ﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾? He said in [al-A'raf: 17]: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾, and he said in [al-Isra': 62]: ﴿I will surely take control of his descendants, except a few﴾. There are three answers to this.

The first: he assumed this, and his assumption was realized, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20]. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

Regarding the cause of that assumption, there are two opinions.

One: when God, Exalted is He, said to him: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and those among them who follow you, all together﴾ [Sad: 85], he knew that he would attain what he wanted. The second: when he caused Adam to slip, he said: "The descendants of this one are weaker than him."

[p. 207] The second answer: the meaning is, "I will surely incite them and strive in that, not that he knew the unseen." This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: it is possible that he had knowledge from the angels, by a report from God, Exalted is He, that most of creation would not be grateful. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. If it is said: Why did he limit it to some of them? He said: ﴿a prescribed portion﴾, and He said: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 17], and he said: ﴿except a few﴾. There are three answers to this.

The first: it is possible that knowledge of the fate of creation came from the angels, as we have explained.

The second: he did not attain from Adam everything he wanted; he hoped for some of his offspring and despaired of others.

The third: when he saw Paradise and Hell, he knew that they were created for those who would dwell in them, so he indicated by the "prescribed portion" the inhabitants of the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verses 120–122:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿He promises them﴾, meaning: Satan promises his allies. There are two views concerning what he promises them.

One: that there will be no resurrection for them (ba'th), as said by Muqatil. The second: victory for them, mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. There are two views concerning what he makes them hope for (yumannihim).

One: deception and false desires, such as saying: "Your life will be long, and you will attain your worldly goals." The second: triumph over the allies of Allah.

﴿He promises them and makes them hope, but Satan promises them nothing except deception. Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾

(p-208) The Exalted's saying: ﴿And Satan promises them nothing except deception﴾, i.e., falsehood by which he deceives them. As for al-mahis (escape), al-Zajjaj said: it is the way out and the refuge. It is said: "hastu 'an al-rajul uhisu" (I deviated from the man). They also related: "jistu ajayid" with the jim and the dad, meaning "hastu" (I deviated). That is not permissible in the Qur'an, even if the meaning is the same, because recitation is a sunnah (prophetic practice transmitted by oral tradition), and what is in the Qur'an is more eloquent than what is permissible. It is said: "hasta ahwasu hawsan wa hiyasatan" when it cut (into the eye); al-Asma'i said: it is said "hassa 'ayn saqarika," meaning: its eye was cut/marked. Al-hawsu in the eye is the narrowness of its back corner. It is also said: "waqa'a fi haysa baysa" (he fell into a difficult situation), and "haza bas" (he fell into what he cannot escape from).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verses 120–122:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿He promises them﴾, meaning: Satan promises his allies. There are two views concerning what he promises them.

One: that there will be no resurrection for them (ba'th), as said by Muqatil. The second: victory for them, mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. There are two views concerning what he makes them hope for (yumannihim).

One: deception and false desires, such as saying: "Your life will be long, and you will attain your worldly goals." The second: triumph over the allies of Allah.

﴿He promises them and makes them hope, but Satan promises them nothing except deception. Those—their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾
