Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 123:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Not by your wishful thinking﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: The people of the religions disputed. The People of the Torah said: "Our Book is the best of books, and our Prophet is the best of prophets." The People of the Gospel said the same. The Muslims said: "Our Book has abrogated every book, and our Prophet is the Seal of the Prophets." So this verse was revealed, and then they were given the choice among the religions by His saying: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾. This was narrated by al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas. To this meaning went Masruq, Abu Salih, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: The Arabs said: "We will not be resurrected, nor punished, nor brought to account." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: The Jews and the Christians said: "None will enter Paradise except us," and the Quraysh said: "We will not be resurrected." So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Ikrimah.

Al-Zajjaj said: The subject of "laysa" (is not) is implicit, and the meaning is: "The reward of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not by your wishful thinking." Something indicating the reward has already occurred, namely His saying: ﴿We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. Regarding those referred to by His saying "your wishful thinking" there are two opinions.

The first: They are the Muslims, according to the majority.

The second: They are the polytheists, according to Mujahid. As for the wishful thinking of the Muslims, it is what has been transmitted of their saying: "Our Book abrogates the books, and our Prophet is the Seal of the Prophets." The wishful thinking of the polytheists is their saying: "We will not be resurrected." The wishful thinking of the People of the Book is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved, and the Fire will not touch us except for a number of days," and "Our Book is the best of books, and our Prophet is the best of prophets." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that entry into Paradise and recompense are by deeds, not by wishful thinking. Regarding the meaning of "evil" (su') there are two opinions.

The first: It is sins. From this is the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can there be righteousness after this verse? ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾. If we do evil, we will be recompensed for it." He said: "May Allah forgive you, O Abu Bakr. Do you not fall ill? Do you not grieve? Do you not suffer hardship? That is what you are recompensed for."

The second: It is shirk (polytheism). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir. Regarding this recompense there are two opinions. The first: It is general, applying to everyone who does evil, for he will be recompensed for it. This is the meaning of the saying of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'A'ishah, and Ibn Jarir chose it, and he cited as evidence the hadith of Abu Bakr that we have mentioned.

The second: It is specific to the disbelievers, who are recompensed for everything they did, whereas the believer is not recompensed for everything he committed. This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri. Ibn Zayd said: Allah promised the believers that He would expiate their misdeeds for them, and He did not promise the polytheists.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector﴾. Abu Sulayman said: Whoever Allah wills to recompense for some of his deeds will not find a protector (waliyy), meaning a close relative, nor a helper who will prevent him from the punishment of Allah and His recompense.

(p-211) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾. Masruq said: When the verse ﴿Not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾ was revealed, the People of the Book said: "We and you are equal." So the verse ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ was revealed, up to the end of the verse. This indicates the connection of faith with righteous action, so neither of them is accepted except with the existence of the other. The mention of "al-Naqir" has already preceded.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 125:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah gave people a choice among the religions through this verse." "Aslama" means "sincerely devoted" (akhlasa). There are two opinions regarding "al-wajh" (the face):

One is that it means the religion. The second is that it means the deed.

Regarding "al-ihsan" (doing good) there are two opinions. One is that it means tawhid (affirming the oneness of God), as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second is standing before Allah by doing what Allah has enjoined, as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding following the religion of Ibrahim there are two opinions. One is following him in tawhid and obedience.

The second is following his law (shari'ah), which was chosen by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

As for the Khalil (close friend), Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Khalil is the chosen one (al-safiyy)." Others said: "The purified one (al-masafi)." Al-Zajjaj said: "He is the lover whose love contains no defect." He said: "It has also been said that the Khalil is the one in need (al-faqir). It is possible that Ibrahim was called the Khalil of Allah because He loved him with complete love, and it is possible that it is because he placed his poverty and need only in Him." "Al-khullah" means friendship, because each of the two friends fills the deficiency of the other. "Al-khullah" with a fatha on the kha' means need, and it was called "khullah" because of the deficiency that afflicts a person in what he needs. The vinegar that is eaten is called "khall" because the taste of sweetness has been lost from it. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Khalil is on the pattern of fa'il from al-khullah, and al-khullah means affection." Some lexicographers said: "Khalil means the lover, and the lover is one whose love contains no deficiency or defect. The meaning is that he loved Allah, and Allah loved him with a love free of any deficiency or defect." It is also said that Khalil means the one in need, so the meaning is: He made him one in need of Him, whose poverty and need descend upon Him alone, not upon anything else.

Regarding the reason Allah took him as a Khalil, there are three opinions.

One of them: He took him as a Khalil because of his feeding people. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "O Jibril, why did Allah take Ibrahim as a Khalil?" He said: "Because of his feeding people with food."

The second: People were struck by a year of drought, so they came to the door of Ibrahim seeking food. He used to receive provisions every year from a friend of his in Egypt. He sent his servants with camels to his friend, but he gave them nothing. They said: "If we load up with sand from this valley, people will see that we have brought provisions." So they filled the sacks with sand, then came to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and informed him. Ibrahim was distressed on account of the people. He slept, and Sarah came, not knowing what had happened. She opened the sacks, and behold, there was fine white flour. She ordered the bakers, and they baked and fed the people. Ibrahim woke up and said: "From where is this food?" She said: "From your Egyptian friend." He said: "Rather, it is from my Friend, Allah, mighty and majestic." On that day Allah took him as a Khalil. Abu Salih narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: He took him as a Khalil because he broke the idols and argued with his people. This was said by Muqatil.
(p-213) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing﴾. That is: His knowledge encompasses everything.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 127:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you concerning women﴾. There are five reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: In the Jahiliyyah they did not give inheritance to women and children. When God prescribed the inheritance shares in this surah, that was difficult for them, so they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it, and this verse was revealed. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: The guardian of an orphan girl would marry her if she was beautiful and he desired her, and he would consume her property. If she was plain, the men would prevent her from marrying until she died, and then he would inherit from her. So this verse was revealed (p-214). Ibn Abi Talhah narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: They did not give women their dowries, and their guardians would take possession of them. When the words of God were revealed, ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾, they asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about this, and this verse was revealed. This is the statement of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her.

The fourth: "A man had an elderly wife, and he had children by her. He wanted to divorce her, but she said: 'Do not do it, and allot to me in each month what you wish, or more.' He said: 'If this is acceptable, it is more beloved to me.' So he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and he said: 'God has heard what you say; if He wills, He will answer you.' Then this verse and the one after it were revealed." Salim al-Aftas narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

(p-215) The fifth: The guardian of an orphan girl, when he desired her wealth and beauty, would not be generous to her in her dowry. So this verse was revealed, and they were forbidden to marry them, or to give them less than the customary dowry of their like. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned it.

His saying: ﴿They ask you﴾, that is, they seek a fatwa (fatwa: a legal ruling), which is the clarification of what is difficult among the rulings. It was said: al-istift'a' (seeking a ruling) is seeking information. The exegetes said: what they asked about was the inheritance of women, for they said: how does a woman inherit, and a small boy?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "ma" is nominative; the meaning is: God gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is also recited to you in the Book gives you a ruling concerning them. This is His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, and so on.

What was recited to them concerning marriage is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾.

Concerning "the orphans of women" there are two views.

The first: They are the orphan women, and the attribute is added to the noun, as you say "the day of Friday" (yawm al-Jumu'ah).

The second: They are the mothers of orphans, and their children who are orphans are attributed to them.

Concerning "what was prescribed for them" there are two views.

The first: It is the inheritance. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid among others. The second: It is the dowry. Then, concerning the addressees of this, there are two views (p-216). The first: they are the guardians of the woman, who used to take her dowry instead of her. The second: the guardian of the orphan girl, who, if he married her, did not deal justly regarding her dowry. Concerning His saying, ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾, there are two views.

The first: "and you desire to marry them" out of desire for their beauty and their wealth. This is the statement of 'A'ishah and 'Ubaydah. The second: "and you turn away from marrying them because of their ugliness, so you keep them" out of desire for their wealth. This is the statement of al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the oppressed among the children﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "al-mustad'afin" is genitive, upon His saying: ﴿what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphans of women﴾; the meaning is: and concerning the children. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means that they used not to give inheritance to small boys or girls, so God forbade them from that, and made clear to every possessor of a share his share.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you stand up for the orphans with justice﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "an" is genitive, so the meaning is: concerning the orphans of women, and concerning that you stand up for the orphans with justice. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means justice in their dowries and their inheritances.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 128:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment (nushuz) or aversion﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: "Sawda feared that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would divorce her, so she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do not divorce me, keep me, and make my day for Aisha.' So he did, and this verse was revealed." This was related by Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas.

The second: The daughter of Muhammad ibn Maslama was married to Rafi' ibn Khadij, and he disliked something in her, either arrogance or jealousy, so he intended to divorce her. She said: "Do not divorce me, and allot to me what you wish." So this verse was revealed. This was related by al-Zuhri, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. Muqatil said: her name was Khuwaylah.

The third: It has already been mentioned from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding the revelation of the verse before it. And Aisha said: It was revealed concerning the woman who is with a man, and he does not increase his attention to her and wishes to part from her, and perhaps she is fond of him or has a child, so she dislikes his separating from her, and she says to him: "Do not divorce me, keep me, and you are free of any obligation regarding me." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Regarding the meaning of "fear of nushuz" there are two opinions. The first: it is knowledge of it when it becomes apparent. The second: caution against its occurrence, from its signs. Al-Zajjaj said: The nushuz of the husband towards the wife is that he mistreats her in companionship, and that he withholds himself from her and her maintenance. Abu Sulayman said: nushuz means turning away from her toward another, and aversion from her, and occupying oneself with someone else.

﴿There is no blame upon them both if they make settlement between themselves﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read: yusalihā (with a fatha on the ya and shaddah), "yusalaha baynahuma." The original is "yatasalaha," and the ta was assimilated into the sad. Asim, Hamza and al-Kisai read: "yuslihā" with a damma on the ya and without shaddah. The commentators said: the meaning is that they establish between themselves a matter with which both are content, and companionship continues between them, such as she being patient with his preference (for another). It is related from Ali and Ibn Abbas that they permitted the two of them to reconcile by her forgoing part of her dower, or part of her days, by allotting it to the other wife. Regarding His saying, ﴿and settlement is best﴾, there are two opinions. The first: it is better than separation, said by Muqatil and al-Zajjaj. The second: it is better than nushuz and aversion, mentioned by al-Mawardi. Qatadah said: whenever she is content with less than what was hers and they agree upon it, it is permissible; but if she refuses, it is not proper for him to keep her in humiliation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And souls are made present to stinginess (shuhh)﴾. "Uhdirat" means: made obligatory. "Shuhh" is excessive greed for a thing. Ibn Faris said: "shuhh" is miserliness together with greed, and two men "tashahha" over a matter when neither wishes it to escape them. Regarding who this stinginess returns to among the spouses there are two opinions. The first: the woman, so the implied meaning is: the woman's soul is made present to stinginess regarding her right from her husband. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: both spouses together; the woman is stingy over her place with her husband, and the man is stingy with himself toward her when another is dearer to him. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Ibn Zayd said: his soul is not content to give her anything so that she releases him, nor is her soul content to give him anything of her wealth so that he inclines toward her.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you do good﴾, regarding which there are two opinions. The first: by patience with the one he dislikes. The second: by good treatment of her in companionship.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you guard (against wrong)﴾, meaning: injustice toward her. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, so He will recompense you for it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 129:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between women﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: You will not be able to make them equal in love, which is the natural inclination of the heart, because that is not within your acquisition. ﴿Even if you are eager﴾ for that, ﴿do not incline entirely﴾ toward the one you love, in maintenance and in turn (p-220) and division. Mujahid said: Do not deliberately do harm, so that you leave the other as one suspended (mu'allaqah). Ibn Abbas said: The mu'allaqah is the one who is neither an ayyim (a woman without a husband) nor a dhat ba'l (a woman with a husband). Qatada said: The mu'allaqah is the one who is imprisoned.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you amend﴾, that is, by justice in division, ﴿and fear Allah﴾ from injustice, ﴿indeed Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of the inclination of hearts.

"And if they separate" — he says: if the woman refuses to permit her husband to prefer the one he inclines toward, and chooses separation, then God will enrich each of them from His bounty. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: He will enrich the woman with a man, and the man with a woman.

Then he mentioned what makes one desire to seek good, saying: "And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you" — meaning the People of the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of the scriptures — "and [instructed] you, [O people of the Qur'an], to fear Allah." It was said: [it means] to affirm His oneness. "And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" — so your opposition does not harm Him. It was also said: to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of the angels, and they are more obedient to Him than you.

We have already mentioned the meaning of "Free of need, Praiseworthy" in Surat al-Baqarah, and the meaning of "Disposer of affairs" in Surat Al 'Imran.

"And if they separate" — he says: if the woman refuses to permit her husband to prefer the one he inclines toward, and chooses separation, then God will enrich each of them from His bounty. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: He will enrich the woman with a man, and the man with a woman.

Then he mentioned what makes one desire to seek good, saying: "And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you" — meaning the People of the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of the scriptures — "and [instructed] you, [O people of the Qur'an], to fear Allah." It was said: [it means] to affirm His oneness. "And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" — so your opposition does not harm Him. It was also said: to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of the angels, and they are more obedient to Him than you.

We have already mentioned the meaning of "Free of need, Praiseworthy" in Surat al-Baqarah, and the meaning of "Disposer of affairs" in Surat Al 'Imran.

"And if they separate" — he says: if the woman refuses to permit her husband to prefer the one he inclines toward, and chooses separation, then God will enrich each of them from His bounty. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: He will enrich the woman with a man, and the man with a woman.

Then he mentioned what makes one desire to seek good, saying: "And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you" — meaning the People of the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of the scriptures — "and [instructed] you, [O people of the Qur'an], to fear Allah." It was said: [it means] to affirm His oneness. "And if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" — so your opposition does not harm Him. It was also said: to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of the angels, and they are more obedient to Him than you.

We have already mentioned the meaning of "Free of need, Praiseworthy" in Surat al-Baqarah, and the meaning of "Disposer of affairs" in Surat Al 'Imran.

(p-221) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means the polytheists and the hypocrites. ﴿And bring others﴾ who are more obedient to Him than you. Abu Sulayman said: This is a warning to the disbelievers. He says: If He wills, He will destroy you, just as He destroyed those before you when they disbelieved in Him and denied His messengers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 134:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world﴾. It was said: this verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who did not believe in the Resurrection and only sought the immediate benefits of this world. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman. Al-Zajjaj said: the polytheists of the Arabs would draw near to Allah so that He would give them some of the good of this world and turn away its evil from them, and they did not believe in the Resurrection. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed them that the good of this world and the Hereafter is with Him. Al-Mawardi mentioned that what is meant by the reward of this world is the spoils of war in jihad, and the reward of the Hereafter is Paradise. He said: the purpose of the verse is to urge the one who strives in jihad to intend the reward of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 135:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice﴾ There are two accounts concerning the occasion of its revelation.

(p-222) The first: "That a poor man and a rich man came to dispute before the Prophet ﷺ, and he was inclined toward the poor man, believing that the poor man would not wrong the rich man, so this verse was revealed." This is the statement of al-Suddi.

The second: that it relates to the story of Ibn Ubayriq, so it is an address to those who argued on his behalf. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. And "al-qiwam" is an intensive form derived from "qa'im" (one who stands firm). And "al-qist" means justice. Ibn Abbas said: "Be persistent in upholding justice in testimony, against whomever it may be, even against yourselves." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the speech is: "Stand firm for justice and bear witness for Allah with the truth, even if the truth is against the witness himself, or against his parents, or his relative. ﴿If he is rich﴾ the one testified for ﴿or poor﴾, Allah is more fitting for him; and if he is poor, Allah is more fitting for him." As for testimony against oneself, it is a person's acknowledgment of what is owed to another from him. The verse has commanded that one should not look to the poverty or the wealth of the one testified against, for Allah the Exalted is more entitled to be considered regarding both of them. Ata said: "Do not show partiality toward the poor, nor magnify the rich, so that you refrain from speaking about him." Among those who said the verse was revealed concerning testimonies were Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Qatada, and al-Dahhak.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not follow desire, lest you deviate﴾ Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: its meaning is: "So do not follow desire, and fear Allah, lest you deviate from the truth." This was said by Muqatil.

The second: "And do not follow desire in order that you deviate," said by al-Zajjaj. The third: "So do not follow desire out of aversion to deviating from the truth." The fourth: "So do not follow desire, and thus you deviate." Al-Mawardi mentioned both of these.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you distort﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Amr, Asim, and al-Kisa'i recited "talwu" with two waws, the first being dammah and the lam being sukun (p-223).

Concerning the meaning of this reading there are three opinions.

The first: that the witness twists his tongue in testimony toward something other than the truth. Ibn Abbas said: "He twists his tongue with other than the truth, and does not establish the testimony in its proper form, or turns away from it and leaves it." This is the view of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: that the judge turns his face toward some of the litigants, or turns away from some of them; this was also related from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that a person twists his neck, turning away from the command of Allah out of his arrogance and obstinacy.

And "aw tu'ridu" [or you turn away] may carry the meaning of "wa tu'ridu" [and you turn away]; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-A'mash, Hamza, and Ibn Amir recited "talu" with one waw, the lam being dammah. The meaning is: "that you take charge of people's affairs, or abandon them," so the address is to the rulers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions.

One of them: "That ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Asad, Usayd (the two sons of Kaʿb), Thaʿlabah ibn Qays, Salam, Salamah, and Yamin, who were believers among the People of the Book, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we believe in you, in your Book, in Moses, the Torah, and ʿUzayr, and we disbelieve in whatever is other than that of the books and messengers.' So this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "That the believers among the People of the Book had a dispute with the Jews when they embraced Islam, so this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Muqatil.

Regarding those addressed by His saying, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: they are the Muslims. This is the saying of al-Hasan. The meaning then is: O you who have believed in Muhammad and the Qur'an, remain steadfast in your faith.

The second: the Jews and the Christians. This is the saying of al-Dahhak. The meaning then is: O you who have believed in Moses, the Torah, and Jesus, the Gospel, believe in Muhammad and the Qur'an.

The third: the hypocrites. This is the saying of Mujahid. The meaning then is: O you who have believed outwardly with your tongues, believe with your hearts.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read "nazzala" (sent down) in ﴿upon His Messenger﴾ and "anzala" (sent down) in ﴿the Book which He sent down before﴾, both with a damma (u-vowel). Nafi ʿ, ʿAsim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "nazala" in ﴿upon His Messenger﴾ and "anzala" in ﴿the Book which He sent down﴾, both with a fatha (a-vowel). The intended meaning of "the Book" in ﴿which He sent down upon His Messenger﴾ is the Qur'an, and "the Book which He sent down before" means every book sent down before the Qur'an. Thus "al-Kitab" here is a noun of genus (ism jins).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 137:

(p-225) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and then disbelieved﴾ — the scholars differed regarding who this verse was revealed about, in three opinions.

The first: that it concerns the Jews. They believed in Moses, then disbelieved after Moses, then believed in ʿUzayr (Ezra), then disbelieved after him in Jesus, then increased in disbelief by rejecting Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It is also related from Qatadah, who said: They believed in Moses, then disbelieved by worshipping the calf, then believed in him after he returned, then disbelieved after him in Jesus, then increased in disbelief by rejecting Muhammad.

The second: that it concerns the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah and disbelieved in the Gospel, and the Christians believed in the Gospel, then abandoned it and disbelieved in it, then increased in disbelief by rejecting the Qur'an and Muhammad. This was narrated by Shaybān from Qatadah. It is also related from al-Hasan, who said: They are a people from among the People of the Book who intended to cast doubt upon the believers; they would display faith and then disbelief, then increased in disbelief by remaining steadfast in their religion. Muqatil said: They believed in the Torah and Moses, then disbelieved after Moses, then believed in Jesus and the Gospel, then disbelieved after him, then increased in disbelief by rejecting Muhammad and the Qur'an.

The third: that it concerns the hypocrites, who believed, then apostatized, then died upon their disbelief. This is the view of Mujahid. Ibn Jurayj related from Mujahid regarding ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ that he said: They persisted in it until they died. Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding ﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾ — so long as they persist in that — ﴿nor would He guide them to a path﴾, meaning: He will not make them guided through their disbelief. He said: The denial of forgiveness was attached to disbelief after disbelief, because a believer who returns to disbelief after having disbelieved is forgiven his earlier disbelief, but when he apostatizes again, he is held accountable for the first disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 138:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Give the hypocrites the good news﴾. Muqatil claimed that when the forgiveness was revealed in Surat al-Fath (p. 226) for the Prophet and the believers, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and a group with him said: "What about us?" So this verse was revealed.

Others said: The hypocrites used to take the Jews as allies, so they were joined with them in the announcement of punishment. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: make the place of their good news a punishment. The Arabs say: "Your greeting is a blow" (taḥiyyatuka al-darb), meaning: this is a substitute for you in place of the greeting. The poet said:

"And horses that have advanced upon them with a cavalry, their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 139:

Allah's words: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they take the Jews as allies in support and assistance.

Allah's words: ﴿Do they seek honor with them?﴾ That is, the might of prevailing over Muhammad and his companions. The meaning is: do they seek protection through them? Muqatil said: this is because the Jews helped the polytheists of the Arabs in fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Zajjaj said: "Do the hypocrites seek honor with the disbelievers?"

Al-ʿIzzah ("honor, might") means protection and intense dominance, and it is derived from their saying: "ʾArḍ ʿizāz" (a hard, barren land). Al-Asmaʿi said: "al-ʿizāz" is the land that does not produce plants. So the interpretation of ʿizzah is dominance and strength to which no humiliation attaches. Al-Khansaʾ said:

"As if they had never been a sanctuary to be protected, when people, at that time, whoever was mighty, plundered."

That is: whoever was strong and dominant seized spoil. It is said: "istaʿazza ʿalā al-marīḍ" (the sick person was overcome), meaning his pain intensified. Likewise the people's saying: "yaʿizzu ʿalayya an yafʿala" (it is hard for me that he should do such), meaning it is difficult for me. And their saying: "qad ʿazza al-shayʾ" (the thing has become scarce) when it cannot be found, meaning it is difficult to find; the root is one.

(p-228) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you in the Book﴾. ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb read "nazala" with a fatḥah on the nūn and the zāy. The exegetes said: what was revealed to them concerns the prohibition of sitting with them. His saying in [al-Anʿām: 68]: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our signs, turn away from them﴾. The hypocrites used to sit with the rabbis of the Jews, who would mock the Qur'an and deny it, so Allah forbade the Muslims from sitting with them. "The signs of Allah" are the Qur'an. The meaning is: when you hear disbelief in the signs of Allah and mockery of them, then do not sit with them until they turn to a discussion other than disbelief and mockery. (Indeed you) if you sit with them while they are upon that, then you (are like them). As to what the likeness consists in, there are two views.

The first: in disobedience. The second: in being pleased with their state, because the one who sits with a disbeliever is not himself a disbeliever. The verse has drawn attention to the warning against sitting with the disobedient. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: Indeed a man sits in a gathering and speaks a word by which he pleases Allah, so mercy reaches him and encompasses those around him; and indeed a man sits in a gathering and speaks a word by which he angers Allah, so wrath reaches him and encompasses those around him. (p-229)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 141:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who wait for you﴾. Abu Sulayman said: This verse was revealed specifically concerning the hypocrites. Muqatil said: The hypocrites used to wait for the believers' misfortunes. If there was a conquest (fath), they would say: "Were we not with you? So give us a share of the spoils (ghanima)." And if the disbelievers had a portion, that is, a dynasty (dawla) over the believers, they would say to the disbelievers: "Did we not gain control over you (nastahwidh alaykum)?" Al-Mubarrad said: The meaning of "Did we not gain control over you" is: "Did we not overpower you in your opinion?" Al-Zajjaj said: "Did we not overcome you by allying with you?" And nastahwidhu (we gain control) in the language means "we take control"; it is said: "hadhat al-ibil" and "hazataha," when you take control of them and gather them. Others said: "Did we not take control over you by aid and support?" Ibn Jurayj said: "Did we not make clear to you that we are upon your religion?"

And regarding His saying: ﴿and We protect you from the believers﴾ there are three views.

One: We prevent them from you by discouraging them from you. The second: by what We teach you of their news.

The third: by turning you away from entering into faith. The purport of the statement is: displaying a favour from the hypocrites over the disbelievers, that is, "Acknowledge this right of ours upon you."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: the believers and the hypocrites. Ibn Abbas said: He means that He delays the punishment of the hypocrites.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾. Concerning it there are three views.

One: that there will be no way for them over them on the Day of Resurrection. Yasi' al-Hadrami narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that a man came to him and said: "Tell me about the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾, while they fight us [and prevail and kill]?" He said: "And Allah will never give the disbelievers, on the Day of Resurrection, a way over the believers." This is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatada.

The second: that the intended meaning of "way" is domination over them; that is, the believers are the ones who prevail, and the final outcome is theirs. This meaning is in the narration of Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that "way" means proof (hujja). Al-Suddi said: Allah has not given them a proof against them, meaning concerning what they did to them of killing and expulsion from their homes. Ibn Jarir said: When Allah promised the believers that He would not cause the hypocrites to enter their place in Paradise, nor the believers the place of the hypocrites, there would be no proof for the disbelievers over the believers, by their saying to them: "You were our enemies, and the hypocrites were our allies, and you have all gathered in the Fire."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 142:

(p-231) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites try to deceive Allah﴾ means: they act the way a deceiver acts. It was also said: they try to deceive His Prophet, and He is the One who deceives them, meaning He requites them for their deception. Al-Zajjaj said: when He commanded that what they displayed be accepted, He was deceiving them by that. It was also said: His deceiving them will take place on the Day of Resurrection by extinguishing their light. We have explained a portion of this in (al-Baqarah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they stand up to the prayer, they stand up lazily﴾ means: they stand up sluggishly. "Kusala" is the plural of "kaslan," and "al-kasal" (laziness) is reluctance toward the command. Abu Imran al-Jawni recited "kasla" with a fatha on the kaf, and Ibn al-Sumaifa recited "kasla" with a fatha on the kaf without an alif. They were this way because they prayed out of fear for their own blood; they hoped for no reward by performing it, and they feared no punishment by abandoning it.

(p-232) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They show off to the people﴾ means: they pray so that people will see them. Qatadah said: "By Allah, were it not for the people, the hypocrite would not pray." Regarding describing their remembrance as "little," there are three opinions.

One: it was called little because it is not accepted. This was said by Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and Qatadah.

The second: because it is for show, and had it been for Allah, it would have been much. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

The third: it is little in itself, because they confine themselves to what is apparent, and not to what is hidden of recitation and glorification. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 143:**

His saying, the Exalted: "Wavering between that." *Mudhabdhab* means one who vacillates between two matters. The root *tadhdhub* means movement and agitation. This is the attribute of the hypocrite (*munafiq*), because he is bewildered in his religion and does not settle on a sound belief. Qatadah said: "They are neither polytheists who openly declare association with Allah, nor sincere believers." Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of "between that" is between Islam and disbelief. They did not show disbelief so that they would be counted among the disbelievers, nor did they truly affirm faith so that they would be counted among the believers. Ibn Abbas said: "And whoever Allah leaves astray, you will never find for him a way to guidance."

Ibn Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The likeness of the hypocrite is that of a lone sheep between two flocks: it goes toward this one once and toward that one once, and it does not know which of them to follow."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 144:

(p-233) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not take the disbelievers as allies﴾. Regarding the meaning of "the disbelievers" there are two opinions.

The first: they are the Jews. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the hypocrites. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: do not make them your intimates (bitana) and your close associates (khassa).

As for al-Sultan (sultan), it means the clear proof (hujja). It is said of the ruler that he is "sultan" because he is the proof of God on His earth. The derivation of "sultan" is from "al-salit" (oil lamp fuel, or oil). "Al-salit" is that by which one is illuminated, and from this the olive oil is called "al-salit." The Arabs use the word sultan both as feminine and masculine. They say: "qadat 'alayka al-sultan" (the authority has decided against you) and "amarat-ka al-sultan" (the authority has ordered you). The masculine usage is more common, and the Qur'an came with it. Whoever uses the feminine has in mind the meaning of "proof" (hujja), and whoever uses the masculine intends the possessor of authority (sahib al-sultan). Ibn al-Anbari said: the estimated sense of the verse is: "Do you wish to give God a clear proof against you, by allying with the disbelievers, which would oblige you to His punishment and earn you His wrath?"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 145:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the ra' (al-darak). 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a sukun on the ra' (al-dark). Al-Farra' said: "They are two dialects." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Jahannam has darak, meaning levels (manazil) and layers (atbaq). So each level of it is a daraka (dark)." Ibn al-Anbari related from some scholars that he said: "The darakat (levels) are like terraces, some beneath others." Al-Dahhak said: "The darj (degrees) is when some are above others, and the dark (depths) is when some are lower than others." Ibn Faris said: "Paradise has darajat (ranks), and the Fire has darakat (depths)." Ibn Mas'ud said regarding this verse: "They are in coffins of iron, closed upon them (mubhamah ['alayhim])." Ibn al-Anbari said: "Al-mubhamah is the one with no locks upon it. It is said: 'a matter is mubham' when it is ambiguous, its meaning and its gate unknown."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will not find for them any helper﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "One who prevents them from the punishment of Allah."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except those who repent﴾. Muqatil said: The occasion of its revelation was that some people said, when the abode of the hypocrites was mentioned: "So-and-so and so-and-so were hypocrites, and they repented. How should they be treated?" So this verse was revealed.

The meaning of the verse: "Except those who repent" from hypocrisy (nifaq), ﴿and amend﴾ their deeds after repentance, ﴿and hold fast to God﴾, meaning they cling firmly to His religion, ﴿and make their religion sincere﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first is that it refers to Islam, and making it sincere means removing associating partners (shirk) from it. This was said by Muqatil.

The second is that it refers to action, and making it sincere means removing the impurities of hypocrisy and showing-off (riya') from it. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then those are with the believers﴾. Regarding the word مَعَ ("with"), there are two views.

The first is that it retains its original meaning, which is accompaniment. Regarding what they are accompanied with the believers, there are two views. The first is in guardianship (wilayah), as said by Muqatil. The second is in religion and reward, as said by Abu Sulayman.

The second is that مَعَ carries the meaning of مِن ("from"), so the sense is: ﴿then those are from the believers﴾. This was said by al-Farra'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 147:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment﴾. "Ma" (what) is an interrogative particle, and its meaning is affirmation (taqrir), i.e., Allah does not punish the grateful believer. The meaning of the verse is: What would Allah do with your punishment if you are thankful for His blessings and believe in Him and His Messenger? Faith is prior in meaning even though it is mentioned later in wording. It is related from Ibn Abbas that what is meant by gratitude (shukr) is monotheism (tawhid).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing﴾. That is, He appreciates the little of your deeds and is Knowing of your intentions. It was also said: Shakir means Accepting (qabil), i.e., He accepts.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 148:

The first view: A guest was hosted by a people, and they treated his hospitality badly, so he complained about them. Then this verse was revealed as a concession (rukhsah) permitting him to complain. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second view: "A man slandered Abu Bakr al-Siddiq while the Prophet (ﷺ) was present. Abu Bakr remained silent toward him several times, then he answered him back. The Prophet (ﷺ) then stood up. Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of God, he insulted me and you said nothing to him, but when I answered him back, you stood up!' He said: 'There was an angel responding on your behalf, and when you answered him back, the angel left and the Devil came.' Then this verse was revealed." This is the view of Muqatil.

The reciters differed over the reading of ﴿إلّا مَن ظَلَمَ﴾ (illa man zalama, "except one who has been wronged"). The majority read it with a dammah on the ظ (ẓā') and a kasrah on the ل (lām), i.e. ẓulima. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Raja', Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Zayd ibn Aslam read both with a fatḥah (zalama).

On the reading of the majority, there are three views regarding the meaning of the statement:

The first: "except when the one wronged invokes a complaint about his wrongdoer, for God has granted him a concession." This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "except when the wronged one takes revenge on his wrongdoer." This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The third: "except when the wronged one informs about the wrong done to him by the one who wronged him." This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

Ibn Jurayj related from him that he said: "except that the guest may openly speak ill of the one who did not host him."

As for the reading of those who read the ظ with a fatḥah, Tha'lab said: it is referred back to the statement ﴿ما يَفْعَلُ اللَّهُ بِعَذابِكُمْ﴾ ("What would God do with your punishment"), except for one who has done wrong. Al-Zajjaj mentioned two views concerning it:

The first: the meaning is "except that the wrongdoer openly speaks evil wrongfully."

The second: "except that you openly speak evil to the wrongdoer." According to this, "illa" in this place is an exceptive particle of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and its meaning is: "but the wronged one may openly speak evil to his wrongdoer. But the wrongdoer may openly speak evil to him, so openly speak evil to him back."

Ibn Zayd said: "except one who has been wronged," meaning one who persists in hypocrisy, so one speaks openly against him until he refrains.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿وَكانَ اللَّهُ سَمِيعًا﴾ ("And God is ever Hearing"), meaning: of the evil speech you openly utter; (ʿaliman, "Knowing") of what you conceal. It has been said: Hearing of the people of the wronged one, Knowing of what is in his heart, so let him fear God and say nothing but the truth.

Al-Hasan said: whoever is wronged is granted a concession to invoke against his wrongdoer without transgressing, such as saying: "O God, help me against him; O God, bring out my right for me; O God, come between him and what he intends."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 149:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whether you disclose good or conceal it⁠﻿—⁠﻿﻿﻿⁠ ... ﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means among the acts of righteousness, such as fasting and giving charity. Some of them said: "If you disclose good" means in place of evil. Most of them hold that the pronoun in "tukhfūhu" (you conceal it) refers to the good. Some of them said it refers to the evil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning⁠﻿—⁠﻿﻿﻿⁠ ... ﴾ Abu Sulayman said: That is, He has never ceased to be one who pardons while having the power to punish; so you too should pardon while having the power to do so.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 150:

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers⦈ — there are two opinions regarding them. (p-240) The first: they are the Jews, who believed in Musa (Moses), in 'Uzair (Ezra), and in the Torah, and disbelieved in 'Isa (Jesus), in the Injil (Gospel), and in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah and Musa, and disbelieved in the Injil and 'Isa; and the Christians believed in the Injil and 'Isa, and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. This was said by Qatadah.

As for the meaning of His statement: ﴿And they wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers⦈, i.e., they wish to separate belief in Allah from belief in His messengers, and belief in Him is not valid while denying His messengers, or some of them. ﴿And they wish to adopt a path between that⦈, i.e., between their belief in some of the messengers and their denial of others, ﴿a way⦈, i.e., a doctrine they follow. Ibn Jurayj said: a religion they adhere to.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the true disbelievers﴾. He mentioned "the truth" (al-haqq) here as an emphasis of their disbelief, to remove the illusion of one who imagines that their belief in some of the messengers would remove from them the designation of disbelief.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the true disbelievers﴾. He mentioned "the truth" (al-haqq) here as an emphasis of their disbelief, to remove the illusion of one who imagines that their belief in some of the messengers would remove from them the designation of disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 153:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾. There are three opinions regarding the occasion of its revelation.

The first: they asked him to send down a Book to them specifically. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: "The Jews and the Christians came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'We will not pledge allegiance to you until you bring us a Book from Allah to so-and-so, that you are the Messenger of Allah, and to so-and-so with a Book that you are the Messenger of Allah.' So this verse was revealed." This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The third: the Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ to send down to them a written Book from the heaven, just as the Torah was sent down to Musa. This is the view of al-Qurazi and as-Suddi.

Regarding the meaning of "the People of the Book," there are two opinions. One: the Jews and the Christians. The second: the Jews.

Regarding the meaning of "a Book sent down from the heaven," there are two opinions.

One: a written Book other than the Qur'an.

The second: a Book confirming his message.

We have explained in (al-Baqarah) the meaning of their asking to see Allah openly, and their taking the calf. And "the clear signs" (al-bayyinat): the signs that Musa brought. If it is said: how did He say, "then they took the calf," when "then" (thumma) implies delay and lateness? Was the taking of the calf after their saying, "Show us Allah openly"? Regarding this there are four answers, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

The first of them: "thumma" is referred back to their earlier action, and the meaning is: "And when We promised Musa forty nights," they also opposed, then they took the calf.

The second: it is advanced in meaning but delayed in wording, and the implied sense is: "They had already taken the calf, then they asked Musa for something greater than that." A similar example is ﴿Throw it to them, then turn away from them and see what they return﴾ [an-Naml: 28], meaning: throw it to them, then see what they return, then turn away from them.

The third: the meaning is: "then they had taken the calf," so the verb "to be" is implied.

The fourth: "thumma" here signifies delay in the reporting and advancement in the action, as one says: "I drank the water, then I ate the bread," meaning: I drank the water, then I inform you that I ate the bread after my informing you of drinking the water.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We pardoned that﴾, i.e., We did not uproot the worshippers of the calf. And "the manifest authority" (as-sultan al-mubin): the clear proof. Ibn 'Abbas said: the hand and the staff. Others said: the nine signs.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 154:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We raised over them the mount (al-Tur) because of their covenant﴾, meaning: because of what they gave to God of the pledge. And "al-mithaq" (the covenant): "They will surely act upon what is in the Torah."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾. Nafi' recited "la ta'dduu" (lā taʿaddūa), with the ʿayn unvowelled and the dal shaddah. Warsh related from him "ta'addu" (taʿaddū), with the ʿayn fathah and the dal shaddah. The rest of the readers recited "ta'du" (taʿdū), light, and all of them put a ḍammah on the dal. We have mentioned this and other matters in (al-Baqarah). And "al-mithaq al-ghalidh" (the solemn covenant): the emphasized pledge.

(p-243) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾. "Ma" here is a reinforcing particle (ṣila mu'akkida). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "so by their breaking their covenant," namely that God took a covenant from them that they would make clear what He had sent down to them concerning the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) and other things. The particle "bi" (by) is governed by the verb that operates in it. His saying, ﴿We forbade them good things﴾ means: because of their breaking their covenant, and the things mentioned after it are what We forbade them. His saying, ﴿for wrongdoing﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying, ﴿for their breaking﴾. God made their recompense for their disbelief that He set a seal upon their hearts. Ibn Faris said: al-ṭabʿ (sealing) is the sealing (khatm), and from this comes "God sealed the heart of the disbeliever," as if He sealed over it so that no guidance or light reaches it, and so he is not granted success in any good. Al-ṭābaʿ is the seal (khātam) with which something is sealed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they do not believe except a few﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: they do not believe, of them, except a few, and these were ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: the meaning is that their faith is little, and this is their saying, "Our Lord is God"; this was said by Mujahid.

Allah's words: ﴿And for their disbelief﴾. Repeating the mention of disbelief serves a purpose, and there are two views concerning it.

The first: He meant, "And for their disbelief in Muhammad and the Qur'an," as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "And for their disbelief in the Messiah, though they had been given good tidings of him," as said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. As for "slander" (buhtan), it is, according to the consensus of the scholars, their accusation of Maryam (Mary) with fornication.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 157–158:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, grammarian and exegete) said: That is, by their claim of having killed him, and they did not kill him, they are punished with the punishment of one who killed, because they killed the one whom they killed believing him to be a prophet. And regarding His saying, ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾, there are two views.

The first: it is part of the saying of the Jews, so the meaning is: "He is the Messenger of Allah according to his claim."

The second: it is part of the saying of Allah, not in the manner of relating it from them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But it was made to appear to them﴾, that is, his likeness was cast upon another.

Regarding the one upon whom his likeness was cast, there are two views.

The first: he was one of those among the Jews who intended to kill him. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that when the Jews gathered to kill Jesus, Gabriel brought him into a small door (khawkha) that had an opening (rawzana), and a man from among them entered behind him, so Allah cast upon him the likeness of Jesus. When he came out to his companions, they killed him, thinking him to be Jesus, then they crucified him. Muqatil and Abu Sulayman also said this.

The second: he was a man from among the companions of Jesus. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that when Allah willed to raise Jesus, Jesus came out to his companions and said: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed in my place and will be in my rank?" A young man stood up and said: "I will." He said: "Sit down." Then he repeated the words, and the young man stood up again, and Jesus said: "Sit down." Then he repeated, and the young man said: "I will," and he said: "Yes, you are that one." So the likeness of Jesus was cast upon him, Jesus was raised, and the Jews came, seized the man, killed him, and then crucified him. Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatada and al-Suddi also held this view.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning it﴾. Regarding those who differed, there are two views.

The first: they are the Jews. In that case, regarding the pronoun in "concerning it" there are two views.

The first: it refers to his killing, so they differed as to whether they killed him or not.

Regarding the cause of their disagreement on this, there are two views.

The first: when they killed the person upon whom the likeness had been cast, the likeness had been placed on his face but not his body, so they said: "The face is the face of Jesus, and the body is the body of another." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: they said: "If this is Jesus, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is Jesus?" meaning the one who entered in pursuit of him. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: the pronoun refers to Jesus, and their disagreement concerning him is the saying of some of them: "He is the son of adultery," and the saying of others: "He is a sorcerer."

The second view regarding those who differed: they are the Christians. In that case, regarding the pronoun in "concerning it" there are two views.

The first: it refers to his killing, whether he was killed or not. The second: it refers to him, whether he is God or not. And regarding the pronoun in "of it" there are two views.

The first: it refers to his killing.

The second: it refers to himself, whether he is God, or of illegitimate birth, or a sorcerer.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Ittiba'a (following) is in the accusative by way of exception, and it is an exception that is not from the first part. The meaning is: they have no knowledge of it except that they follow assumption. If it were in the nominative, it would be permissible, taking their knowledge to be the following of assumption, as the Arabs say: 'Your greeting is the striking.'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not kill him﴾. Regarding the pronoun "him" there are three views.

The first: it refers to assumption, so the meaning is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty. This is the saying of Ibn Abbas.

The second: it refers to knowledge, that is: they did not kill [the knowledge of it] with certainty. One says: "I killed him with certainty," and "I killed him with knowledge [of the opinion and the report]." This is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba. Ibn Qutayba said: The root of this is that killing a thing occurs through subjugation, domination and overpowering. So their knowledge of the killing of the Messiah was not knowledge that encompassed them; it was only assumption.

The third: it refers to Jesus, so the meaning is: they did not truly kill Jesus. This is the saying of al-Hasan. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Certainty" is delayed in meaning, so the sense is: "They did not kill him, but Allah raised him to Himself with certainty."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 4, verse 157–158:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah"﴾. Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, grammarian and exegete) said: That is, by their claim of having killed him, and they did not kill him, they are punished with the punishment of one who killed, because they killed the one whom they killed believing him to be a prophet. Ibn Qutayba said: The root of this is that killing a thing occurs through subjugation, domination and overpowering.
